In the eighteenth century, Storgata as far as Brugata and Brugata onward to the Akerselva were understood as one street called Vaterlands Storgade. Today's canonical place is the named Storgata route, not Torggata, Youngstorget, the Folketeater quarter or the social territory at the Brugata intersection.

The northern section became continuous with the city when Nybrua opened in 1827. The area south of Brugata was incorporated into the city in 1784, and the areas farther north in 1839. Trade, crafts, inns and housing grew along the approach road. The street therefore records both suburban expansion and the gradual incorporation of the area into the city.

Storgata became a major tram corridor. Rails still occupy the same street space as platforms, pavements, deliveries and entrances. The 2018–2021 upgrade added new rails and foundations, wider pavements, two new stops, drainage measures and a 200-metre technical tunnel. Storgata stop opened on 21 June 2021 and in 2026 is served by lines 12, 15, 17 and 18.

Individual addresses preserve different histories. Number 23 housed the city's post office from 1813 to 1832; number 25 contained Olympia cinema and later Scala Teater; and the masonry building at number 27, dating from 1837, housed both a Catholic chapel and a printing office. At number 39 a Stolperstein commemorates the Jewish businessman Philipp Gosias, who lived there before he was deported in 1943 and killed at Auschwitz.

A landmark complex is the Folketeater building at Storgata 21–23, designed by Christian Morgenstierne and Arne Eide and inaugurated in 1935. It has its own canonical place, but its street frontage remains a visible layer along Storgata. At the other end, Nybrua is likewise a separate place and the physical endpoint that completed the route in 1827. Storgata can be read as the line connecting these addresses and crossings, where transport, commerce, memory and everyday movement continue to share the same narrow urban space.

ullevål_hageby.name: Ullevål Garden City
ullevål_hageby.desc: Ullevål Hageby was planned after Kristiania municipality bought the Store Ullevål farm in 1909. Oscar Hoff won the planning competition in 1913, and between 1915 and 1922, 119 buildings with 654 flats were erected. Damplassen became the centre of a residential area with front gardens, co-operative shops, fairy-tale street names and a later resistance history tied to XU and the Pelle group.
ullevål_hageby.popupDesc:
Kristiania municipality bought the Store Ullevål farm in 1909 to obtain land for housing. In 1913, 425 decares were set aside for a garden city, and architect Oscar Hoff won the planning competition. The plan drew on the English garden city movement's idea of low houses, private or semi-private gardens, green streets and a local centre. Development was organised through the Kristiania Garden City Company.

Between 1915 and 1922, 119 buildings were erected with a total of 654 flats, office premises and nine co-operative shops. The development includes villas, semi-detached houses, four-family houses and longer terraces, mainly in masonry. Harald Hals and Adolf Jensen contributed to the final architecture after the initial plans for co-operative building societies for each block proved difficult to carry out. The houses were given a clear Nordic neo-Baroque character, with variation in roofs, gables, entrances and front gardens.

Damplassen became the centre of the scheme. The name refers to two older fish ponds on the site. One was called Svenskedammen, the Swedes' pond, because Swedish prisoners of war are said by tradition to have worked there around 1809. Shops and services surrounded the square, so residents could do their daily shopping within the area. Many streets were named after fairy tales, such as Askeladdveien and Soria Moria, while Tiurveien, Elgveien and Hjorteveien refer to wildlife.

The garden city gradually became more closely tied to the rest of Oslo. The tram reached the area in 1925, and the Sognsvann Line opened in 1934. Public transport made it possible to combine life in small houses with gardens with work and education elsewhere in the city. Ullevål Hageby therefore did not become an isolated suburb, but a planned residential district with clear boundaries and several connections.

During the occupation several resistance members lived here. The XU leader Arvid Storsveen had his home at John Colletts allé 16. Several young people from the garden city joined the Pelle group, which carried out sabotage operations against German enterprises in 1944–45. The brothers Hans and Kåre Andersen, Ludvig Hansen and Sverre Nielsen were executed at Akershus on 9 February 1945. A memorial by Joseph Grimeland, unveiled in 1948 at Ullevål school, honours 26 fallen from the school district.

Ullevål Hageby is thus more than an attractive low-rise area. The street network shows a concrete housing-policy experiment from the 1910s, Damplassen shows how retail and community were built into the plan, and the memorial at the school ties the peaceful gardens to organised resistance and loss during the Second World War.

barcode.name: Barcode
barcode.desc: The Barcode row was built in Bjørvika from 2008 to 2016 between Oslo Central Station and Dronning Eufemias gate. Buildings of up to 22 storeys stand as narrow slabs with passages between them. The complex holds around 180,000 square metres of offices, some 10,000 workplaces and 400 homes. Its height, density and DNB's three connected headquarters buildings made the project one of the country's most contested pieces of urban development.
barcode.popupDesc:
Barcode, also known as the Opera Quarter, lies between the rail yards at Oslo Central Station and Dronning Eufemias gate. The row of high-rises was built mainly from 2008 to 2016 as the commercial part of the new Bjørvika development. The site previously held railway tracks, warehousing and road structures close to the old E18. Once the through traffic was moved into the Bjørvika Tunnel, the area could be built as a new part of the city centre.

The name refers to the placing of the buildings. Narrow volumes of up to 22 storeys stand close together like the lines of a barcode, but are separated by streets and passages that give glimpses between the railway and the fjord. The complex as a whole holds around 180,000 square metres of office space, some 10,000 workplaces and 400 homes. The density made it possible to gather a great deal of activity close to Oslo S, but at the same time created a tall wall along the northern side of Dronning Eufemias gate.

Barcode was not designed by a single architectural practice. MVRDV, DARK Arkitekter and A-lab developed the overall concept, while several Norwegian and international practices designed individual buildings. The row includes the PwC building, the KLP building, the Deloitte building, the MAD building and DNB's headquarters. Variation in height, width, façade material and window pattern was intended to make each volume legible while giving the whole row a unified silhouette.

DNB's headquarters consists of three buildings: the west and central buildings from 2012 and the east building from 2014. MVRDV, a-lab and DARK were involved in the design. The buildings are connected underground and in places by bridges across the passages. The bank moved its headquarters from Aker Brygge to Bjørvika in 2013. The move gathered several thousand employees and made Barcode a new centre of gravity for finance and office work.

Between the high-rises run Trelastgata, Rostockgata and other new streets. Trelastgata is named after the timber shipping that once took place in the area. The passages were meant to let light and views through the row and connect Oslo S to the fjord. At ground level there are shops, eating places, a kindergarten and entrances to homes and offices, but activity varies sharply between the working day and the evening.

The new street names also tie the project to older and more recent history. Trelastgata refers to the large-scale timber shipping from Bjørvika, while Rostockgata is named after the Hanseatic town of Rostock. Dronning Eufemias gate takes its name from the medieval queen Euphemia of Rügen. The high-rises therefore stand in a street network that tries to give the newly built area historical references.

The project provoked extensive protests. Critics described the row as a high-rise wall that took away views and left the fjord front dominated by offices. A petition gathered more than 30,000 signatures. Supporters pointed to architectural variation, high land utilisation and workplaces beside the country's largest transport hub. Both sides remain visible: Barcode gives Oslo a striking skyline and many short passages, but also presents a dense spine between the rail yard and the new fjord city.

tjuvholmen.name: Tjuvholmen
tjuvholmen.desc: Tjuvholmen was zoned in 2004 following the winning proposal "Utsyn" by Niels Torp Arkitekter and built out from 2005 to 2014. The former harbour area was extended from 33 to 51 decares and gained around 900 homes. The Astrup Fearnley Museum, the sea bath, the sculpture park and the viewing tower all opened in 2012.
tjuvholmen.popupDesc:
Tjuvholmen had several functions long before the area became a new fjord district. Toftes Gave, a rescue institution for children, was built here in 1844. In 1874 Christiania's first public socialist meeting was held on the islet. The area was later used for harbour operations, warehouses, workshops and businesses dependent on the waterfront.

The original islet covered around 33 decares. When the harbour operations were to be moved and the site developed, the area was filled out to about 51 decares. A design competition was decided in 2002. The proposal "Utsyn", developed by Niels Torp Arkitekter together with Selvaag, won. The zoning plan was adopted in 2004, and construction began the following year.

The development was carried out by Tjuvholmen KS, owned by the Selvaag Group and the Aspelin Ramm Group. The area gained around 900 homes, a significant share of them planned as rental housing, in addition to offices, a hotel, retail and restaurants. Tjuvholmen allé was laid out as a 16-metre-wide diagonal main street. Canals, bridges and smaller streets divide the area into Odden, Holmen and Skjæret and make the water visible between the buildings.

Culture and public outdoor spaces were an integrated part of the agreement and the plan. At the outermost point the Italian architect Renzo Piano designed the Astrup Fearnley Museum. The museum opened in the autumn of 2012 and is Piano's only project in Scandinavia. Its curved glass roof ties several building volumes together and continues over the walkways towards the fjord.

The same year saw the opening of the sea bath, the sculpture park and the Tjuvtitten viewing tower. The bathing facility has steps, piers and platforms where the public can come right down to the water. The sculpture park lies on Skjæret outside the museum. These public facilities mean that people without a home, hotel room or office on Tjuvholmen can still use the outermost fjord front.

The main development was finished around 2012, while the final parts were completed towards 2014. The new area houses around 1,500 residents and 1,700 workplaces. Housing, workplaces, restaurants, galleries and promenades lie close together, and expensive private buildings meet publicly accessible walking routes and bathing places.

Tjuvholmen therefore gathers an unusually long series of changes in a small area: a children's rescue institution, a socialist public meeting, a harbour, land reclamation, property development, an international art museum and a public sea bath. The planned openness towards the fjord exists side by side with one of Oslo's most expensive residential areas, and this combination is visible at every meeting between promenade, museum, hotel and residential façade.

damstredet_telthusbakken.name: Damstredet and Telthusbakken
damstredet_telthusbakken.desc: Damstredet and Telthusbakken preserve two connected timber-house environments from before the masonry city. Damstredet is named after the Sculptor's Pond and holds houses from the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries; Henrik Wergeland lived here in 1839–41. Telthusbakken was built up by the poor before 1800 on a steep remnant of the town common and was formally surveyed in 1815–16.
damstredet_telthusbakken.popupDesc:
Start at Sigrun Bergs plass, where Damstredet meets Akersveien. Beneath the square lay the Sculptor's Pond until it was filled in during 1851–52; the pond gave the street the name it took over from the older designation Bergfjerdingens Gade. The change of name lets you read three layers in one place: the former suburb of Bergfjerdingen, the sculptor Meyer family's smallholding and today's memory of the textile artist Sigrun Berg.

Walk down Damstredet and compare the houses, not just their colours. At numbers 1–3 stands Solberg, built and altered in several stages. Henrik Wergeland lived on the ground floor as a newlywed in 1839–41, and the stable of his horse Veslebrunen is preserved behind the house. His writing cabin, by contrast, was moved to the Norwegian Museum of Cultural History in 1902. One courtyard thus shows use, preservation and the fact that heritage can be separated from its original setting.

At Damstredet 2 a darker history lies at street level. The motor mechanic Sigurd Dickman lived here with his family in the first years of the war. He was deported on the Donau on 26 November 1942 and died at Auschwitz on 15 February 1943; a stumbling stone has been laid in his memory. His brother Rolle and Rolle's wife Johanne escaped to Sweden. Look down without turning the house into a backdrop: the memorial stone ties the peaceful street to persecution, flight and loss.

Further down stands Rabarbraslottet, the Rhubarb Castle, a house built and rebuilt in stages through the nineteenth century. The name refers to a gardener and a large rhubarb bed. Its restoration in the 1950s prompted the restoration of several more houses, and the textile artist Sigrun Berg later lived here and ran a weaving studio opposite. The idyllic appearance is therefore the result of work, rebuilding and conservation choices, not an untouched pocket of time.

Cross Akersbakken to Telthusbakken. The name comes from a military tent house by Old Aker Church. This steep remnant of the town common was poorly suited to cultivation and was not distributed as ordinary smallholdings. Towards the end of the eighteenth century poor people took over plots they regarded as ownerless; before 1800 the northern side was built up as far as the church. Surveying and title deeds in 1815–16 made ownership more formal.

Finish at the Egebergløkka allotment garden and look back towards the church. The green slope, the low houses and the uneven sequence of the street show how terrain shaped settlement before larger zoning plans took over. At the same time the area is still a residential environment: stay in the public street, do not photograph into windows, and leave stairs, gardens and gates as the residents' private space.

Read the two streets together, but not as if they were identical. Damstredet speaks particularly of Bergfjerdingen, craftsmanship, the change of name and conservation; Telthusbakken speaks of the town common, marginal ground and the formalisation of plots. Between them, Akersbakken, Old Aker Church and Vår Frelsers cemetery tie the place into a rich walk across the Aker ridge.

deichman_bjorvika.name: Deichman Bjørvika
deichman_bjorvika.desc: Deichman Bjørvika opened on 18 June 2020 as Oslo's new main library, designed by Lund Hagem Arkitekter and Atelier Oslo. The 13,500-square-metre building has six levels, around 450,000 books, a cinema, workshops, music rooms and a podcast studio. In the Silent Room one new manuscript is stored each year until the Future Library publishes the whole collection in 2114.
deichman_bjorvika.popupDesc:
Oslo's public library was founded in 1785 with the book collection of the ironworks owner and chancery councillor Carl Deichman. The institution grew into a network of district libraries, and the main library moved into a monumental building of its own at Hammersborg in 1933. When the Fjord City and Bjørvika were being planned, the library was given a new site between Oslo Central Station and the Opera House.

Lund Hagem Arkitekter and Atelier Oslo won the architectural competition in 2009. The site was cramped and lay above complicated infrastructure. The architects therefore let the upper floors cantilever out beyond the footprint. The large cantilevers gave more floor area without filling the whole ground-level square and created covered zones by the entrances.

The building has six levels and an area of around 13,500 square metres. Some 450,000 books stand alongside newspapers, films, games and digital collections. The building also holds a cinema, stages, meeting rooms, music rooms, sewing machines, 3D printers, workshops and a podcast studio. The library thus functions as book store, workplace, cultural centre and production space all at once.

Three diagonal light wells cut through the floors. They carry daylight from the façades and entrances into the middle of the building and make several levels visible to one another. The folded roof and the open stairs create long sightlines towards the city, the fjord, the Opera House and the rail yard at Oslo S. The interior is organised so that quiet reading zones, events and noisier workshops can share the same building.

Deichman Bjørvika was due to open on 28 March 2020. The coronavirus closure postponed the opening, and the public was admitted on 18 June. The move ended the main library's 87 years at Hammersborg. The new address, Anne-Cath. Vestlys plass 1, ties the building to the writer who wrote about, among others, Grandmother and the Eight Children.

One of the most unusual rooms is the Silent Room for Katie Paterson's art project Future Library. Every year from 2014 to 2114 an author delivers an unpublished manuscript that is to remain unread. The room is clad in timber from the forest felled when a thousand new spruce trees were planted in Nordmarka to provide paper for the future publication. The library thus holds books from the past, tools for today's public and texts no one may read for roughly a hundred years.

var_frelsers_gravlund.name: Vår Frelsers cemetery
var_frelsers_gravlund.desc: Vår Frelsers cemetery was laid out in 1807 and taken into use in the summer of 1808, outside the dense city. Paths, trees and grave memorials show how Christiania grew, how prosperous families displayed status, and how public memory was shaped. The Grove of Honour, the urn graves and today's wreath-layings make the landscape more than a collection of famous names: here the city is still choosing who and what to remember.
var_frelsers_gravlund.popupDesc:
Vår Frelsers cemetery begins as a boundary in the city. It was laid out in 1807 and taken into use in the summer of 1808, on the town common outside the dense built-up area of Christiania. A ban on burials inside churches and new requirements for burial grounds outside market towns had moved the question of the dead into both hygiene and town planning. When the cemetery served as Christiania's common burial ground from 1811 to 1833, the area had to be extended in step with the city.

Follow the paths and read how the landscape is ordered. Tall memorial stones, stone frames, ironwork and family graves made the status of prosperous families visible to visitors. Other graves are smaller and more anonymous. Compare Vår Frelsers with Ankerløkken: there the pauper graves dominated after the site became a permanent burial ground in 1839. The cemetery is therefore not a neutral register of everyone who lived in the city, but a landscape shaped by economy, belonging and the right to hold a grave.

The city's growth also left traces in buildings and use. A mortuary chapel with a sexton's dwelling was built in 1864, and the cemetery was extended several times until 1881. The chapel provided a dedicated place for storage and ceremonies. From 2004 it was consecrated as an Orthodox church, so that a building raised for nineteenth-century funeral practice took on a new religious use.

In 1903 the idea of a dedicated Grove of Honour for significant women and men was put forward. The grove gathered some graves and had others moved in, but many well-known figures lie outside it. Henrik Wergeland, Camilla Collett and Ivar Aasen are found elsewhere in the cemetery, while Henrik Ibsen, Bjørnstjerne Bjørnson, Edvard Munch, Christian and Oda Krohg, Marcus Thrane, Martin Tranmæl, Carl Joachim Hambro, Viggo Hansteen and Rolf Wickstrøm, among others, are marked in the Grove of Honour. The selection shows that public honour is not only about who the dead were, but about whom later generations chose to raise up.

Nor do the graves stand silent. On 17 May speeches are held and wreaths laid at Wergeland, Bjørnson, Ibsen, Hansteen and Wickstrøm, among others. New speakers tie older lives to questions of democracy, freedom of expression and community. The cemetery thereby becomes a public stage for the use of history, while remaining a place for grief, urn interments and quiet visits.

Protection changes how the landscape can be used. Temporary listing was introduced in 1969, and from 2009 urn graves became available again. The City of Oslo states that anyone may be buried here, but that the provision applies to urn graves. The municipality has also halted new allocations of reused graves with existing memorials while the monuments are surveyed, assessed and restored under the conservation plan. Memory, practical cemetery management and heritage protection thus meet in the same stones.

Read the place as a physical archive, but also as an edited narrative. Trees, paths and grave memorials leave traces of almost two hundred years of urban growth, class, family life, art and politics. What has been preserved, moved, wreathed or reused shows that commemorative culture is constantly negotiated. Ask therefore both whom you find, whom you do not find, and what values the markings around the graves express.

vigelandsparken.name: The Vigeland Park
vigelandsparken.desc: The Vigeland Park holds over 200 sculptures in bronze, granite and wrought iron, designed by Gustav Vigeland across more than 40 years. The city council set aside the area in Frogner Park in 1924. The bridge opened in 1940, the 17-metre Monolith with 121 figures was finished in 1942, and the Fountain was filled with water in 1947.
vigelandsparken.popupDesc:
The Vigeland Park is Gustav Vigeland's life's work and holds over 200 sculptures in bronze, granite and wrought iron. The work stretched across more than forty years. Vigeland modelled the figures and also designed the park's architectural framework of bridges, stairs, gates, terraces and long sightlines. The complex was therefore planned as a single whole, not as a collection of individual statues.

The starting point was the Fountain, originally intended for Eidsvolls plass in front of the Storting. In 1924 the city council decided that it should instead be erected in Frogner Park. The plan gradually grew to encompass a sculpture-lined bridge, the Monolith plateau and several gates and side structures along one continuous axis.

The great granite block for the Monolith came from the Iddefjord and was raised on the site in 1928. Vigeland had made a full-scale clay model in 1924–25. Around one million measuring points were transferred from the model to the stone. The stonemasons Ivar Broe, Nils Jönsson and Nils Kjær worked for thirteen years on the 17-metre column.

The Monolith consists of 121 intertwined human figures. Children, adults and elderly bodies climb, support one another and press together up the column. The work was finished in 1942, a year before Vigeland died. Around the plateau stand 36 granite groups showing people of different ages and in different relationships.

The bridge received 58 bronze sculptures. When it opened on 7 July 1940, 46 of them were in place. Among the figures stands "Sinnataggen", the Angry Boy, who has become one of Norway's best-known sculptural motifs. The bridge figures are placed on the parapets so that visitors move between them rather than viewing them from one fixed point.

The Fountain was installed and brought into operation in 1947. Around 1,800 cubic metres of water pass through the system every hour. Bronze trees with human figures surround the basin, while the reliefs beneath them depict a cycle of life. The wrought iron gates were put in place in 1952, and later works including The Clan, a self-portrait with the sculpture Triangle and the work Surprised were added to the complex.

The park was formally opened on 2 June 1993, several decades after its best-known parts were already in use. The monumental axis functions at the same time as an ordinary public park. Tourists, runners, school classes and picnickers move through an artwork built in stages from the 1920s until after Vigeland's death.

voienvolden.name: Vøienvolden
voienvolden.desc: Vøienvolden in Maridalsveien is Oslo's most complete surviving smallholding complex, with a farmyard and buildings from the eighteenth century. The main building took its present form around 1790. Sverre and Ingrid Udnæs began a comprehensive restoration with architect Magnus Poulsson in 1917, while the Society for the Preservation of Norwegian Ancient Monuments took over the farm in 1954 and uses it as a museum, office and meeting place.
voienvolden.popupDesc:
Vøienvolden lies as a farmyard behind a gate in Maridalsveien, surrounded by Sagene's dense tenement blocks and traffic. The property was originally part of the Vøyen farm and of Christiania's town common. The common was established in 1629 as shared land for cultivation, grazing and livestock outside the built-up town.

In 1683 the alderman Johan Pettersen Bergmand was granted a large private enclosure here. The site developed into a løkke, a rural property used by townspeople for agriculture, recreation and household needs. The oldest parts of today's farm complex date from the eighteenth century. The main building took essentially its present form around 1790.

The farmyard holds a dwelling house, farm buildings, outbuildings and a garden. The completeness of the ensemble makes Vøienvolden Oslo's most fully preserved smallholding complex. While sawmills, textile factories and workers' housing transformed the landscape along the Akerselva in the nineteenth century, farming continued here. The city grew around the property without erasing the structure of the yard.

The distiller Gabriel J. Udnæs bought Vøienvolden in 1829. The farm became a meeting place for Haugeans, who emphasised religious gatherings, work and commercial activity outside the established state church. The Udnæs family kept the property through several generations.

Sverre Udnæs and his wife Ingrid took over the farm in 1913. In 1917 they began a comprehensive restoration and engaged architect Magnus Poulsson. He removed an extension facing the garden and designed a new side wing with a kitchen and maid's room. The work was early building conservation: the aim was to make the house usable without removing its historic character.

The Society for the Preservation of Norwegian Ancient Monuments took over Vøienvolden in 1954. The society works on the conservation of buildings and cultural environments and has used the farm as a base for its activity in Oslo and Akershus. The buildings house offices, exhibitions, meetings, courses and guided tours, while the yard and garden are used for markets and events among other things.

The contrast remains sharp. One walks through the gate from the traffic of Maridalsveien and the dense city into a farmyard with timber houses, outbuildings and a garden. Vøienvolden shows not a reconstructed village but an actual smallholding complex that remained standing while the industrial and residential district of Sagene closed in around it.

romsaås.name: Romsås
romsaås.desc: Romsås was built as a satellite town in 1970–74 with 2,600 flats across six residential clusters. The Romsås team designed blocks of three to eight storeys between forest and hills, while car traffic was kept to the perimeter. The shopping centre opened in 1972, and the metro station followed in 1974 in a rock cavern 55 metres underground.
romsaås.popupDesc:
Before the satellite town was built, Romsås was an area of farming and forestry with agriculture, quarries and a growing population of stonecutters and industrial workers. Plot sales began in the 1880s, but the area long kept a scattered character. In the 1960s the City of Oslo expropriated large areas in order to carry out a comprehensive housing plan on the heights north of Grorud.

A dedicated architectural collective, the Romsås team, was given responsibility for the plan. The group consisted of Alex Christiansen, Trygve Kleiven, Randi Kippgen, Olav Holm, Nils A. Rosland and Alf Bastiansen. Between 1970 and 1974 around 2,600 flats were built in blocks of three to eight storeys. The housing was distributed across six clusters: Tiurleiken, Orremyr, Ravnkollen, Emanuelfjell, Svarttjern and Røverkollen.

The clusters were placed between knolls, forest and viewpoints. Footpaths tied the housing together, while car traffic was largely routed around the area and into parking structures at the perimeter. The solution was meant to give children and adults continuous routes without crossing the main roads. The blocks are uniform, but the changes in elevation and the terrain make them appear differently from place to place.

Romsås shopping centre opened in 1972, gathering retail and services at the heart of the area. The metro station opened in 1974 as part of the Grorud Line. It lies in a rock cavern 55.1 metres beneath the centre and was designed by Håkon Mjelva. The station and its concrete work received the Concrete Award in 1976. Access by long escalators makes the distance between underground transport and the housing on the heights physically noticeable.

The development also included schools, a nursing home and a church. Romsås nursing home opened in 1975. Several schools were built in and around the clusters, but pupil numbers and organisation changed, and some were later closed. Romsås church was consecrated in 1976, burned in 1986 and was replaced by a new church in 1995.

At Svarttjern a bathing place and park were later laid out, opening in 2009. The area shows how the original plan continues to be supplemented with new functions. Romsås can therefore be read as one continuous project: old stone industry, municipal expropriation, six residential clusters, traffic separation, an award-winning rock station, schools, a church and a nature and bathing area close to the blocks.

rodelokka.name: Rodeløkka
rodelokka.desc: Rodeløkka is named after the dean Frederik Rode, who bought a plot here in 1854. Gunsmith Hans Olsen from Vågå parcelled out the area from 1859, and the timber-house district was built outside the masonry-building requirement in the 1860s and 1870s. After a long clearance dispute, Oslo decided in 1988 to preserve an area of 137 properties.
rodelokka.popupDesc:
Dean Frederik Rode bought thirteen decares of Dælenenga in 1854. He moved a house here from Gjerpen and gave the plot its first clear ownership history. Five years later he sold the property to gunsmith Hans Olsen from Vågå. Olsen began dividing the ground into small plots, and the new residential district was first called Vågeby after his home parish. The name Rodeløkka took hold later, after the previous owner.

The houses were mainly built in the 1860s and 1870s, while the area still lay outside Christiania's city boundary and its masonry-building requirement. Timber construction was therefore possible in a way no longer permitted in the dense city. Small dwellings, workshops, outbuildings and narrow streets grew up for workers and craftsmen. Rodeløkka school opened as early as 1860 and at its peak had around 600 pupils, a clear sign of how fast the population was growing.

The district was incorporated into Christiania in 1878. Later it also gained a tramway. An electric tram line to Rodeløkka opened in 1900 and closed in 1949. A new route ran through the area from 1955 to 1961. Although the tram disappeared, the street widths and the small-scale timber structure remained, in contrast to the larger masonry blocks and road schemes around them.

During the twentieth century many houses were considered substandard and ripe for clearance. Demolition plans triggered prolonged protests in the 1970s and 1980s. Rode's old summer house was moved from Tromsøgata 7 to Langgata 30 in 1984, so that the building could be preserved even though its original setting was lost. Four years later the municipality adopted a conservation area covering 137 properties.

The continuous timber-house environment that remains is therefore not merely an accidental relic of an old suburb. It is the result of plot subdivision from 1859, building outside the masonry requirement, a history of schools and trams, and a concrete fight against clearance. Rodeløkka tells both why small timber houses could arise here and why they are still standing.

The conservation decision covered not only individual fine houses but a whole pattern of plots, back yards, outbuildings and streets. It is that coherence that makes Rodeløkka different from a museum of relocated buildings. The area still shows how a working-class suburb outside the city boundary could be organised in small units before masonry tenements came to dominate the inner city.

vaalerenga.name: Vålerenga
vaalerenga.desc: Vålerenga grew up as a suburb along Strømsveien from the 1830s, acquiring timber houses, masonry blocks, a school and a church. The 1902 church burned in 1979 and reopened in 1984. The E6 long carried heavy through traffic between the houses, until the Vålerenga Tunnel opened in 1987 and 1989 and Strømsveien was closed to through traffic in 1992.
vaalerenga.popupDesc:
Vålerenga grew up as a suburb along Strømsveien from the 1830s. By the time the area was incorporated into Christiania in 1878, extensive timber housing already existed. The houses had been built before the masonry requirement and the city's stricter regulation reached the district. Masonry blocks followed, particularly between 1887 and 1911, along with some apartment blocks in the 1930s. Vålerenga therefore consists of several housing types from different phases, not only the well-known timber houses.

Vålerenga school was built in 1893–95. The church opened in 1902 and became a clear landmark above the steep streets. In 1979 the church burned, leaving only the masonry walls standing. The rebuilt church was consecrated in 1984. The fire created a marked break in the district's history, but the building kept its site and much of its outward form.

From 1926 to 1967 the tram ran through the district. After the tram disappeared, car traffic became a far heavier burden. Strømsveien was part of the E6, and in the 1970s and 1980s large volumes of through traffic passed between timber houses, school and homes. The road created noise, insecurity and a physical barrier through the dense residential area.

Plans for extensive clearance had existed since 1929. Poor housing standards in some buildings and the heavy traffic load were used as arguments for demolition. At the same time, opposition to removing the historic environment grew. The Vålerenga Tunnel opened in two stages in 1987 and 1989 and moved much of the through traffic underground. In 1992 Strømsveien was closed to through traffic.

Once the traffic was gone, the street took on an entirely different function, and much of the older building stock was rehabilitated rather than demolished. Vålerenga therefore shows how a residential district can change without all its houses being replaced. Timber suburb, masonry city, school, church fire, tramway and motorway lie as concrete layers in the same neighbourhood.

The change to Strømsveien is the clearest physical difference between then and now. The same route that first carried suburban traffic and later the E6 through the neighbourhood became a local street after the tunnel. School routes, homes and the local environment could then function without the former stream of through traffic. The traffic rerouting thus became a conservation measure as well.

vinderen.name: Vinderen
vinderen.desc: Vinderen grew into a villa district and suburban centre after the Holmenkollen Line opened in 1898. The school district was established in 1904, a psychiatric clinic opened in 1906, and Ove Bang and Arne Korsmo produced a zoning plan in 1935. The Conditori building from 1901 burned in 2008 and was replaced by a new building in 2012.
vinderen.popupDesc:
Vinderen takes its name from the Vinderen farm, but today's residential district and local centre were shaped by the Holmenkollen Line. When the line opened in 1898, it became possible to live far from the centre and still commute quickly into town. Villas, shops and public institutions appeared around the station. Development gathered particular pace in the 1920s and 1930s.

The Vinderen school district was established in 1904. Two years later the Vinderen psychiatric clinic opened, later becoming part of the University of Oslo. School and health services gave the area functions extending beyond housing. Ove Bang and Arne Korsmo produced a zoning plan in 1935, in a period when new roads and houses were to be arranged around the railway and the growing local centre.

Retail concentrated near the station. Vinderen Conditori opened in 1901 in the building that became known as the Conditori building. The café became a local meeting place across several generations. The building burned in 2008 and was demolished the following year. A new building was completed in 2012, so that one of the oldest institutions by the station continued on a site where the original building was gone.

Other buildings show how the centre developed in stages. The pharmacy building came in 1916, and Vindernhuset was erected in 1937. The old station building was later incorporated into the Vinderntorvet shopping centre, built in 1985–86. The railway history itself thus became part of a newer retail centre.

Vinderen is therefore more than a low-density villa area. The place consists of a railway from 1898, a school district from 1904, a psychiatric clinic from 1906, commercial buildings from several periods and a zoning plan from 1935. The fire at the Conditori building also shows that historic meeting places can survive as businesses even when the building disappears. The whole district is a clear example of how a suburban railway could create both housing and a local centre.

The various dates around the station show how gradually the centre came into being. The café arrived only three years after the railway, the pharmacy fifteen years later, and Vindernhuset followed in the interwar years. The 1980s shopping centre built further on the same site. Vinderen was thus not planned complete in one go, but grew through many small institutional and commercial additions.

ullern.name: Ullern
ullern.desc: Ullern church opened in 1903, and the area became its own parish in 1906. The Smestad Line arrived in 1912, the Røa Line in 1935 and the connection towards Kolsås in 1942. Bestum school, Ullern sports ground, the Radium Hospital and Ullern upper secondary school made the district more than a villa area.
ullern.popupDesc:
Ullern takes its name from the Ullern farm and was long characterised by farms and smallholdings west of the city. Ullern church opened in 1903, and in 1906 the area was separated from Vestre Aker as its own parish. The church and the parish boundary gave the scattered area a clearer local centre before large-scale housing construction gathered pace.

Public transport made the development possible. The Smestad Line opened in 1912. The line was extended towards Røa in 1935, and the connection towards Kolsås came in 1942. Villa areas grew up around the stations, from which residents could commute to the centre. At the same time Ullern never became simply a collection of large detached houses. Terraced houses, stepped terrace blocks and apartment blocks from various parts of the twentieth century also appeared.

Several institutions came to matter for the whole city. Bestum school opened in 1921, and Ullern sports ground followed in 1922. Ullern upper secondary school was established in 1931. The same year the Radium Hospital opened as the country's specialist hospital for cancer treatment. The hospital brought patients, staff and medical activity to an area otherwise often associated with quiet residential streets.

Large office and business areas later appeared near Lysaker and Skøyen. Ullern thereby gained workplaces and traffic flows that do not fit the classic picture of a pure suburb. Railway, schools, sport, hospital and offices tie the residential areas to the rest of the city.

The housing environment is therefore more mixed than the reputation of a uniform villa suburb suggests. Older villas, post-war terraced houses, terrace blocks and newer apartment buildings stand side by side. The Smestad Line, the Røa Line and the Kolsås connection explain why the built-up area could spread across such a large territory, while the institutions explain why people travel to Ullern without living there. The place's history is carried by this mixture: farmland, church parish, railway suburb, school environment, sport, cancer treatment and modern workplaces.

The dates 1903, 1912, 1921, 1922 and 1931 show how quickly the area moved from scattered farmland to organised city district. First came the church, then the railway, the school, the sports ground, the upper secondary school and the Radium Hospital. Each institution drew new daily journeys to the place and made Ullern less dependent on the city centre for work, education, treatment and leisure.

spikersuppa.name: Spikersuppa
spikersuppa.desc: The reflecting pool at Spikersuppa was designed by Arnstein Arneberg and opened in 1956 as a gift from Christiania Spigerverk. The sculptures Deer Group and Playing Children arrived in 1958. The pool was demolished during metro construction in 1974–75 and rebuilt, before Narvesen funded the ice rink that opened in 1994 and gained the nickname "Narvisen".
spikersuppa.popupDesc:
Spikersuppa is the popular name for the reflecting pool in the middle of Eidsvolls plass, between the Storting and the National Theatre. The scheme was designed by city hall architect Arnstein Arneberg and opened in 1956. Christiania Spigerverk, the nail works, financed the pool as a gift to the city, and the connection to the factory quickly gave the place the name still used more often than the formal one.

The pool was shaped as a long, shallow sheet of water with a fountain. On a small island stands Arne Vigeland's sculpture group Deer Group, installed in 1958 together with a group of trees. The same year Arne Durban's Playing Children arrived at the pool's edge. Water, trees and figurative sculptures made the central part of Eidsvolls plass a clear place to linger, not merely a passage along Karl Johans gate.

The original scheme had a dramatic interruption when the metro tunnel between Nationaltheatret and Sentrum station was to be built. The pool was demolished in 1974–75 to make room for the construction work beneath the city centre. Once the tunnel was finished, Spikersuppa was rebuilt. The place therefore shows an urban space literally taken apart and put back together above one of the capital's most important transport tunnels.

In 1994 Narvesen financed an artificial ice rink in the pool. The winter facility quickly acquired the nickname "Narvisen". The same surface is therefore used in two entirely different ways through the year: as a reflecting pool with a fountain in the summer half of the year, and as a skating rink when the cold arrives. The sculptures and the shape of the pool are fixed, while the activities change with the season.

Its location gives a relatively small scheme great public significance. The Storting lies on one side, the National Theatre on the other, and Karl Johans gate carries large pedestrian flows past the square. Christmas markets, concerts, political demonstrations and everyday lingering constantly add new activities around the pool. People may pass on their way to work, meet someone by the ice or stop in front of a stage during an event.

Spikersuppa is therefore the result of several concrete interventions: an industrial company's gift, Arneberg's park architecture, two sculptures from 1958, demolition during metro construction and Narvesen's winter rink from 1994. The name sounds informal, but the place gathers industrial history, public art, transport construction and seasonally driven city life in the middle of the country's most symbolic central corridor.

bankplassen.name: Bankplassen
bankplassen.desc: Bankplassen emerged as a ceremonial public square after the lower fortifications were removed from the mid-1820s. Around the compact square, three generations of Norges Bank buildings, a vanished theatre and later museum use can be read as separate historical layers. Public art, trees and seating edges give the street level a scale of its own and make the square more than a frame around the institutional buildings.
bankplassen.popupDesc:
Bankplassen is the square itself between Kirkegata, Kongens gate and Myntgata, not the sum of the buildings around it. The area was released when the lower fortress ramparts and glacis were removed from the mid-1820s. A ceremonial setting was developed here for the young state's civil and military institutions, and the square was named after Norges Bank, the central bank.

The oldest bank building on the square was completed in 1828 to designs by Christian Heinrich Grosch. The Christiania Theatre opened on the opposite side in 1837 and stood there until 1899. The two buildings were separate institutions, but their façades made Bankplassen a space where state-building, finance and the performing arts met.

The Society for the Welfare of the City of Oslo laid out park planting between the theatre and the old bank in 1860. The Engebret Café had by then established itself on the square and became a meeting place for the circle around the theatre. When the theatre building was demolished, the site was used for Norges Bank's new headquarters, which opened in 1906.

The bank building from 1828 later acquired a new institutional history as the National Archives and then the architecture museum. Sverre Fehn's pavilion today links Grosch's building to the former archive store, and the complex opened as the National Museum – Architecture in 2008. Norges Bank's present head office on another side of the square was inaugurated in 1986.

That same year Brynjulf Bergslien's statue of the actor Johannes Brun was moved to Bankplassen. It stands close to where the Christiania Theatre once was and makes a vanished theatrical layer visible in today's square. Newer sculptures by Marit Krogh and István Lisztes are tied to granite blocks, benches and the passage in Revierstredet, where art and physical security measures are woven together.

What is distinctive about Bankplassen lies in how several independent institutions face the same small public space. Walk around the square and compare Grosch's classicism, the bank building from 1906, the head office from 1986 and the small artworks at street level. The shift from fortress terrain to a space of finance, culture and everyday life then becomes readable without confusing the neighbouring buildings with the square itself.

christiania_torv.name: Christiania Torv
christiania_torv.desc: Christiania Torv was the political, civic and commercial centre of the new town of Christiania, laid out beside Akershus Fortress after the fire of 1624. The town hall and cathedral stood here, and the square gathered the market, a public water post and public punishment before its central market functions gradually moved to Stortorvet. The name Christiania Torv was adopted in 1958, and after many years of heavy traffic the square was rehabilitated in the 1990s; Wenche Gulbransen's fountain sculpture Christian IV's Glove arrived in 1997.
christiania_torv.popupDesc:
After the great fire in Oslo in August 1624, Christian IV decided that the town should be moved to the area beside Akershus Fortress and built as Christiania. The new town was given a regulated street grid, and Christiania Torv became a political, civic and commercial centre through its first hundred years. The square originally had an almost square form. Oppdag Kvadraturen describes how it was placed near a high point in the town, so that church and town hall gained a visible position in the townscape.

Holy Trinity Church was consecrated here in 1639. The Old Town Hall was completed beside the square in 1641, and before the town hall was built the town's courthouse stood on the square. At the centre of the square lay the public water post "Vandkunsten", from which citizens could, for a fee, lay private water pipes to their houses. The pillory and the "kak", a post with a neck iron used for public flogging, also stood here. The square was moreover used at times as a place of execution, so that trade, the exercise of authority and punishment all took place in the same public space.

The Christiania market was held on the square in January and February from the 1640s until 1736. When Holy Trinity Church burned down in 1686, it was decided to build a new cathedral outside the Kvadraturen; it was completed at Stortorvet in 1697. In 1736 the market too was moved to Stortorvet. Christiania Torv thereby gradually lost its role as the town's natural centre and was later referred to as the Town's Old Square or Gammel-Torvet.

St. John's Church stood beside the square from 1878 to 1929 on the site where Holy Trinity Church had been. The name Christiania Torv was adopted in 1958. In 1964 the square was enclosed and paved and at the same time given a new water feature. After many years of heavy traffic, the square was rehabilitated in the 1990s.

In 1997 Wenche Gulbransen's fountain sculpture Christian IV's Glove was placed at the centre of the square, on the spot associated with the older water feature. The work uses the story of Christian IV and the founding of the town as its motif, but the sculpture is not historical documentation of a literal thrown glove. The design of the square was awarded the City of Oslo Architecture Prize in 2003.

The Old Town Hall from 1641 still stands beside the square, and the Anatomy Building also faces the space. Rådhusgata and Øvre Slottsgate meet at the square. Together, the preserved street geometry, the buildings, the fountain and the traces of church, market and public authority mean that several of Christiania's historical functions can still be read in one small square.

slottsparken.name: The Palace Park
slottsparken.desc: Slottsparken was laid out from 1838 as a romantic landscape park around the Royal Palace, with palace architect H.D.F. Linstow as its central planner. The park covers around 220 decares and holds some 1,000 trees. The Queen's Park from 1751 was incorporated in 1840, and the Guard House in Swiss chalet style was built in 1845–49.
slottsparken.popupDesc:
Slottsparken was laid out at the same time as the Royal Palace and developed from 1838. Palace architect Hans Ditlev Franciscus Linstow took an active part in the planning. While the Palace Square and the palace façade were given a monumental, classical form, the park was shaped as a romantic landscape inspired by English garden art.

The paths wind through undulating lawns, large groups of deciduous trees and smaller sheets of water with fountains. The park covers around 220 decares and holds some 1,000 trees, many with roots going back to the first phase of planting. The form was intended to give constantly changing views rather than one strict symmetrical axis. The Palace may therefore disappear behind tree crowns and reappear as one follows the paths.

An older rococo garden from 1751 was bought and incorporated in 1840. This part is today's Queen's Park and still has a more secluded role than the rest of the green space. The Palace was completed in 1849, but the park took its main form through the 1840s and 1850s. Parkveien was laid out along the outer edge and helped define the new boundary to the west and north-west.

The Guard House by the Palace Square was built in 1845–49 and is regarded as one of Norway's oldest buildings in the Swiss chalet style. By Wergelandsveien stands Grotten, the house the state made available to Henrik Wergeland in 1841. The buildings show that the park consists not only of natural forms but also of small houses connected with guard duty, art and national representation.

During the Second World War, air raid shelters were built along Wergelandsveien and Parkveien and in the Queen's Park. These installations laid a layer of civil defence beneath the peaceful landscape park. Above ground the area continued to be a central frame around the Palace and the political power relations under the occupation.

In the spring of 1966 Norway's first open drug scene arose in Slottsparken. Nisseberget became associated with youth rebellion, hippie culture and later with the history of how open drug environments were moved and pushed onwards through the city. This layer is less visible than the palace architecture, but is documented in public inquiries and archive material.

The park has been open to the public throughout. It is used as a shortcut, a place to walk, a meeting place and a setting for national ceremonies. Slottsparken thus gathers royal representation, romantic garden art, old trees, wartime civil defence, a writer's house and informal youth scenes within the same continuous green space.

botsparken.name: Botsparken
botsparken.desc: Grønland Park, commonly called Botsparken, was laid out in 1916–17 on land the Penitentiary handed over to the city in 1912. The park lies in front of the 1851 prison and forms the western end of Klosterenga. The Hovinbekken stream, culverted in the 1920s, was reopened through the new art and water park in 2023.
botsparken.popupDesc:
Botsparken is the everyday name for the western part of Grønland Park, directly in front of the long wall of the former Penitentiary. The prison opened in 1851 as a national prison for male long-term inmates. Its Norwegian name, Botsfengselet, referred to a penal idea in which isolation, labour and religious influence were to lead the inmate to penance and improvement.

In 1912 the prison handed over land to the city. The park was laid out in 1916–17 and quickly gained importance in a dense working-class district with little open space. Its official name is Grønland Park, but the closeness of the prison made "Botsparken" the established everyday name. The open lawn and the trees stand in clear contrast to the wall and the closed prison buildings.

Eastwards the green corridor continues as Klosterenga between the prison grounds and the housing in Gamle Oslo. The park therefore functions both as a local place to spend time and as part of a longer connection. Walking routes tie Grønland to the areas towards Galgeberg and Gamlebyen. Its narrow form means one is constantly aware of the nearby housing, institutions and traffic.

The Hovinbekken stream once ran through the area but was culverted in the 1920s. From the 1990s the sculptor Bård Breivik developed a plan for a sculpture park in which water, stone and vegetation would form one continuous work of art. The project became protracted and was not completed in Breivik's lifetime.

After his death the work was carried on by, among others, sculptor Kristian Blystad and architect Jørn Skaare. Klosterenga park opened in its new form in 2023. The Hovinbekken was brought back as an artificial stream some 700 metres long, and stonework, bridges, seating and watercourses were integrated into the green corridor. The City of Oslo has described the project as the largest single municipal investment in art since the Vigeland Park.

Botsparken lies at the entrance to this scheme. The place therefore gathers three very different kinds of infrastructure: the prison wall and its penal history, the neighbourhood park from 1916–17, and the reopened stream with public art from 2023. What began as ceded prison land has become a connection between Grønland, Klosterenga and Gamlebyen with room for play, rest, movement, water and art.

stensparken.name: Stensparken
stensparken.desc: Stensparken follows a 500-metre limestone ridge between Korpehaugen and Blåsen. The park name became official in 1891, and the scheme was completed in 1943. Here stand Fagerborg Church from 1903, air raid shelters from 1961–62, the Sigrid Undset sculpture from 1991 and the listed functionalist urinal "Kjærlighetskarusellen", an important site in Oslo's queer history.
stensparken.popupDesc:
Stensparken lies between Pilestredet, Stensgata, Thereses gate and Sporveisgata. The park follows a limestone ridge some 500 metres long, with Korpehaugen to the south and Blåsen to the north. Blåsen is the park's highest point, 81 metres above sea level. The elevation gives views across the city, while the lime-rich bedrock creates drier and more species-rich slopes than in many other parks in inner Oslo. The park area is around 48 decares.

The name comes from the Sten farm, which in the Middle Ages was monastic land under Nonneseter. The area was later known as Natmandshaugen. The name Stensparken became official in 1891. The first landscaping took place around 1890–1900 with money from the spirits monopoly, but the work took several decades. In the 1930s came a fountain, better access to Blåsen, playgrounds, a paddling pool, roundabouts, a shelter and small children's urinals. The park was only completed in 1943.

Fagerborg Church was built in the south-western part of the park and consecrated on 22 December 1903. Hagbarth Schytte-Berg designed the church in Østfold granite with neo-Romanesque and neo-Gothic features. The altarpiece is by Jo Visdal, the stained glass by Max Roth and the font by Lars Utne. The church originally had 860 seats. During the Second World War the bell tower was used as a meeting place for the resistance movement.

The park's most unusual monument stands towards Sporveisgata. City architect Harald Aars designed the functionalist public urinal built in 1937. It became known as "Kjærlighetskarusellen" (the carousel of love) and served as a meeting place for queer men at a time when homosexuality was a criminal offence and later strongly socially condemned. The urinal was listed in 2009, converted into a light installation by Per Barclay in 2022 and marked with a blue plaque in 2023.

Air raid shelters were built beneath Blåsen in 1961–62. A masonry house from 1886, erected behind the later demolished Reiersen smallholding, became a youth house in 2021. In 1991 Kjersti Wexelsen Goksøyr's sculpture of Sigrid Undset was unveiled in the park. It ties the place to the writer who grew up nearby.

The park's long completion meant that the ideals of several periods were laid one on top of another. The early paths and planting were supplemented by the functionalist play and service buildings of the 1930s, while later measures have brought catering, art and youth activity. The park also gained everyday functions. The uppermost playground had a paddling pool that could be used as an ice rink in winter, and a large shelter in functionalist style. A smaller illuminated fountain was installed below Blåsen in the 1930s. Since 2010 there has been outdoor catering in the park.

Stensparken is therefore not merely a green gap between St. Hanshaugen, Bislett and Fagerborg. On the same ridge are traces of monastic land, park politics, church decoration, resistance work, civil defence, literature and queer history. The different layers still lie physically close together between Blåsen, the church, the playgrounds and the urinal.

nydalen.name: Nydalen
nydalen.desc: The Nydalen Cotton Mill was founded in 1845, and the Christiania Nail and Rolling Mill followed in 1853. A distinct industrial community of around 2,000 workers grew up around the factories. Textile production ended in 1963, the industrial area opened as Nydalen Park in 1990, the metro arrived in 2003 and BI in 2005. Today housing, offices and culture lie between the brick factories and the Akerselva.
nydalen.popupDesc:
In the Middle Ages Nydalen was called Fallandadalen, the valley of the waterfalls. Until the mid-nineteenth century the area was mostly forest, farmland and a few sawmills along the Akerselva. Industrialisation began when Adam Severin Hiorth founded the Nydalen Cotton Mill in 1845. The first spinning mill was completed in 1847, and from 1864 came weaving sheds, a dye works and a bleachery. Nydalens Compagnie could in time carry out the entire process from raw cotton to finished cloth.

The Christiania Nail and Rolling Mill was established in 1853 and developed a different production line of nails, steel wire and rolled ironware. The two industrial complexes used the water power of the Akerselva, but each also created a large working community. Around 2,000 workers lived in or near Nydalen. The companies built workers' housing, a school and other institutions, and the area long functioned as an industrial community of its own outside the dense city.

The Gjøvik Line gained a stop at Nydalen in 1947. At the same time industry began to lose its dominant position. Textile production at Nydalens Compagnie was reduced from the 1950s and ceased in 1963. The nail works continued longer, but this activity too was gradually wound down or moved. When the production of wire nails was finally moved to Sweden, the valley's continuous industrial history was over.

Transformation began before the last factories had gone. Old brick buildings were rehabilitated from 1986, and the industrial area opened as Nydalen Park in 1990. A dedicated municipal sub-plan secured the riverbanks as a public park corridor. Avantor became the largest property developer, and factories and warehouses gained new users in media, technology, culture and services. The National Touring Theatre and the National Concert Institute took over the old iron store at Gullhaug torg, among other buildings.

The greatest change came with public transport and education. The metro station, designed by Kristin Jarmund, opened in 2003. The BI Norwegian Business School moved into its new complex in 2005, and the metro ring line was completed in 2006. Nydalen upper secondary school, housing, a hotel, shops and office buildings followed. Solsiden and Nydalen Qvarter gave the area a large permanent population.

Nydalen also became a media and cultural location. TV 2, TVNorge, the Book Club, publishers and printing businesses established themselves in the area at various times, while the National Touring Theatre gained production premises in a former industrial building. Development has continued beyond the first transformation phase. Park Vest opened in 2017. Vertikal Nydalen, designed by Snøhetta, was completed in 2023 as a 65-metre mixed-use building with restaurants, offices and 41 flats. The building shows that Nydalen remains a testing ground for high density and mixed functions.

Today's Nydalen is therefore built from both preservation and replacement. Factory façades, ponds and bridges stand beside metro entrances, tall office buildings and newer housing. The Akerselva, which first supplied power to the machines, now serves as park, walking route and principal space in a district where industrial labour has been replaced by education, media, technology and services.

sorenga.name: Sørenga
sorenga.desc: The Sørenga pier was long a quay area and depot for empty containers before housing construction began in 2009. A canal turned the pier into an island, and the promenade opened the old harbour front to pedestrians. At its outer end, Sørenga sea bath opened in June 2015 with a beach, a diving tower, a 50-metre sea pool and a 190-metre floating concrete structure.
sorenga.popupDesc:
Sørenga lies on the former Øra, a low shore and harbour area just outside the medieval town of Oslo. Through the twentieth century the waterfront was filled in and used for quays, warehousing and transport. The Sørenga pier ended up as a large, fenced-off depot for empty containers. The shape of the long pier is still visible, but almost all of its use has been replaced.

When Oslo adopted the Fjord City in 2000, harbour operations were to be moved and large parts of the waterfront opened for housing, culture and public promenades. The 2008 Fjord City plan set the framework for the transformation. At Sørenga, housing construction began in 2009. New blocks were built around a canal that cut the pier free from the mainland and turned the area into an island connected by bridges. Around 800 homes were finished or being occupied a few years later.

The promenade was carried around the whole of Sørenga and linked the area to the continuous Harbour Promenade. Between the residential blocks lie small squares, piers and passages down to the water. The former container quay therefore did not become purely private residential land; the outer edge was to remain accessible to anyone wishing to walk, sit by the fjord or swim.

Sørenga sea bath opened on 25 June 2015. The facility was designed by LPO arkitekter in collaboration with landscape architects Kristine Jensens Tegnestue and consulting engineers Dr.techn. Olav Olsen. The floating concrete structure was built in a dry dock at Fredrikstad Mekaniske Verksted by AF Gruppen, towed into the Oslo Fjord and anchored at the outer end of the pier. The structure is roughly 190 metres long and 28 metres wide and weighs around 4,650 tonnes.

The sea bath has a child-friendly sandy beach, lawns, seating, showers and a diving tower. The open swimming pool is 50 metres long and divided into eight lanes. A protective stone fill of about 140,000 cubic metres dampens the waves and made it possible to establish the beach and the calmer bathing areas. Timber decks and ramps tie the water surface to the promenade.

Sørenga quickly became one of the most used areas in the Fjord City, particularly on warm summer days. In a few years the place went from an inaccessible container depot to a dense residential area and a public bathing facility. The same harbour form that once kept the city out now serves as pier, promenade and gateway to the fjord.

majorstuen_tbanestasjon.name: Majorstuen metro station
majorstuen_tbanestasjon.desc: Majorstuen station opened on 16 March 1898 as the terminus of the Holmenkollen Line, Norway's first electric suburban railway. The Smestad Line followed in 1912, the Underground Line to Nationaltheatret in 1928 and the Sognsvann Line in 1934. Majorstuhuset gathered station, shops and offices, while the station today distributes all metro lines between the centre and the lines west and north.
majorstuen_tbanestasjon.popupDesc:
Majorstuen was the terminus when the Holmenkollen Line's first section to Slemdal opened on 16 March 1898. The line was Norway's first electric suburban railway and was initially run as a tramway from the city boundary up towards the hills. The first station was simple, with a goods shed, tracks and tram sheds by Slemdalsveien. Smallholdings, small houses and eating places still surrounded the site.

The name Majorstuen is older than the railway. Around 1750 there was a small cottage under the Nedre Blindern farm, associated with an officer nicknamed "the major". The place later developed into an excursion spot and restaurant. When the railway arrived, the old place name also became the name of the station and eventually of the whole district that grew up around it.

The Smestad Line opened in 1912 and made Majorstuen the crossing point of two suburban railways. At the same time the station gained a small timber building in national neo-Baroque style, designed by Kristofer Lange. Passengers could change between the lines, while depots and workshop functions made the area a technical centre for traffic heading west.

The great change came in 1928. The Holmenkollen and Smestad Lines were carried through the 1.92-kilometre Underground Line from Majorstuen via Valkyrie plass to Nationaltheatret. Majorstuen thus ceased to be a terminus and became the gateway between the tunnel section beneath the centre and the open suburban railways. The station was rebuilt, and a new depot was added.

Majorstuhuset was begun in 1930 and completed around the opening of the Sognsvann Line in 1934. The large building gathered ticket sales, waiting rooms, shops, offices and flats above the track area. The station thereby gained an urban frontage towards Kirkeveien and Slemdalsveien, while the tracks, platforms and depots still lay open behind the façade.

The western suburban railways were later connected to the unified metro network. In 1992 Majorstuen received new platform canopies, fencing and a ticket kiosk, among other improvements. Today all metro lines stop here. Trains share tracks through the centre but branch towards Frognerseteren, Kolsås, Østerås, Sognsvann and the Ring. The station of 1898 therefore remains the system's most important distribution point west of the centre.

nationaltheatret_stasjon.name: Nationaltheatret station
nationaltheatret_stasjon.desc: The Nationaltheatret metro station opened in 1928 as the terminus of the Underground Line from Majorstuen. The railway station arrived with the Oslo Tunnel in 1980 and was extended from two to four tracks in 1999 before the airport express service began. Beneath the Palace Park, trains, metro, art and three entrances meet at a hub just 1.4 kilometres from Oslo Central Station.
nationaltheatret_stasjon.popupDesc:
Nationaltheatret holds two stations from different chapters of Oslo's transport history. The metro station opened in 1928 when the Holmenkollen and Smestad Lines were carried from Majorstuen through the 1.92-kilometre Underground Line. It lay beneath the city centre and was the terminus for the western suburban railways, with entrances close to the National Theatre and Karl Johan.

The Underground Line made it possible to bring travellers from the villa and excursion areas in the west right into the city core without filling the streets with more trams. Nationaltheatret kept its role as terminus until the tunnel was extended eastwards to Stortinget in 1987. The western lines were then connected to the eastern metro through the centre.

The railway station opened in 1980 together with the Oslo Tunnel between Oslo Central Station and Skøyen. The tunnel for the first time tied the formerly eastern and western railway systems together beneath the city. Nationaltheatret lies 1.4 kilometres from Oslo S and became a central stop for local and regional trains without a new station building having to be built above ground in the townscape.

The first railway hall had two tracks. Before the opening of Oslo Airport Gardermoen and the airport express service, a new parallel tunnel was blasted. In 1999 the extended station was completed with four tracks, a larger concourse and new public areas. Tracks 1 and 2 lie in the older hall and are mainly used by trains heading west, while tracks 3 and 4 lie in the newer hall and take traffic eastwards.

LPO arkitekter designed the extension. New entrances were established from Ruseløkkveien and Henrik Ibsens gate, in addition to the connection towards the centre. The entrance at Henrik Ibsens gate was later awarded a diploma from the Houen Foundation. Steel, glass and concrete characterise the spaces, and works by Bård Breivik, Anne-Karin Furunes and Katrine Giæver, among others, are integrated into the complex.

Nationaltheatret has three entrances and indoor transfer between railway and both metro directions. Above the station lie the Palace, the Palace Park, the National Theatre and the capital's ceremonial street. Beneath them lies a transport complex built in stages in 1928, 1980 and 1999, where old suburban railways, metro, local trains and airport express services meet without being visible from the street.

olaf_ryes_plass.name: Olaf Ryes plass
olaf_ryes_plass.desc: The municipality bought the open field in 1863, the square was named after officer Olaf Rye in 1864, and the park was laid out in 1890. The Eilert Sundt bust from 1892, the fountain from 1927 and continued use as a local meeting place make several historical layers visible in the same park space.
olaf_ryes_plass.popupDesc: Olaf Ryes plass is the bounded park and square between Markveien, Grüners gate, Thorvald Meyers gate and Sofienberggata. The municipality bought the open field in 1863, named the square after Olaf Rye in 1864 and laid out the park in 1890. Mathias Skeibrok’s bust of social researcher Eilert Sundt was erected in 1892, and the fountain followed in 1927. Parkteatret at number 11 is important neighbouring context, not part of the canonical square surface. Photographs from 1903 and 2009 show historical layers rather than an exact optical before-and-after pair. Dated 2026 programmes document current event use without turning it into a permanent property of the place. The four streets also act as ownership checks: the paths, vegetation, bust and fountain belong to the square narrative, while surrounding façades and businesses remain separate places or neighbouring context.

birkelunden.name: Birkelunden
birkelunden.desc: Birkelunden was laid out in the 1860s as part of Thorvald Meyer's development of Grünerløkka and given free to the municipality in 1882 on condition that the park never be built on. The 16.3-decare park was later reorganised for play and activity, gained today's bandstand in 1926 and several artistic and commemorative traces, and forms part of the far larger Birkelunden cultural environment listed in 2006.
birkelunden.popupDesc:
Birkelunden is a 16.3-decare park in Grünerløkka, bounded by Seilduksgata, Toftes gate, Schleppegrells gate and Thorvald Meyers gate. The park was laid out by the landowner Thorvald Meyer in the 1860s as part of the planning and parcelling out of Grünerløkka. In 1882 Meyer handed Birkelunden over free of charge to the municipal parks department, on condition that the park never be built on.

The park was reorganised in 1916–20 to make room for play, playground equipment and a skating rink. Today's bandstand was built in 1926 to designs by architect Otto Hald following an architectural competition. A water basin was laid out in 1927–28.

The name has also changed form: the park was called Birkelunden from the start, was given the official form Bjerkelunden in 1926, and regained Birkelunden in 1955. The Norwegian Pensioners' Association describes how Jack Johnsen gathered 10–12 pensioners on a bench in Birkelunden, and how 18 people founded Friends in Bjerkelunden in 1937. The City of Oslo moreover describes Birkelunden as an arena for the labour movement's mass rallies in the early twentieth century.

Ørnulf Bast's bronze group Foals was erected in 1953. A bust of Jack Johnsen was raised in 1984, and the park received work on its basin and planting in 1984–86. In 1989 Nils Aas's memorial to Norwegians who fought with the International Brigades in the Spanish Civil War was raised in Birkelunden.

Birkelunden must at the same time be distinguished from the larger Birkelunden cultural environment. The cultural environment was protected on 28 April 2006 following a listing process that began in 1996. The Directorate for Cultural Heritage states that the cultural environment covers about 116 decares and includes the park itself, Grünerløkka school, Paulus Church and 15 blocks with 139 tenement buildings. The 116 decares describe the conservation area around and including the park, not Birkelunden's own park surface of 16.3 decares.

In 2026 the City of Oslo lists the bandstand with power outlets and drinking fountains among the facilities in Birkelunden. The park's own history can be read through its bounded green surface, the reorganisation for play, the bandstand, the history of its name and the memorials, while the tenements, the school and the church belong to the larger cultural environment around it.

akerselva.name: The Akerselva river
akerselva.desc: The Akerselva runs from Lake Maridalsvannet through Nydalen, Sagene and Grünerløkka towards Bjørvika. Around 20 waterfalls powered mills, sawmills, paper factories, spinning mills and workshops. Industry left the river heavily polluted, but the Akerselva Environmental Park was established from 1986, and walking routes, parks and reused factories turned the former production axis into a continuous urban and natural corridor.
akerselva.popupDesc:
The Akerselva carries water from Lake Maridalsvannet through Nydalen, Sagene, Grünerløkka and the city centre towards the fjord. The river course cuts across the strike of the bedrock and forms many bends and around 20 waterfalls. The drops made the river one of Oslo's most important energy sources before electricity. Grain mills are documented from the Middle Ages, and frame saws arrived in the sixteenth century.

Timber, log floating and sawmills created great fortunes in the seventeenth century. Bentse Brug began paper production in 1696 as Norway's first paper mill. From the 1840s came a far larger wave of industry. Nydalens Compagnie, Hjula Weaving Mills, Graah's Spinning Mill, Myrens Workshop, Christiania Spigerverk, Lilleborg Fabriker and numerous smaller businesses built close to the falls. Workers' housing, schools, shops, mission houses and associations grew up around the factories.

The river was at once power source, transport route, sewer and boundary. The first municipal sewage was discharged straight into the water, and industry released chemicals and waste. Salmon, trout and the freshwater pearl mussel disappeared. On a short stretch between Ankerbrua and Marcus Thranes gate there were 25 direct sewage outlets. Factory fences and closed sites moreover made many parts of the riverbank inaccessible.

From the 1980s water quality improved, and fish were released. Discharges nonetheless continued to do great damage. Phosphoric acid killed life below the Idun factories in 1988, sulphuric acid from the Spigerverket killed around 25,000 salmon and trout in 1990, and a chlorine leak from the Oset treatment plant destroyed almost all life in the river in 2011. Midgardsormen, a new sewage system that opened in 2014, reduced discharges during heavy rain.

The Akerselva Environmental Park was established in 1986 on the initiative of environment minister Sissel Rønbeck. The aim was to secure a belt 200–600 metres wide between Maridalsvannet and Vaterland, safeguard the industrial history and open the banks for outdoor life. The 1990 municipal sub-plan gave legal protection to the river space, parks, vegetation and a range of buildings and bridges. Around 240 decares with 31 structures and areas were designated for conservation.

Deindustrialisation made it possible to give the factories new functions.
