deichman_grunerlokka.desc: Deichman Grünerløkka is based at Schous plass and has since 1914 been a district library, reading room and local cultural venue. The branch combines lending and guidance with events, debates and activities. The place's literary significance lies in long-standing public access, not in the memory of one particular writer.
deichman_grunerlokka.popupDesc:
Deichman Grünerløkka opened in 1914 and is based at Schous plass 10. The branch is a district library, not a former main library or a private literary salon. The map point covers the library building and the local institution that has for generations given residents access to books, newspapers, information and workspaces.

The library's fundamental function is to make knowledge and literature available without an obligation to buy. The collection changes with language, media, population composition and reading habits. Lending is therefore only one part of the work; guidance, reading rooms, digital services and help in finding reliable information are equally important public tasks.

The branch also functions as a literary stage and a local meeting place. Readings, conversations, courses and small events can make room for established writers and new voices alike. The programme varies over time, so the place should not be described as though one particular type of event or list of participants were permanent.

The building at Schous plass ties the library to Grünerløkka's urban development. The area has passed through industry, working-class district, immigration, upgrading and commercial pressure. The library's public and functions have changed along with the neighbourhood, while the principle of free public access has provided continuity.

The place must be distinguished from Deichman Bjørvika, which is the main library, and from specialised services such as Biblo Tøyen. The strength of the Grünerløkka branch lies in its closeness to everyday life: it serves a local community and can adapt collections and activities to needs that are not necessarily visible in a central major institution.

On site the user can examine how entrance, collections, noticeboards and workspaces organise a public reading community. The central literary question is not only which books stand on the shelves, but how an institution creates lasting access to language, stories, information and encounters between people with different experiences. The branch's history shows how a district library can both preserve institutional continuity and change its working methods as neighbourhood, media and public needs alter. This delimitation makes it possible to use the place as a source without mixing documented events, later commemorative culture, institutional use and interpretations that require evidence of their own.

kulturkirken_jakob_litteratur.name: Kulturkirken Jakob
kulturkirken_jakob_litteratur.desc: Kulturkirken Jakob at Hausmanns gate 14 is a former church that has served as a cultural venue since 2000. Literature appears here through poetry, readings and cross-disciplinary events. The place is not a writer's memorial, but a room where text meets music, performance and audience.
kulturkirken_jakob_litteratur.popupDesc:
Kulturkirken Jakob lies at Hausmanns gate 14 and is a former church building that has been used as a cultural venue since 2000. Literature is one part of the activity, alongside music, performing arts and other events. The map point covers the building and its cultural use, not a permanent literary exhibition or one particular body of work.

The church interior gives readings and poetry particular acoustic and visual conditions. Height, reverberation, light and the placing of the audience affect how the voice is perceived. A text usually read in silence can become collective and bodily when performed. The staged space therefore helps create meaning.

The conversion from church to cultural centre is an example of a change of function. The building's religious history does not disappear when new activities move in. Architecture, symbols and former rituals still form a frame around concerts and literary events. The programming can use, challenge or try to soften that inheritance.

The place must be distinguished from the House of Literature, an institution built around literary public life through a continuous programme, and from the libraries, which manage collections and free access to information. Kulturkirken is first and foremost a venue. Literature's presence varies with the events calendar and must not be presented as permanent daily activity.

Cross-disciplinary productions can combine poem, music, image and performance. The text is then not merely content but material within a composite work. That opens new entrances to literature, while the adaptation must be distinguished from the original work's wording, genre and historical context.

On site the user can observe how a former church organises audience and stage. A good question is how the room changes a reading: what happens to pace, intimacy and authority when the text sounds in monumental architecture? Kulturkirken Jakob shows that literary public life is also created through acoustics, programming choices, ticketing and temporary encounters. The programme history must be examined through archives, posters and organiser sources if specific writers or performances are to be tied to the building. The general venue identity is stable, but each literary encounter is temporary and cannot be inferred merely from the premises being called a cultural church.

norli_universitetsgata.name: Norli Universitetsgata
norli_universitetsgata.desc: Norli Universitetsgata is a central bookshop at Universitetsgata 22–24, represented by the shop's named point because the address covers several entrances. The place ties literature to commerce, selection and events. Historical continuity must be documented precisely and not inferred automatically from the age of the chain or the premises.
norli_universitetsgata.popupDesc:
Norli Universitetsgata is based at Universitetsgata 22–24. Because the address covers several official points, History GO uses the shop's named map object as its physical anchor. The place is an active bookshop in the city centre, not a library, writer's home or archive. Its literary role rests on sales, selection, guidance and events.

The bookshop connects the reader to publishers, distributors and a commercial market. The shelves show editorial choices and economic conditions alike: storage space, purchasing agreements, topicality and demand affect which books become visible. A large range does not mean that all languages, genres or small publishers receive equal space.

Staff can make the market more accessible through recommendations and expertise. Events, signings and launches create encounters between authors and readers, but also form part of marketing. The bookshop's public role is therefore real, while the business depends on sales and profitable operation.

Claims that the place is among the city's oldest or has been a continuous gathering point since the nineteenth century must be tied to documented activity, name, address and ownership. A bookshop chain, a set of premises and a particular branch can have different historical timelines. The year given in a place file should not be used as proof on its own.

The location near the university, theatres and central cultural institutions gives an audience of students, staff, tourists and city users. That proximity does not, however, automatically explain the shop's range or historical significance. Such matters must be examined through catalogues, advertisements, photographs, accounts and the institution's own archives.

On site the user can see how books are grouped, profiled and priced. A good question is who decides what meets the customer first. Norli Universitetsgata shows that literary circulation does not stop when the manuscript becomes a book; it continues through distribution, shop space, staff, marketing and the reader's choice among many competing titles. The shop can also be compared with online retail and digital reading platforms. The physical space gives immediate eye contact with covers, tables and categories, while algorithmic shops order visibility in other ways. Both systems shape the discovery of literature and should be examined critically.

sigrid_undset_statue.name: The Sigrid Undset statue
sigrid_undset_statue.desc: The Sigrid Undset sculpture in Stensparken, made by Kjersti Wexelsen Goksøyr and unveiled in 1991, honours the writer who received the Nobel Prize in Literature. The monument is documented in the park, but the current coordinate lacks unambiguous plinth verification and must not be presented as millimetre-precise. The map point is provisionally an approximate display anchor.
sigrid_undset_statue.popupDesc:
The Sigrid Undset statue stands in Stensparken and was unveiled in 1991. The sculpture is by Kjersti Wexelsen Goksøyr and honours the writer and Nobel laureate Sigrid Undset. Municipal sources document the monument in the park, but the current map coordinate lacks unambiguous plinth verification and should be treated as approximate.

Undset is known particularly for historical novels, among them the trilogy about Kristin Lavransdatter, but she also wrote contemporary novels, short stories, essays and biographical texts. She received the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1928. Her work examines faith, responsibility, desire, family and room for action across historical periods.

A monument can turn an extensive body of work into one recognisable portrait. The artist's choice of body, face, clothing and posture affects how the writer is remembered. The sculpture does not directly show the medieval research, the narrative technique or the conflicts within the works. It is a later visual interpretation of literary significance.

The placing in Stensparken gives the memorial an everyday green urban space rather than a museum setting. Connections to places where Undset lived or moved must be documented separately; proximity alone does not prove that the park was a central workplace. The monument's documented identity must be kept apart from biographical assumptions about the area.

The unveiling in 1991 also says something about posterity's canon. Undset's status as a Nobel laureate gives strong institutional authority, but the monument still selects one person among many writers. A critical reading can examine how gender, prize status, national history and sculpture policy affect who becomes visible.

On site the user can look for the sculpture without trusting the map point's precision blindly, and then compare the monument with Undset's own texts. A good question is what the sculpture emphasises and what it leaves out. The memorial opens literary history, but scholarly understanding requires the works, the biography and source criticism. The coordinate discrepancy should be used pedagogically, not hidden. A digital map can give an impression of accuracy that the sources do not support. The user must therefore distinguish between the securely documented park, the securely identified monument and the provisional point that merely aids the search. The uncertainty is to be corrected in a separate coordinate exercise with an inspectable source.

ruth_maier_minne.name: The Ruth Maier memorial
ruth_maier_minne.desc: The stumbling stone at Dalsbergstien 3 commemorates Ruth Maier, the Austrian Jewish refugee, diarist and poet who was deported from Norway and killed at Auschwitz in 1942. The memorial ties her own writing to her last Oslo address, without reducing her life to the arrest and the murder.
ruth_maier_minne.popupDesc:
The Ruth Maier memorial is a stumbling stone at Dalsbergstien 3, the address where she lived before her arrest and deportation in November 1942. The map point is a documented address anchor, not a claim of millimetre-precise placement of the stone. The memorial lies in the pavement and meets passers-by in an ordinary residential environment.

Ruth Maier came to Norway as a Jewish refugee from Austria. She wrote diaries, poems and letters and developed a close friendship with the poet Gunvor Hofmo. The texts document thoughts, relationships, artistic ambitions and the experience of exile. They make her visible as a writing person, not merely as a victim in a statistic.

She was arrested by Norwegian authorities, deported on the Donau and killed at Auschwitz. The memorial must state this clearly, but without sensationalism or unnecessary detail. Responsibility and the course of events must rest on documented sources. Formulations that turn the deportation into an abstract European tragedy can obscure the Norwegian complicity.

The stumbling stone follows a commemorative principle in which the name is returned to the person's last freely chosen home. The small metal plate competes with the pace of the city and can be overlooked, worn down or covered. It is precisely this everyday placing that makes the history hard to isolate as something that only happened elsewhere.

The diaries were published after her death and are edited material. The reader must distinguish between the original entry, later selection, translation, publication and public reception. A private document becomes literature and historical source through a chain of preservation and editorial choices.

On site the user can read the name and the dates and then seek out Maier's own texts. A good question is how a brief memorial in the pavement can open a whole life without closing it in the role of victim. The stumbling stone connects literature, biography, persecution and local responsibility at one concrete address. The memorial also demands respect for the fact that the address remains part of other people's everyday lives. Visits should take place from the public pavement without turning the home into a sight. An ethical reading of the place combines attention, documentation and restraint towards both the dead and today's residents.

alf_proysen_statue_nittedal.name: Alf Prøysen Statue – Nittedal Cultural Center
alf_proysen_statue_nittedal.desc: Sivert Donali's bronze monument of Alf Prøysen. The statue previously stood by Oslo Spektrum and was moved to Nittedal Cultural Center in 2019.
alf_proysen_statue_nittedal.popupDesc: This large bronze figure of Alf Prøysen, created by Sivert Donali, was unveiled in Brumunddal in 2014 during the marking of Prøysen's centenary. It honors Prøysen in the heart of Ringsaker and stands as a clear symbol of his importance to Norwegian culture as both lyricist and storyteller. The statue stood for many years by Oslo Spektrum, but in 2019 it was moved to Nittedal Cultural Center, where it also marks the center's role as an active hub for cultural outreach and community life.

proysenhuset_rudshogda.name: Prøysen House – Rudshøgda
proysenhuset_rudshogda.desc: The cultural center built by Alf Prøysen's childhood home in Rudshøgda, a national dissemination center for his life and works.
proysenhuset_rudshogda.popupDesc: Prøysen House is located by Alf Prøysen's childhood home in Rudshøgda and serves as a living center for sharing his songs, stories, and cultural heritage. The area around the house includes paths, installations, and settings that recreate the world Prøysen grew up in and connect visitors directly to the landscape that shaped his artistic work.

inger_hagerups_plass.name: Inger Hagerups plass
inger_hagerups_plass.desc: Inger Hagerups plass is the turning circle at the end of Hagapynten in Haugerud, named after the poet who lived in the area for nearly forty years. The place marks a real local connection, but is above all a named residential and everyday space, not a museum or a writer's house.
inger_hagerups_plass.popupDesc:
Inger Hagerups plass lies at the end of Hagapynten in Haugerud and functions as a turning circle and address area. It is named after the poet Inger Hagerup, who lived in the district for nearly forty years. The map point covers the documented square, not an arbitrary neighbouring address or a preserved writer's home open to the public.

Hagerup wrote poetry for adults, poems for children, radio plays and translations. She could combine precise rhythm and accessible language with political seriousness, love, unrest and play. The local naming gives an entrance to this broad body of work, but the square does not represent one particular poem or a single literary period.

The connection between person and place is stronger than at a square that has merely been given a famous name. Hagerup lived much of her adult life in Haugerud, apart from the war years in Sweden, and later moved to sheltered housing at Romsås. All the same, concrete claims about her writing work must be supported by biographical sources.

A place name works through everyday use. Residents, visitors, post, maps and transport repeat the name even when the writing is not discussed. In this way literary history becomes part of local orientation. At the same time the area acquires meanings of its own through residential life, traffic, neighbourliness and changes that have nothing to do with Hagerup.

The square also shows how literary commemorative culture can be moved out of the centre. Many national monuments stand close to institutions of power and culture, while Hagerup's name is anchored in an outer city area where she actually lived. That gives local identity, but must not be used to turn all of Haugerud into a backdrop for one person.

On site the user can examine signage, buildings and the function as a turning circle. A good question is what the name does to the experience of an ordinary residential space. Inger Hagerups plass shows that literary geography consists not only of museums and statues, but also of everyday places where biography, local environment and collective memory meet. The naming year of 1999 belongs to commemorative culture, not to the beginning of Hagerup's relationship with Haugerud. By distinguishing between period of residence, naming decision and present-day use, the place can give precise knowledge both about a writer's biography and about how a local community chooses to honour a former neighbour.

oscar_braaten_statuen.name: The Oskar Braaten bust
oscar_braaten_statuen.desc: The bronze bust of Oskar Braaten stands by Beierbrua in the landscape he depicted along the Akerselva. Arne Durban's monument was unveiled in 1961 and ties the writer's working-class stories to a concrete industrial setting. The bust is a later memorial, not evidence that particular scenes played out at the plinth.
oscar_braaten_statuen.popupDesc:
The Oskar Braaten bust stands by Beierbrua over the Akerselva. The bronze portrait is by Arne Durban and was unveiled in 1961. The map point covers the artwork itself, not an earlier misplaced point in Glads vei. The memorial lies in a landscape closely tied to Braaten's depictions of working-class environments.

Braaten wrote about factory girls, workers, families and everyday life on the east side. The play Ungen is among his best-known works, but his writing also includes novels, short stories and other plays. He turned social conflicts and spoken idiom into literary material, though the texts cannot be treated as direct photographs of reality.

The placing by the river gives the monument a strong geographical frame. Factories, housing, bridges and work routes along the Akerselva shaped the environments Braaten knew. All the same, one must distinguish between the general industrial landscape, documented biographical places and fictional addresses or characters in the works.

The bust is an interpretation by posterity. Face, posture, plinth and placement make the writer a public representative for a whole milieu. That can make working-class literature visible, but can also gather many people's experiences into one famous man. The monument must therefore be read together with sources about both the artwork and the environments it is meant to commemorate.

Hønse-Lovisa's house lies nearby and shows a different kind of connection between Braaten and the place. There a real workers' dwelling has been named through fiction and film. The bust, by contrast, is an explicit memorial. The two points should be compared without confusing character, writer, building and monument.

On site the user can study the view towards the river and ask why the bust stands precisely here. The scholarly point is how literary geography is made from text, historical landscape and later commemorative culture alike. The Braaten bust gives an entrance to working-class history, but requires reading beyond the heroic portrait. The portrait can moreover be compared with Braaten's own descriptions of people along the river. Where the bust gathers identity into one face, the texts distribute attention among many characters, voices and social positions. The difference shows what monument and narrative can each do in their own way.

alexander_kiellands_plass.name: Alexander Kiellands plass
alexander_kiellands_plass.desc: Alexander Kiellands plass received the writer's name in 1914 and was laid out as a park in 1918. The place is an everyday urban space, not a Kielland museum: the literary connection lies in the name and in how the city uses a writer to give identity to a public meeting place.
alexander_kiellands_plass.popupDesc:
Alexander Kiellands plass is the park between Uelands gate, Maridalsveien and Waldemar Thranes gate. The area was named after the writer Alexander L. Kielland in 1914 and laid out as a park in 1918. The map point represents the whole park area, not one statue, building or address along its edge.

Kielland was a novelist, short-story writer, dramatist and social critic, known for sharp depictions of power, double standards, schooling and the bourgeoisie. The square nonetheless does not document that he lived or wrote here. The literary link is the naming decision: the city made the writer part of its public geography.

Naming is a form of canon-making. When a writer's name is repeated on signs, stops, maps and in everyday speech, literary history becomes embedded in daily life. Many who use the park may know the name better as a place than as a writer. That shows how commemorative culture can survive independently of active reading.

The park also has its own history as a local meeting place. Play, catering, passage, lingering and neighbourhood life give the area meanings that do not come from Kielland's books. A literary name does not control how the place is used. Urban space develops through plans, maintenance, conflicts and daily routines.

The place must therefore be distinguished from a writer's museum, a workplace and a monument. What exists here is first and foremost a named public space. Kielland's life and work must be examined through books, archives and biographical sources, while the park can be used to study how the city chooses who is to be visible in the street network.

On site the user can read the name signs, follow the park's boundaries and observe today's use. A good question is what happens when a critical body of writing becomes a stable place name. The name honours Kielland, but the square also shows how literary fame is transformed into practical orientation and local belonging. The park's literary value therefore lies not in authentic traces of Kielland's life, but in the name's lasting place in the city's orientation and collective memory. This delimitation makes it possible to use the place as a source without mixing documented events, later commemorative culture, institutional use and interpretations that require evidence of their own.

vg_huset.name: The VG building
vg_huset.desc: The VG building at Akersgata 55 is an active newsroom anchor for a paper founded in 1945 and later developed into a continuous digital news operation. Reporters, desk, photography, video, sport and publishing systems come together here. The place turns tabloid prioritisation, front-page work, push alerts and the attention economy into concrete working processes.
vg_huset.popupDesc:
The VG building lies at Akersgata 55, in the middle of Norway's historic newspaper street. This is an active newsroom building where news is assessed, investigated, edited and published around the clock. Reporters, desk staff, photographers, video journalists, duty editors and development teams work in parallel streams towards web, mobile and other surfaces.

VG was founded in 1945, but today's media work is shaped by the shift from printed newspaper to continuous digital publishing. The front page is no longer a single sheet of paper each morning. The web front, push alerts, live studio, video clips and running updates can change many times while a story develops.

Tabloid journalism is about clear prioritisation, compression and appeal, but the word does not automatically describe poor journalism. Headlines, images and angles must quickly explain why a story matters. At the same time, competition for attention can reward conflict, emotion and a focus on individuals. Editorial checking routines must therefore work under time pressure.

The place is also part of a larger press cluster. Aftenposten's historic main address at number 51 and Dagbladet's former newspaper building at number 49 have canonical records of their own. The proximity shows a long press history, but the buildings, periods and editorial identities must not be merged into one general "Akersgata place".

History GO uses Akersgata 55 as the VG building's concrete address anchor. The record does not represent every location the paper has used since 1945, the whole corporate group around the newsroom, or every story VG publishes. The façade is the entrance to a working environment; on its own it says little about the quality of any individual journalistic decision.

Observe from the public street and compare the building with the historic press addresses around it. Then examine a VG front page over time: which stories move up or down, which images are swapped, and when is a push alert sent? In this way agenda-setting power becomes visible as a series of editorial choices. Attention is a scarce resource, but the public is not passive; readers click, share, criticise and influence further prioritisation. Measurements of traffic and response give the newsroom rapid knowledge of its audience, but numbers alone do not explain why a story matters. Journalistic judgement must still weigh interest against documentation, harm and public value.

salt.name: SALT
salt.desc: SALT at Langkaia is a cultural venue established in 2014, built around temporary timber structures, stages, food service and sauna culture by the fjord. Concerts, club nights, talks and events make the site a flexible urban space in Oslo where the music programme, social use and temporary architecture work together.
salt.popupDesc:
SALT lies at Langkaia, between the city centre, the Opera House and Akershus Fortress, and was established in 2014. The venue consists of several temporary structures and programming surfaces close to the fjord. History Go uses the actual grounds of the named cultural venue as its map anchor, not Havnelageret or the whole of Langkaia.

Music is one of several interwoven functions. Concerts, club nights, talks, art, food service and sauna culture may use the same outdoor and indoor spaces at different times. This mixture makes the venue flexible, but the presentation should not reduce the place to sauna, food or nightlife alone.

Temporary architecture does not mean an absence of infrastructure. Stages need power, sound, lighting, rigging points, audience flow, safety and weather protection. Movable or simple structures can be adapted faster than permanent buildings, but they demand continuous maintenance and planning for wind, cold, precipitation and neighbours.

The fjord setting affects both atmosphere and production. Views, weather, boat traffic and proximity to central thoroughfares make the cultural activity visible to passers-by. At the same time, sound carries across water and open surfaces. Programming, opening hours and technical solutions must therefore take a wider urban environment into account.

History Go treats SALT as a cultural venue in its own right, separate from the Opera House, Akershus Fortress and the general Fjord City sites around it. The year 2014 refers to the establishment of the project, not the erection of a single permanent building. Changes to tents, stages and installations are part of the site's identity.

Observe from public areas how timber structures, passages and stages organise movement towards the water. Respect access and event boundaries. Compare SALT with a permanent concert building: temporariness can open room for experiment, but it also creates uncertainty about longevity, investment and the use of public urban ground. The venue's history shows how a time-limited project can acquire lasting cultural significance. Programme archives can also reveal whether the flexibility actually produces genre diversity, or whether certain activities dominate. There is a difference between architectural impermanence and institutional continuity: structures can be replaced while organiser expertise, audience habits and the place name become steadily more established in the city's wider cultural life over time.

det_norske_teatret.name: Det Norske Teatret
det_norske_teatret.desc: A theatre and music venue in central Oslo, central to Norwegian performing arts and musical productions.
det_norske_teatret.popupDesc: Det Norske Teatret is a central theatrical institution in Oslo with a distinct profile in Nynorsk performing arts. The building houses large productions, smaller stages and a steady flow of audiences through the city centre across the year. Here language policy, choice of repertoire and stage-technical production come together in daily institutional operation, not only in anniversary narratives. On this site the relationship between language, power and cultural work becomes concrete in a working theatre.

blaa.name: Blå
blaa.desc: Blå at Brenneriveien 9C is a club and concert venue by the Akerselva river, established in 1998 and particularly important for jazz, improvisation, electronica and alternative club culture. The riverside space, the backyard and the indoor stage form a single music environment where programming, audience and an industrial urban landscape shape one another.
blaa.popupDesc:
Blå is at Brenneriveien 9C, close to the Akerselva river, and was established in 1998. History Go uses the named venue as its precise anchor, not the Vulkan area, the river course or the whole of Brenneriveien. The venue has a clear identity of its own within a larger cultural and industrial environment.

The programming profile is associated above all with jazz, improvisation, electronica, club music and alternative expression. Such a profile does not arise automatically from genre labels. Booking, technical expertise, financial risk, artist networks and audience trust determine which concerts can actually take place and which scenes are able to develop.

The physical setting is part of the experience. The riverside space, the backyard, the entrance and the indoor stage are used together, but they are not the same place as the Akerselva as a nature and city route. Sound, queues, weather and movement between outdoors and indoors shape how an evening is organised.

Blå also functions as social infrastructure. Musicians, promoters, technicians, DJs and audiences meet across projects and genres. Small and mid-sized venues can make room for improvisation, unfinished expression and artistic risk that is harder to test in the largest concert halls.

The year 1998 refers to the establishment of the venue, not the construction year of the whole complex. Food service and nightlife are part of the operation, but they should not replace the music history. The record represents this specific venue and its programming culture, not every business in the area or every event along the river.

Observe from public areas how the entrance, the backyard and the riverbank create transitions between urban space and concert space. Compare Blå with Rockefeller and John Dee: different capacity, acoustics, booking and audience culture give different musical possibilities. The place shows that live culture is sound, labour, economics, networks and belonging all at once. Club nights also create informal spaces for learning, where audiences discover artists and musicians hear each other's work. A concert programme is a historical document as well: over time, posters, artist lists and recurring club concepts can show which genres grew, met or disappeared from Oslo's nightlife, and how audiences found their way to this place.

rockefeller.name: Rockefeller Music Hall
rockefeller.desc: Rockefeller Music Hall at Mariboes gate 5B is a central concert venue established in 1986. The hall fills the space between intimate clubs and the largest arenas, and through a continuous Norwegian and international programme it has become an important institution for touring, audience building and popular music history in Oslo.
rockefeller.popupDesc:
Rockefeller Music Hall is at Mariboes gate 5B and opened in 1986. Across several decades the venue has run a dense programme of Norwegian and international artists. History Go uses the main hall as its precise anchor, not the whole block or every business connected to the same promoter environment.

Its capacity places Rockefeller between intimate club venues and the largest halls. This middle scale matters in the touring economy: artists can reach a large audience without the production demands of an arena, while the promoter still has to handle extensive sound, lighting, security, staffing and ticket logistics.

A concert evening rests on a long chain of work. Booking, contracts, promotion, transport, rigging, soundcheck, security, food service and load-out must be coordinated before and after the performance itself. The audience sees the stage, but the institution's continuity depends on the skilled work that makes repeated productions possible.

Rockefeller is therefore also an archive of Oslo's popular music history. Programme posters, ticket data, reviews and audience memories can show which genres, artists and touring routes have found room over time. A single famous concert moment nevertheless does not represent the institution's full significance.

John Dee at number 5A is a separate, smaller venue with a different sense of space and programming function. Sentrum Scene is a larger city-centre arena with different audience flows and set-ups. Close organisational or geographical connection does not mean the three venues should be merged into one marker.

Observe from the public street how the entrance, queuing zones and goods access are organised in a dense city-centre block. Compare the programme with smaller and larger venues: capacity affects artist selection, ticket economics and the audience experience. Rockefeller shows how music history is created through artistic expression, professional labour, commercial risk and repeated urban use alike. An established venue can be conservative and innovative at the same time: continuity provides resources and an audience, while booking choices decide whether new expression actually gets through. Audience habits matter too: repeat visits, prior knowledge and expectations shape how a venue is perceived. Institutional history must therefore be read across many seasons, not only through anniversaries and sold-out nights or individual artists' breakthroughs on this particular Oslo stage.

john_dee.name: John Dee
john_dee.desc: John Dee at Mariboes gate 5A is an intimate club and concert venue attached to the Rockefeller environment, established in 1997. The smaller scale creates close contact between artist and audience and makes the venue important for new bands, narrower expression and tours that do not require a larger room.
john_dee.popupDesc:
John Dee is at Mariboes gate 5A and was established in 1997. It is the smaller venue in the environment around Rockefeller, but it has its own entrance, sense of space and programming profile. Shared operation and infrastructure do not make the room merely a space inside Rockefeller Music Hall.

The intimate capacity changes the concert. The distance between stage and audience is short, reactions register quickly, and small differences in sound level, lighting and positioning can affect the whole experience. The audience becomes not just a crowd, but a visible and audible part of the performance.

John Dee is often used by new artists, narrower genres and established names who want a smaller format. That does not mean the venue is merely a step on the way to something bigger. Some forms of expression work best at club scale, and artistic significance cannot be measured directly in tickets sold.

The operating economics also differ from larger halls. Capacity, ticket price, staffing, technical production and touring costs have to be balanced differently. A small venue can reduce certain costs, but it has fewer tickets to spread them across and less room for financial error.

History Go models John Dee and Rockefeller as separate canonical places. Numbers 5A and 5B lie very close together and belong to the same venue ecosystem, but the rooms differ in scale, address and audience experience. Sentrum Scene is again a larger arena with different logistics and a different programming function.

Look at the entrances and the building's organisation from the public street, and compare how audience queues, deliveries and artist access have to be handled. This is an active workplace, so access boundaries must be respected. John Dee shows that a smaller venue is not just a reduced grand hall, but a musical form of its own. Closeness can produce a stronger response, but it also makes greater demands on dynamics, sound control and audience behaviour. Concert archives and programme posters can also show how alternative scenes build continuity through many small nights, not only through occasional sold-out highlights and names.

sentrum_scene.name: Sentrum Scene
sentrum_scene.desc: Sentrum Scene at Arbeidersamfunnets plass 1 is a large concert and event venue established in 1992. The hall fills the level between club venues and the largest arenas, with flexible standing and seated configurations. Its location, capacity and broad programme make the place central to Oslo's touring and audience logistics.
sentrum_scene.popupDesc:
Sentrum Scene is at Arbeidersamfunnets plass 1 and was established as a concert venue in 1992. The hall is larger than John Dee and Rockefeller, but smaller than the city's biggest arenas. History Go uses the specific hall and address as its anchor, not the whole square or the city-centre area.

Capacity affects which productions fit. Standing concerts can gather a dense and energetic audience, while a seated set-up changes sightlines, movement and atmosphere. Stage, dressing rooms, bars, escape routes and technical zones must be adaptable to different artists and event types.

The central location is part of the venue's function. Audiences arrive from Torggata, public transport hubs and the surrounding city-centre streets. Large arrivals and rapid departures have to be handled without bringing the whole urban space to a halt. Queues, security and timing therefore affect both the concert experience and the neighbours.

The programme spans genres and may also include other stage events. Breadth does not mean that all productions are alike. Sound levels, set design, audience culture and economics vary, and the promoter has to translate a tour's technical requirements into the building's concrete possibilities.

Sentrum Scene is a canonical identity in its own right. Rockefeller and John Dee are nearby and may belong to the same promoter and touring environment, but they have different addresses, sizes and spatial qualities. Organisational connections should not erase the differences between the physical venues.

Observe from public areas how audience queues, deliveries and the entrance are distributed around the building. Compare a concert poster with the set-up the event requires. Sentrum Scene shows that live music is not only about the artist and the song, but about capacity, logistics, safety, economics and public transport. A larger hall also changes the relationship between audience and artist: distance, screens, lighting and shared reactions become more important in creating closeness. Historical programme listings can show how the venue's role shifts with the touring market, genre trends and audience expectations. Flexibility is therefore not just furnishing, but an institutional ability to handle very different productions without the place losing its distinct local identity as a music venue.

oslo_gassverk.name: Oslo Gasworks
oslo_gassverk.desc: Supplied the city with gas for lighting and heating from 1858 — a symbol of industrialization and modernity.
oslo_gassverk.popupDesc:
Oslo Gasworks in Grønland was the core of the city’s gas supply from the mid-19th century. From here, energy went to street lighting, industry, and households before electricity took over.

In History Go, the site is important because it shows how technical infrastructure and energy systems made industrialization possible, and how such facilities changed work, urban growth, and everyday life.

havnelageret.name: Oslo Havnelager
havnelageret.desc: Oslo Havnelager organised large-scale goods flow between ships, quay, warehouse and city in a building of roughly 27,000 m². The site shows storage capacity, foundation work and supply power, but also how heavy port infrastructure can be reshaped into a modern office and service product.
havnelageret.popupDesc:
Oslo Havnelager was built in 1916–1920 as a very large warehouse building at Langkaia. Some 27,000 m², direct proximity to the quay and extensive foundations of 1,550 long concrete piles made it possible to organise goods on a large scale on demanding harbour ground. The same qualities made the building strategic as a materiel depot during the war.

In 1982–1985 the building was modernised and converted into offices. Later changes of ownership, upgrades and tenant fit-outs have carried that conversion forward. Today Langkaia 1 is marketed as a full-service building with offices, reception, canteen, meeting rooms and a gym. Havnelageret can therefore be used to analyse capacity, supply risk, change of use, the office market, space efficiency and investment across the building's life cycle.

The professional quiz questions distinguish documented facts from explicit scenarios. Calculations of floor area, pile quantity, storage capacity and return are learning exercises with visible assumptions, not new historical claims.

tollbukaia.name: Tollbukaia
tollbukaia.desc: Oslo’s historic customs area — a meeting point for ships, trade, and control at the harbor.
tollbukaia.popupDesc: For more than a hundred years, Tollbukaia was one of Oslo’s most central harbor locations for customs, control, and the flow of goods. Ships from Norway and abroad met here, and the area functioned as a link between maritime transport, trade, and the city’s growing business life. The quay is a concrete reminder of how Oslo was shaped by imports, exports, and maritime connections — an industrial hub that connected the city to the world.

oslo_posthus.name: Oslo Posthus
oslo_posthus.desc: Oslo Posthus was the main terminal of the capital's postal system, bringing sorting, dispatch, public services and administration together. The site shows how transport networks, division of labour and terminal capacity were later succeeded by a capital-intensive conversion into housing, commercial space and public-facing functions.
oslo_posthus.popupDesc:
The main post office at Dronningens gate 15 opened in 1924 and was the Postal Service's main terminal in the Oslo postal district until 1975. The building gathered sorting, dispatch, public services and administration, and linked the city to shifting transport networks from steamships and railways to modern distribution. After the terminal period, a post office, a directorate and a museum continued until 2004, so the transition happened in stages.

Linstow bought the Posthus block in 1999 for 275 million kroner. The conversion had to take account of the façades, the postal dispatch hall and the staircases, while the block gained 211 homes, roughly 7,000 m² of commercial space and new public-facing functions. The site therefore offers concrete material for capacity analysis, project economics, financing, mixed use, portfolio strategy and tenant mix.

The professional part of the quiz uses only documented claims about the place as its starting point. All new financial and capacity calculations are clearly stated scenarios in NOK and should be assessed with their assumptions, uncertainty and the limits of what can be concluded.

telegrafbygningen.name: Telegrafbygningen
telegrafbygningen.desc: The Telegraph Building brought the country's telegraph and telephone connections together in one large system of work and technology. The site shows information flow, manual telephone operation and automation, and also how critical infrastructure was later reshaped into offices and public-facing business.
telegrafbygningen.popupDesc:
The Telegraph Building was erected for the Telegraph Service in 1916–1924 and served as the main exchange and administrative building for telegraphy and telephony. Close to a thousand female telephone operators worked at the exchanges during the occupation, and the building shows how labour-intensive early telecommunications were. The annexe with an automatic exchange from 1966 marks the shift towards higher technical capacity and fewer manual connections.

The 2019–2021 refurbishment covered a whole block complex of 16,670 m². Historical qualities were combined with offices, shops, food service and events. The site can therefore be used to examine project economics, capacity management, internal control, property value and how a formerly society-critical infrastructure acquires a new business model.

The quiz's first fourteen questions provide ordinary knowledge of the place. After that the player works with documented conditions, explicit NOK scenarios, calculations and professional decisions, without confusing educational scenarios with historical facts.

vinmonopolet_lager.name: Vinmonopolet Central Warehouse
vinmonopolet_lager.desc: Built in 1930 in a functionalist style — an expression of state control of trade and production.
vinmonopolet_lager.popupDesc: Vinmonopolet’s central facility was built at Hasle in 1933 as a functionalist bottling and warehouse building designed by Otto Valentin Juell and Otto Legaard Scheen. The following year, they received the Houen Diploma for the work. The main building covers 10 decares, is built in iron and brick, and is regarded as a major work of Norwegian functionalism. At opening, the facility was the largest industrial building in the Nordic region, with modern production, storage, bottling, and dispatch of spirits. During the war, the German occupation authorities seized parts of the area for storage. Arcus took over operations in 1996 and moved out in 2011. The facility was protected in 2011 and later converted into housing and the Vinslottet shopping center, opened in 2019.

nrk_huset_marienlyst.name: The NRK building at Marienlyst
nrk_huset_marienlyst.desc: The NRK building at Marienlyst is a historic and active broadcasting complex with studios, newsrooms, control rooms and technical infrastructure for radio, television and digital platforms. The place has gathered Norwegian public service broadcasting across several generations and shows how journalism, programme production, archives, set design and distribution must be coordinated physically.
nrk_huset_marienlyst.popupDesc:
NRK's complex at Marienlyst is a large production environment, not a single studio hall. The address Bjørnstjerne Bjørnsons plass 1 gathers buildings and functions developed over several periods. Radio, television and later digital publishing formats have placed different demands on space, technology, security and workflow.

Broadcasting makes media production particularly dependent on coordination. Journalists, presenters, producers, photographers, sound staff, lighting designers, editors, set designers and technicians must work towards precise transmission times. Control rooms and studios connect human decisions to cameras, microphones, archive systems and distribution networks.

Marienlyst has been a central physical anchor for Norwegian public service broadcasting across several generations. News, cultural programmes, entertainment, drama, radio and live broadcasts have been produced here. That does not mean all NRK content comes from this address; regional offices, external productions and recordings elsewhere are a fundamental part of the institution.

Public service broadcasting also entails a public mandate. Programme choices, language, accessibility, emergency preparedness and coverage of the whole country must be weighed against different audience needs. The building makes parts of this work physically visible, but editorial credibility is created through source work, checking routines and open discussion, not through the institution's size alone.

The year 1938 marks the early development of the broadcasting complex at Marienlyst and must not be read as the construction year of all of today's building parts. Conversions, technological shifts and new forms of production have laid several time layers over the site. History GO uses the main address as a combined anchor for the complex, not as a coordinate for each studio.

This is a workplace with restricted access. Observe from public areas and note how the complex differs from an ordinary office building: entrances, technical zones, transport and building volumes reveal production needs. Compare radio's aural public sphere, television's visual staging and the web's continuous publishing. Marienlyst shows that "the broadcast" always has a material reverse side. Archives and the reuse of older recordings give the complex an additional dimension of time. Production is not only about live transmission, but also about storing, retrieving and setting earlier sound and images into new contexts within a national media history.

jernbaneverkstedet_lodalen.name: Lodalen Railway Workshop
jernbaneverkstedet_lodalen.desc: Maintenance workshop from the 1890s — the lifeline of train traffic in the Oslo area.
jernbaneverkstedet_lodalen.popupDesc: Since the 1890s, Lodalen Railway Workshop has been one of Norway’s most central facilities for operating and maintaining trains. Locomotives and carriages were repaired, modernized, and prepared for service here, and the workshop functioned as a technical backbone for rail traffic in the capital region. The area is a key part of industrial and transport history along the east side of the city.

grunnlovsbygget_bankplassen.name: The Old Norges Bank
grunnlovsbygget_bankplassen.desc: Erected in 1828 — the country's first central bank and a symbol of economic nation-building.
grunnlovsbygget_bankplassen.popupDesc:
Norges Bank was established in 1816, two years after 1814, with its head office in Trondheim and branches in Christiania among other places. When the necessary silver fund could not be raised through voluntary contributions, the capital was instead secured through compulsory deposits — the so-called silver tax. The Christiania branch got its own building at Bankplassen in 1828, designed by Christian H. Grosch, and the house became one of the important public institutional buildings of the young Norwegian state.

When the head seat of Norges Bank was moved from Trondheim to Christiania in 1897, Grosch's building first served as the head office. The bank then moved on to the new building at Bankplassen 4 in 1906. The house at Bankplassen 3 is also known as the scene of Ole Høiland's famous burglary on New Year's night 1835–1836.

Today the building houses the National Museum – Architecture. The museum opened here in 2008 after restoration and with a new exhibition building designed by Sverre Fehn. The site thus ties together monetary and state building, criminal history and Norwegian architectural history in one and the same building.

akershus_kaier.name: Akershus Quays
akershus_kaier.desc: The artery of trade in old Christiania — goods, fish, coal, and timber arrived here from around the world.
akershus_kaier.popupDesc:
Akershus Quays were a main arena for unloading, transshipment, and shipping of goods to and from Oslo. The quays connected maritime transport to railways, roads, and warehouse operations in the city.

In History Go, the site is important for understanding the harbor as an engine of the urban economy, not just as a waterfront.

akershus_energi.name: Akershus Energy Heating
akershus_energi.desc: Produces district heating and energy for the region—a modern successor to the era of hydropower.
akershus_energi.popupDesc:
Akershus Energy Heating is part of the modern energy supply in the metropolitan region through district heating and technical networks. The facility links energy production to waste, distribution and city operations.

In History Go, the place is important as an example of the city's material foundation: energy as continuous infrastructure.

ovre_foss.name: Øvre Foss – Hjula Weaving Mill
ovre_foss.desc: One of the Nordic region's largest textile plants—founded in 1855, with women's labor and steam engines that shaped Sagene.
ovre_foss.popupDesc:
At Øvre Foss/Hjula, hydropower, textile production and factory labor were gathered on a large scale. The facility is linked both to technological modernization and to the emergence of a dense working-class district in Sagene.

In History Go, the place is used to connect industrial history, labor history and urban transformation along the Akerselva.

oslo_mek.name: Akers mekaniske Verksted
oslo_mek.desc: Akers mekaniske Verksted at Pipervika built ships and machinery on the site that is Aker Brygge today.
oslo_mek.popupDesc: Akers mekaniske Verksted moved to Holmen at Pipervika in 1854 and became one of Oslo's most important production environments for shipbuilding, engines and maritime industry. The old shipyard area is Aker Brygge today. The site shows how heavy industry, seafaring and skilled labour shaped the capital's economy, and how a large production area was later reshaped into offices, retail, food service and city life.

schous_bryggeri.name: Schous Brewery
schous_bryggeri.desc: Schous Brewery traces its official founding to 1821, took Christian Julius Schou's name after his 1837 takeover and moved production to Schousløkken in 1873. Brewing ended in 1981; surviving industrial buildings now form part of a mixed culture, education, hospitality and office quarter.
schous_bryggeri.popupDesc:
Schous Brewery grew from Johannes Thrane's earlier brewery. Jørgen Young took it over in 1821, the official founding year, and Christian Julius Schou bought and modernised it in 1837.

The brewery mastered cold-fermented Bavarian beer in 1843. Production moved to Trondheimsveien 2 in 1873, where brewing, yeast production, storage, bottling and distribution became parts of a large industrial system.

Schous and Frydenlund entered De Sammensluttede Bryggerier in 1962. Production and the Schous brand ended in 1981. Some buildings were demolished, while others were converted for offices, education, culture, rehearsal spaces, restaurants and new small-scale brewing.

ringnes_bryggeri.name: Ringnes Brewery
ringnes_bryggeri.desc: Ringnes & Co. was founded at Thorvald Meyers gate 2 in 1876 by Amund Ringnes, Ellef Ringnes and Axel Heiberg, and production began in 1877. The brewery pioneered cultivated yeast strains in Norway. Production moved to Gjelleråsen in 2001; surviving buildings now house Ringnes offices, a museum and Ringnes Brygghus.
ringnes_bryggeri.popupDesc:
Ringnes & Co. was founded on Grünerløkka in 1876 and began production the following year. Amund Ringnes led brewing and technical operations, while Ellef Ringnes handled the outward-facing business role.

From 1887 to 1890, Olav Johan Sopp led the laboratory. Ringnes became Norway's first brewery to cultivate its own yeast strains and use pure-culture yeast in production.

Production moved to Gjelleråsen in 2001. Much of the factory quarter became Ringnes Park, while surviving brewery buildings gained new uses including offices, a museum and a brewpub.

st_halvard_bryggeri.name: St. Halvard Brewery
st_halvard_bryggeri.desc: Historic brewery at Pilestredet 75C, established as Nora Bryggeri in 1877 and later run as St. Halvards Bryggeri and Nora Mineralvand-Fabrik before its closure in 1918.
st_halvard_bryggeri.popupDesc:
Brewing at Pilestredet 75C began in 1877 as Nora Bryggeri. From 1882 mineral water was also produced under the Nora name, and after several company changes the plant was named St. Halvards Bryggeri og Nora Mineralvandfabrik in 1905. The brewery closed in 1918, when the Nora business moved on to Maridalsveien 3.

History Go models this as the historical brewery site at Pilestredet 75C. The official address point is used as a documented historical place anchor for the address where the business stood, not as a claim that the point is the centre of a preserved 1877 building.

oslo_kornmagasin.name: The Grain Magazine at Akershus Fortress
oslo_kornmagasin.desc: The grain magazine at Akershus Fortress was erected in 1788 as a concrete storage building for grain and provisions. The building was later put into use as a penal labour institution and then became part of Akershus county prison, showing how the same physical complex could shift role from supply infrastructure to penal institution.
oslo_kornmagasin.popupDesc:
The grain magazine at Akershus Fortress is inventory 0008 in the protected fortress complex and is documented as erected in 1788. Its original function was the storage of grain and provisions. In 1820 the building was fitted out as a penal labour institution, and it later became part of Akershus county prison.

In History Go the site is used as a concrete example of how state supply, storage and institutional power could be gathered in the same building environment, and how a building can take on entirely new functions through history.

akershus_slott_bakeriet.name: The Bakery at Akershus
akershus_slott_bakeriet.desc: A state-run bakery that supplied the garrison and townspeople in the 19th century—operated as a craft enterprise.
akershus_slott_bakeriet.popupDesc:
The bakery at Akershus supplied military and civilian environments with bread production at a time when local production was decisive. The site shows the interaction between state needs, craft production and urban distribution.

In History Go, it is used as an example of early business operations at the boundary between institution and market.

oslo_kraftselskap.name: Oslo Lysverker Headquarters
oslo_kraftselskap.desc: Monumental headquarters erected for Oslo Lysverker in 1931, where the city's energy supply gained a distinct administrative and representative base.
oslo_kraftselskap.popupDesc:
Christiania Elektricitetsværk started the city's municipal electricity supply in 1892, with the first power station at Rosenkrantz' gate 14. The undertaking later developed into Oslo Lysverker, and in 1931 the agency gained a new monumental headquarters at Sommerrogata 1.

In History Go this place record represents the headquarters building of 1931 itself, not Oslo Lysverker as an abstract institution, the whole power grid or the first power station of 1892. The building nevertheless makes energy history physically legible: administration, technical control and the city's growing power system were given a distinct architectural address here.

grensen_kjopesenter.name: Grensen – shopping street
grensen_kjopesenter.desc: From colonial goods and manufactured wares to modern shops — the main street of trade since the 1800s.
grensen_kjopesenter.popupDesc:
Grensen has long been a dense commercial street in the city centre, with shops, deliveries and a high flow of customers. The area shows how trade concentrates along central movement axes.

In History Go the site is used to ask about consumption, goods flow and changes in city-centre retail.

vippetangen_fisketorg.name: The Fish Hall at Vippetangen
vippetangen_fisketorg.desc: The large fish hall at Vippetangen is a concrete harbour and industry building for the receipt, sale and distribution of fish. The fish market was moved to Vippetangen in 1905, while today's larger hall was erected in 1932–33 and opened in December 1933.
vippetangen_fisketorg.popupDesc:
The fish market was moved to a new fishing harbour at Vippetangen in 1905. The first fish hall here was later succeeded by today's larger complex, erected in 1932–33 and opened on 9 December 1933. The building brought receipt, processing and wholesale trade in fish together in a modern harbour facility.

In History Go this record represents the Fish Hall at Akershusstranda 23 itself, not the whole of Vippetangen or the historical fishing harbour as an area. The older fish market history is used as prehistory to the specific building.

frysja_industriomrade.name: Frysja Industrial Area
frysja_industriomrade.desc: Hydropower from the Akerselva already drove sawmills and mills here in the 18th century—an active industrial area still today.
frysja_industriomrade.popupDesc:
The Frysja area by the upper Akerselva had early hydropower-based industry with mills and sawmills, later a more mixed business use. The place shows long industrial lines from a production economy to transformed urban land.

In History Go, Frysja is relevant for understanding industrial continuity and restructuring at the city's edge.

norges_varemesse.name: Norges Varemesse – Sjølystsenteret
norges_varemesse.desc: Historical trade fair and exhibition complex at Sjølyst, where Norges Varemesse was based from 1962 until the move to Lillestrøm in 2002.
norges_varemesse.popupDesc:
Norges Varemesse opened Sjølystsenteret, also called Messehallen, at Drammensveien 154 in 1962. For four decades the complex was one of the country's most important meeting places for industry, trade, product launches, public fairs, conferences and large cultural events.

The History Go record represents this specific Oslo site and the period 1962–2002, not the Norges Varemesse foundation across its whole history from 1920, and not today's NOVA Spektrum in Lillestrøm. After the move, Messehallen was demolished, and the former exhibition property was developed as Sjølyststranda. Today's Messepromenaden runs through the area where the complex stood and preserves the trace of the fair's name.

bryn_industriomrade.name: Bryn Industrial Area
bryn_industriomrade.desc: One of the oldest industrial areas in eastern Oslo—factory halls, warehouses and railways in close interaction.
bryn_industriomrade.popupDesc:
Bryn Industrial Area developed as an eastern production and logistics zone close to rail and main roads. Here, factories, warehouses and transport were gathered into an efficient business structure.

In History Go, the area is used to ask how infrastructure determines where industry and labor are located in the city.

gronlikaia.name: Grønlikaia
gronlikaia.desc: Former container and harbor area—a symbol of the city's modern logistics and transport.
gronlikaia.popupDesc:
Grønlikaia was a central container and harbor area in the modern part of the Port of Oslo. The quay represents large-scale logistics, international trade and space-demanding transport infrastructure.

In History Go, the place is important for understanding the tension between port operations, urban development and the transformation of waterfront business land.

myrens_verksted.name: Myrens Workshop
myrens_verksted.desc: Founded by Jens Jacob and Andreas Jensen in 1848, Myrens Workshop moved to the Akerselva site in 1854 and supplied machinery to mills, sawmills, wood-processing and fish-processing industries. Production in Oslo ended in 1988; the preserved factory complex is now used for offices, media, training and hospitality.
myrens_verksted.popupDesc: Myrens Workshop grew from a small mechanical shop into a supplier of turbines, steam engines and industrial machinery. Kværner acquired the company in 1928, and exports represented 80 percent of turnover in 1973. After the 1988 closure, the factory buildings were adapted for service and property uses while the industrial fabric remained visible.

christiania_seildugsfabrik.name: Christiania Sailcloth Factory
christiania_seildugsfabrik.desc: Started in 1856—supplied sailcloth and textiles to shipping and industry. One of Oslo's largest workplaces in the 19th century.
christiania_seildugsfabrik.popupDesc:
Christiania Sailcloth Factory was a major producer of textiles and sailcloth linked to shipping and industrial markets. The factory illustrates labor-intensive production and export-oriented business in the 19th-century city.

In History Go, the place is used to connect factory labor, material production and harbor economy.

lilleborg_fabrikker.name: Lilleborg Fabrikker
lilleborg_fabrikker.desc: A/S Lilleborg Fabriker was founded in 1897 as a continuation of older factory activity by the Akerselva river. The historical industrial area housed oil and soap production among other things, and later developed into a central Norwegian producer of detergents and consumer goods.
lilleborg_fabrikker.popupDesc:
Lilleborg's industrial history by the Akerselva has several time layers. Older activity existed on the property long before the company A/S Lilleborg Fabriker was founded in 1897: an oil mill from 1833 and a soap factory from 1842 are part of that prehistory. The plant later grew into a large industrial area for soap, detergents and consumer goods among other products.

Most of the production buildings were later demolished or rebuilt when the area was transformed into housing and new urban functions. History Go therefore uses the documented factory gate at Sandakerveien 54 as an explicit entrance and display anchor for the historical factory complex, not as a geometric centre for the whole former industrial area.

alnaelva.name: Alnaelva
alnaelva.desc: City river running from Alungsjøen through Groruddalen and the eastern boroughs to its present outlet at Kongshavn, marked by industry, culverting and later environmental restoration.
alnaelva.popupDesc:
The Alnaelva is Oslo's longest river and runs from Alungsjøen through areas of heavy industrial history, dense settlement and more recent restoration of blue-green corridors. Along the river you find technical interventions, tunnelled stretches and sections where the water and the nature corridor have been opened up again. Today's flow ends at Kongshavn, while the Vannspeilet water mirror in Middelalderparken marks the historical outlet landscape towards Sørenga and Bjørvika.

In History Go the Alnaelva is important as an example of how urban development, environmental management and local history meet in one watercourse. Questions should connect the river's role as a nature corridor on the east side with the history of intervention, closure and reopening.

The river has also been referred to as the Loelva; this is a historical or alternative name for the Alna and not a separate watercourse of its own.

alnaelvstien.name: The Alna Trail – Svartdalen and Bryn
alnaelvstien.desc: A continuous stretch of the Alna Trail through Svartdalen and Bryn, explicitly modelled as eleven named OSM segments.
alnaelvstien.popupDesc:
This specific part of the Alna Trail follows the Alna through Svartdalen and on towards Bryn. The route consists of gravel and asphalt sections, a pedestrian and cycle path, boardwalk and several bridges, among them the suspension bridge in Svartdalsparken. The stretch shows how a recreational path has to adapt to a ravine valley, a river course, a railway and dense urban structure alike.

History Go models here the actually mapped, continuous Alna Trail component of around 1.64 kilometres. The record should not be read as a complete geometric model of every recreational path along the whole Alnaelva.

trosterud_friomrade.name: Lille Wembley
trosterud_friomrade.desc: A state-secured outdoor recreation area at the entrance to Østmarka at Haugerud, laid out for play, activity, the natural environment and local recreation.
trosterud_friomrade.popupDesc:
Lille Wembley lies at the entrance to Østmarka at Haugerud and is a public outdoor and activity area for the local neighbourhood. The area began as a small gravel pitch, but in 2020 it was laid out as a meeting place for play, activity, grilling and social gathering. The surrounding woodland was cleared and measures were taken for the natural environment and insects, while parts of the area serve as a municipal dog training area.

The site fits the original History Go intention far better than the synthetic name "Trosterud friområde": a concrete, named and publicly accessible local recreation area between the residential city and the forest.

furuset_haugerud_skogbelte.name: Haugerudparken
furuset_haugerud_skogbelte.desc: Municipal open space at Haugerud with woodland, paths, seating, grills and activity areas, secured for general outdoor use.
furuset_haugerud_skogbelte.popupDesc:
Haugerudparken is a municipal open space at Haugerud that combines woodland and local nature with paths, places to stay and activity. The park was developed in stages with vegetation work, a main walkway, cross paths, seating areas, grills and a fire pit, and the area was secured by the state for outdoor recreation purposes. New activity measures followed later, among them an unlit cycle track built as a gravel course.

The History Go marker uses this physically mapped cycle track as an internal park anchor. The point therefore represents a documented site inside Haugerudparken, not a claim about the park's geometric centre or its full outer boundary.

hellerud_gard.name: Nedre Hellerud – historical farm site
hellerud_gard.desc: The historical farm site of Nedre Hellerud, anchored in the land register to gnr. 143 / bnr. 3 at Hellerud gårdsvei 7.
hellerud_gard.popupDesc: Nedre Hellerud is one of the historical farms that arose after the division of Nordre Hellerud. History Go uses Hellerud gårdsvei 7 as a source-backed anchor for the historical land-register site gnr. 143 / bnr. 3. The point documents where the historical farm site is anchored in today's land register and address system, but is not in itself evidence that the building standing there today is the original eighteenth-century farm building.

alnabru_jernbane_og_logistikk.name: Alnabru Freight Terminal
alnabru_jernbane_og_logistikk.desc: Norway's largest rail freight terminal and a national hub for intermodal goods transport in Groruddalen.
alnabru_jernbane_og_logistikk.popupDesc: Alnabru freight terminal is the hub of Norwegian rail freight transport. Bane NOR describes the terminal as the Nordic region's largest rail freight terminal, with loading and unloading tracks, stabling tracks, through tracks and large areas for containers and semi-trailers. The marker has been moved from a general point west of the terminal to the representative point of the specific, named OSM terminal polygon.

frysjadammen.name: Oset lock bridge – the dam complex at Maridalsoset
frysjadammen.desc: Historical timber bridge and regulating point at Maridalsoset, where the Maridalsvannet lake passes into the Akerselva river.
frysjadammen.popupDesc:
Oset lock bridge lies at Maridalsoset and is a preserved part of the regulating complex where the Maridalsvannet passes into the Akerselva. The timber bridge was erected in 1859, and the regulating gate for the water flow sat in the bridge structure itself. The newer Oset service bridge lies immediately upstream and makes the historical lock bridge physically identifiable in today's landscape.

In History Go the site matters because it makes the connection between natural conditions, technical intervention and urban development concrete: how water has to be controlled before it reaches the denser boroughs further south.

seilduksfabrikken_nydalen.name: Upper Spinning Mill (Nydalens Compagnie)
seilduksfabrikken_nydalen.desc: The Upper Spinning Mill of 1856 by the Akerselva, erected for Nydalens Bomuldsspinderi.
seilduksfabrikken_nydalen.popupDesc:
The Upper Spinning Mill was erected in 1856 as the major expansion of Nydalens Bomuldsspinderi. The building housed 14,000 new spindles and made the complex one of Christiania's largest spinning environments. The engineer Oluf Nicolai Roll planned and designed the expansion as part of the factory's technical system.

The Akerselva runs in a culvert beneath the spinning mill. The site therefore shows with particular clarity how factory building, machinery and watercourse were constructed as a single production unit. The established technical ID is retained for compatibility reasons, but the place is not Christiania Seildugsfabrik, which stood at Øvre Foss in Fossveien.

nydalsdammen.name: Nydalsdammen
nydalsdammen.desc: An old bathing pond and the former upper water intake for Nydalens Compagnie in the Akerselva.
nydalsdammen.popupDesc:
Nydalsdammen is an old bathing pond and was the upper water intake for Nydalens Compagnie. Before the textile industry put the water power to use, Nygaard's sawmill stood on the west side of the pond. The site therefore shows how a dammed stretch of river could form a direct part of the factory's power and water system.

After the industrial period the pond was cleaned and reopened in 1991, and the area was given lawns and planting in 1992. Today Nydalsdammen is a municipal bathing spot and part of the Akerselva's public green corridor. Water quality and current conditions can change, particularly after heavy rain, so current signage and municipal advice must always be followed.

stilla_nydalen.name: The river stretch below Nydalsdammen
stilla_nydalen.desc: A stretch of the Akerselva just below Nydalsdammen, where the water passes from the dammed pond surface into a narrower course with vegetated banks.
stilla_nydalen.popupDesc:
The map point lies about 100 metres below Nydalsdammen and shows the transition from the dammed pond surface to the onward river course through Nydalen. Here the water speed, the shape of the banks, tree crowns, roots and public movement can all be read as parts of the same urban watercourse.

The technical ID stilla_nydalen is older and is retained for compatibility. The historical place name Stilla belongs to the bathing pools in the upper Akerselva, from Grandalen north of Nydalsbakken towards Brekkefossen, and not to this point below Nydalsdammen. The display name has therefore been corrected without moving the coordinate.

bjoelsenfossen.name: Bjølsenfossen
bjoelsenfossen.desc: The Akerselva's highest waterfall, used for sawmilling, water supply and the milling industry.
bjoelsenfossen.popupDesc:
Bjølsenfossen, also called Bjølsenfallet, is the Akerselva's highest waterfall, with two drops totalling more than 16 metres. The fall is natural, but the water flow is controlled from the Bjølsen dam and the lock complex above it. In the 1600s the fall powered the Sandaker sawmill, and Gerhard Treschow founded the Bjølsen sawmill in 1701.

The city's water intake lay in the Bjølsen dam from 1860 to 1867. From 1884 the fall was closely tied to Bjølsen Valsemølle. The water was carried through penstocks to turbines, and the preserved power plant could develop around 1,200 horsepower. Mill production continues in the area, while the fall itself lies largely within an active industrial area with limited public access.

bjoelsenparken_elvenaer.name: Advokat Dehlis plass – the green space
bjoelsenparken_elvenaer.desc: Small public green space at Advokat Dehlis plass, with lawn, trees, a monument and hard street edges.
bjoelsenparken_elvenaer.popupDesc:
The technical site was previously listed, incorrectly, as "Bjølsenparken (river-adjacent part)". The coordinate belongs to Advokat Dehlis plass at the junction of Maridalsveien and Bentsebrugata, south-east of the actual Bjølsenparken. The square was named in 1934 after the jurist and co-operative pioneer Ole Dehli. The monument by Asbjørg Borgfelt was raised in 1946.

The natural value lies in the small green urban space: lawn, trees and vegetated edges meet asphalt, traffic, a school and dense building. The site shows how even a small green area can give shade, take up some rainwater and work as a local place to stay and an ecological link on the way towards the Akerselva.

glads_molle.name: Glad's Mill
glads_molle.desc: Protected paper mill from 1736 and Norway's oldest preserved factory building in timber.
glads_molle.popupDesc:
Glad's Mill at Sandakerveien 10A was erected in 1736 as the Lower Paper Mill by the trading house Collett & Leuch and the merchant Iver Elieson. The panelled log building with a mansard roof is the oldest remaining factory building along the Akerselva and is described by the City of Oslo as Norway's oldest preserved factory building in timber.

The mill was operated together with Bentse Brug from 1748 to 1798. Fredrik Glad took over in 1798, and the building was later named after him. Paper production ceased in the 1870s. From 1880 Glad's Mill formed part of Hjula Væverier, which installed a power station in the basement and transmitted energy to the factory on the opposite side of the river. The building later housed gramophone record production and F. J. Stenersen's printing works, among other things. It was protected in 1967 and restored in 1992.

voienfossen.name: The Vøyen Falls
voienfossen.desc: Three waterfalls in the Akerselva that powered a grain mill, spinning mills, a weaving mill and mechanical industry.
voienfossen.popupDesc:
The Vøyen Falls are not a single drop but three historical power points in the Akerselva between Bentsebrua and Sannerbrua. In the 1850s the Lower Vøien Grain Mill stood at the river's 15th fall of 16 feet, Hjula Væverier at the 16th fall of 22 feet and Vøien Cotton Spinning Mill at the 17th fall of 28 feet. Together the sequence of falls carries the river some 20 metres down through thresholds such as Hjulafossen, Labakken and Våghalsen.

Knud Graah and Niels O. Young bought the fall rights at Nedre Vøyen in 1844. Vøien Cotton Spinning Mill came into operation in 1846 with 70–80 workers, 2,372 spindles and an overshot iron wheel. On the opposite side Halvor Schou built Hjula Weaving Mill to drawings by Oluf Nicolai Roll. The weaving mill was given a 65-horsepower turbine from Myrens Verksted and capacity for 400 looms.

Foss Spinderi and Den Norske Hesteskosømfabrik show that the falls also powered other industrial ventures. Textile production was later wound up, but the factory buildings and the waterfall landscape still make the transition from natural power to industrial city physically legible.

voien_gard_voienvolden.name: Vøienvolden Farm
voien_gard_voienvolden.desc: Protected smallholding and farm complex from Christiania's town common, preserved as a tight four-sided courtyard at Maridalsveien 120.
voien_gard_voienvolden.popupDesc:
Vøienvolden farm at Maridalsveien 120 is the preserved smallholding Nedre Vøien, not the older Vøyen farm and not the Vøyen Falls.
