Antena 1 remains a central news and current-affairs channel, with fado broadcasts and in-depth journalism, while Antena 2 and Antena 3 cultivate classical and contemporary music respectively. The site is useful for reading how the infrastructure of radio shifted from propaganda tool to democratic public sphere.

lisbon_arquivo_rtp.name: Arquivo RTP
lisbon_arquivo_rtp.desc: RTP’s audiovisual archive, attached to the broadcaster’s main complex on Avenida Marechal Gomes da Costa. The archive holds television and radio recordings from 1957 onwards, and is a central part of Portuguese sound and image memory.
lisbon_arquivo_rtp.popupDesc: Arquivo RTP manages the audiovisual material of the Portuguese public-service broadcaster Rádio e Televisão de Portugal and is housed at RTP’s main complex on Avenida Marechal Gomes da Costa. The archive contains television recordings from the start of television broadcasting in 1957 and radio recordings from Emissora Nacional and RDP from 1935 onwards, including news bulletins, sport, documentary, drama and entertainment. After 1974, RTP has worked on restoration, digitalisation and publication of parts of the archive through the platforms RTP Memória and RTP Arquivos, and the institution collaborates with the Cinemateca Portuguesa, ANIM and research communities in preserving audiovisual heritage. The archive is a crucial source for research on Portuguese contemporary history, from Estado Novo propaganda and the colonial wars to the Carnation Revolution, democracy and contemporary politics and culture. The site can be read as a case of how a public-service broadcaster also functions as a memory institution, and how the public sphere manages its own sound and image residues.

lisbon_diario_de_noticias.name: Diário de Notícias building
lisbon_diario_de_noticias.desc: Historic headquarters of the newspaper Diário de Notícias, founded in 1864 and for a long time one of the most influential Portuguese dailies. The monumental editorial building on Avenida da Liberdade is a visible trace of 20th-century Portuguese press modernity.
lisbon_diario_de_noticias.popupDesc: Diário de Notícias was founded on 29 December 1864 and for long stretches was the leading daily newspaper in Portugal, especially in the 20th century. The newspaper’s headquarters on Avenida da Liberdade is a large, block-shaped editorial building from the middle of the 20th century, with marked towers and facades that place the press distinctly on Lisbon’s ceremonial axis. Under the Estado Novo, Diário de Notícias functioned both as a regime-controlled public sphere and as a space for journalistic work under censorship, and after 1974 the newspaper went through several changes of ownership, takeovers and editorial reorganisations in parallel with the digitalisation of the European press. The building remains strongly associated with the newspaper’s identity and is a good place to read how the printed press of the 20th century built itself as a physical industry in the city centre, with printing presses, editorial offices and distribution at the same address. The site invites reflection on the relationship between editorial public sphere, regimes and commercialisation.

lisbon_lusa.name: Lusa – Agência de Notícias de Portugal
lisbon_lusa.desc: Portugal’s national news agency, founded in 1987 following the merger of earlier agencies. Lusa supplies text, photography and video to Portuguese and Portuguese-language media around the world, and is a central part of the country’s media infrastructure.
lisbon_lusa.popupDesc: Lusa – Agência de Notícias de Portugal was formally established in 1987 through the merger of the earlier agencies ANOP and NP, and is Portugal’s most important national news agency. Its headquarters is in Rua Dr. João Couto in the Sete Rios area, and Lusa has correspondents in all the former Portuguese colonies and in several major capitals, so that the agency forms a coherent linguistic and editorial network across the Portuguese-speaking world. Lusa supplies dispatches, photography, audio and video to virtually every Portuguese newspaper, broadcaster and online outlet, and is therefore a decisive but often invisible infrastructure of the Portuguese public sphere. As a partly state-owned agency, the institution is regularly involved in debates about funding, editorial independence and the narrow Portuguese media economy. Lusa is useful for reading how news is produced behind the headlines and how a small European linguistic community tries to hold its own media structure together.

lisbon_rtp.name: RTP – Rádio e Televisão de Portugal
lisbon_rtp.desc: Headquarters of Portugal’s state public-service broadcaster, covering both television and radio. RTP is central to the Portuguese media public sphere, to the history of television and to the democratisation after 1974.
lisbon_rtp.popupDesc: Rádio e Televisão de Portugal (RTP) is Portugal’s state public-service broadcaster and operates several television channels (RTP1, RTP2, RTP3, RTP Memória, RTP Internacional, RTP África) and radio stations under Antena 1, Antena 2 and Antena 3. Television itself began broadcasting from Portugal on 7 March 1957, while broadcasting in radio form has an even longer history under the Estado Novo regime, when Emissora Nacional functioned as the regime’s state broadcaster. After the Carnation Revolution in 1974, RTP was reorganised as a public-service broadcaster with responsibility for media pluralism in the public sphere, and the institution plays a central role in the shift from propaganda apparatus to democratic public sphere. The headquarters lies in the Avenida Marechal Gomes da Costa area in the north of the city and contains studios, editorial departments and technical production facilities. RTP is a central reference point for Portuguese media, television history and the debate over the role of public-service broadcasting in a democratic society.

lisbon_faculdade_de_ciencias.name: Faculdade de Ciências da Universidade de Lisboa
lisbon_faculdade_de_ciencias.desc: Faculty of natural sciences at the Universidade de Lisboa, located on the Cidade Universitária campus in Campo Grande. The faculty teaches and researches in physics, mathematics, biology, geology, chemistry and computer science, and is a central institution in Portuguese basic research.
lisbon_faculdade_de_ciencias.popupDesc: The Faculdade de Ciências da Universidade de Lisboa (FCUL) was founded in 1911 as part of the young republic’s reorganisation of higher education, and originally had its base in the buildings of the former Escola Politécnica in Príncipe Real. From the 1980s onwards, the faculty gradually moved to the Cidade Universitária in Campo Grande, where modern research and teaching buildings bring together mathematics, physics, chemistry, biology, geology and computer science. FCUL houses several research institutes, including in astrophysics, biodiversity and data, and is one of the main providers of natural-science expertise for Portuguese schools, public administration and industry. The site is useful for reading how basic research, teacher education and institution-building are linked in a small European country, and how the historic shift from the 19th-century polytechnic tradition to today’s research university has shaped Portuguese science.

lisbon_instituto_higiene_medicina_tropic.name: Instituto de Higiene e Medicina Tropical
lisbon_instituto_higiene_medicina_tropic.desc: Medical research and teaching institute in Junqueira, founded in 1902 as Escola de Medicina Tropical. The institute was built to serve the colonial health service and is today part of the Universidade NOVA de Lisboa, with a focus on global health.
lisbon_instituto_higiene_medicina_tropic.popupDesc: The Instituto de Higiene e Medicina Tropical (IHMT) was founded in 1902 as Escola de Medicina Tropical, built to train doctors and researchers who would work in the Portuguese colonies in Africa and Asia. The institute lies on Rua da Junqueira on the Belém axis and has, since the early 20th century, been central in Portuguese research on malaria, sleeping sickness, parasitic diseases and public health in tropical territories. After 1974, the institution was reorganised as a university institute within what is today the Universidade NOVA de Lisboa, with emphasis on global health, cooperation with former colonies and research on tropical diseases in a wider international framework. IHMT is a good place to read the link between colonial health service, medical research and global health, and how scientific institutions manage both inherited assets and critical renewal. The building houses historical collections and laboratories that provide insight into early-20th-century medical infrastructure.

lisbon_instituto_ricardo_jorge.name: Instituto Nacional de Saúde Doutor Ricardo Jorge
lisbon_instituto_ricardo_jorge.desc: State public-health institute with research and reference laboratories, with roots back to 1899 and its main complex on Avenida Padre Cruz. The institute is central to the surveillance of epidemics, environmental health and biomedical research in Portugal.
lisbon_instituto_ricardo_jorge.popupDesc: The Instituto Nacional de Saúde Doutor Ricardo Jorge (INSA) goes back to 1899, when a state institute for hygiene and bacteriology was set up in the wake of a bubonic plague epidemic in Porto. The institution is named after the physician Ricardo Jorge, who led the modern work on urban hygiene and disease prevention in Portugal around 1900. INSA is today headquartered on Avenida Padre Cruz in northern Lisbon and functions as a national reference laboratory in fields such as microbiology, water quality, food and chemical safety, epidemiology and genetics. The institute plays a central role in the surveillance of infectious diseases, for example during influenza seasons, HIV/AIDS and the COVID-19 pandemic, and is an important part of Portugal’s preparedness. The site is useful for reading the link between city, disease and state science – from the 19th-century hygiene movement to today’s biomedical laboratory state.

lisbon_instituto_superior_tecnico.name: Instituto Superior Técnico
lisbon_instituto_superior_tecnico.desc: Portugal’s largest engineering school, founded in 1911 and located on the Alameda campus in central Lisbon. IST trains engineers in fields including civil engineering, electrical engineering, physics and computer science, and is a cornerstone of the country’s technical research and education infrastructure.
lisbon_instituto_superior_tecnico.popupDesc: Instituto Superior Técnico (IST) was founded on 23 May 1911 as part of the reorganisation of higher education under the young Portuguese Republic and received in the 1930s its distinctive campus around Avenida Rovisco Pais, designed in part by Pardal Monteiro. The school trains engineers in civil, mechanical, electrical, chemical, physics, computer-science and, later, biomedical and aerospace engineering, and is today the largest unit at the Universidade de Lisboa in technology. IST has been central to the modernisation of Portuguese industry, telecommunications, energy supply and infrastructure, and the research institutes linked to IST take part in international collaborations from particle physics to climate and artificial intelligence. The campus is also a concrete arena for reading how the Portuguese technical elite has been shaped and how the engineering profession has been linked both to the modernisation of the Estado Novo and to the building of the democratic welfare state.

lisbon_jardim_botanico_tropical.name: Jardim Botânico Tropical
lisbon_jardim_botanico_tropical.desc: Botanical garden in Belém, laid out in 1906 as Jardim-Museu Agrícola Colonial. The garden was built for colonial tropical agricultural research and is now part of the Universidade de Lisboa, while remaining an important critical site of memory for Portuguese colonial history.
lisbon_jardim_botanico_tropical.popupDesc: The Jardim Botânico Tropical in Belém was laid out from 1906 as the Jardim-Museu Agrícola Colonial and was linked to the Instituto Superior de Agronomia and the colonial administration’s effort to systematise tropical plant and agricultural knowledge. The garden holds species from the Portuguese colonies in Africa, Asia and South America and functioned historically as a research garden, a demonstration garden and a symbolic landscape of the colonial project, in particular during the colonial Exposição do Mundo Português in 1940. Today, the garden is part of the Universidade de Lisboa and is used for research, teaching and public outreach, while remaining a concrete site for reading the link between botany, agricultural science and colonial history. The area abuts the Mosteiro dos Jerónimos and Praça do Império, and the design itself of the garden, with its ponds, pavilions and colonial stone art, can be read as material trace of an empire that no longer exists.

lisbon_laboratorio_nacional_engenharia_c.name: Laboratório Nacional de Engenharia Civil
lisbon_laboratorio_nacional_engenharia_c.desc: State research laboratory for civil engineering and infrastructure, founded in 1946 and located near Avenida do Brasil. LNEC has played a central role in the development of bridges, dams, earthquake safety and large infrastructure projects in Portugal.
lisbon_laboratorio_nacional_engenharia_c.popupDesc: The Laboratório Nacional de Engenharia Civil (LNEC) was established by decree in 1946 and built up from the late 1940s onwards near Avenida do Brasil in the northern part of Lisbon. The institute was set up to provide a scientific basis for Portuguese construction projects in roads, bridges, ports, dams and buildings, and has since played a central role in research and advisory work on public infrastructure. LNEC has been involved in projects such as the Ponte 25 de Abril, the Vasco da Gama Bridge, large dams in the Tagus and Douro systems and in the analysis of earthquake, flood and coastal risk. The complex houses test halls, a wind tunnel, shake tables, hydraulic model basins and materials laboratories, and is one of the largest applied research facilities in Portugal. The site can be read as a case of how the postwar state invested in technical-scientific capacity in order to build modern infrastructure, and how the earthquake-prone city of Lisbon still depends on engineering research.

lisbon_museu_nacional_de_historia_natura.name: Museu Nacional de História Natural e da Ciência
lisbon_museu_nacional_de_historia_natura.desc: University museum of natural history and the history of science in Príncipe Real, attached to the Universidade de Lisboa. The building houses botanical, zoological and geological collections, as well as a historic 19th-century physics-chemistry laboratory.
lisbon_museu_nacional_de_historia_natura.popupDesc: The Museu Nacional de História Natural e da Ciência (MUHNAC) lies on Rua da Escola Politécnica in Príncipe Real and administers collections that go back to the Escola Politécnica of 1837 and the former Museu Bocage. The building combines historic teaching rooms, a preserved 19th-century physics-chemistry laboratory, a botanical garden complex and extensive zoological, geological and anthropological collections. After a fire in 1978 and subsequent restoration, the institution was reorganised as a university museum and is today a central arena for research in the history of science and for public knowledge dissemination in Portugal. The site is a good starting point for reading how naturalist classification, teaching and colonial collecting were built into 19th-century state science.

lisbon_observatorio_astronomico.name: Observatório Astronómico de Lisboa
lisbon_observatorio_astronomico.desc: State astronomical observatory in the Tapada da Ajuda, opened in 1861. The site was built for positional astronomy, timekeeping and state science, and today is a research unit under the Universidade de Lisboa.
lisbon_observatorio_astronomico.popupDesc: The Observatório Astronómico de Lisboa was founded following the mid-19th-century reorganisation of Portuguese astronomy and opened its new observatory building in the Tapada da Ajuda in 1861. The main building was designed to house a meridian circle and other instruments for positional astronomy, and the institution was central to establishing national timekeeping, coordinate systems and maritime navigation support. The observatory was part of a network of European observatories that supplied data for star catalogues and geodetic measurements, while also being a knowledge institution under the Portuguese monarchy and later the republic. After light pollution made observation in Lisbon difficult, research was redirected toward theory, data analysis and collaboration with other observatories, and the unit is today attached to the Universidade de Lisboa. The building with its classical architecture and preserved instruments is a concrete reminder of how state, science and infrastructure were intertwined in the 19th century.

lisbon_pavilhao_do_conhecimento.name: Pavilhão do Conhecimento
lisbon_pavilhao_do_conhecimento.desc: Interactive science centre in the Parque das Nações, opened in 1999 in the premises of one of the Expo 98 pavilions. The centre is part of the Ciência Viva network and is aimed in particular at children, young people and school classes.
lisbon_pavilhao_do_conhecimento.popupDesc: The Pavilhão do Conhecimento – Centro Ciência Viva opened in 1999 as the first large interactive science centre in Portugal, housed in one of the pavilions built for the Expo 98 world exhibition. The building, designed by João Luís Carrilho da Graça, lies centrally in the Parque das Nações together with the Oceanário, the Pavilhão de Portugal and the Gare do Oriente. The centre is part of the national Ciência Viva network, which since the late 1990s has built interactive science centres across the country to strengthen public understanding of natural science and technology. The Pavilhão do Conhecimento is particularly oriented toward school classes, children and families, and is an example of how modern science communication shifts from static exhibitions to hands-on learning and partnership with schools. The site can be read as a deliberate part of the Expo 98 legacy, in which the ocean and knowledge form the frame for a new scientific citizenship.

lisbon_torre_do_tombo.name: Arquivo Nacional da Torre do Tombo
lisbon_torre_do_tombo.desc: Portugal’s national archive, with roots in the Middle Ages and its current concrete building from 1990 next to the Cidade Universitária. Torre do Tombo holds documentation ranging from medieval diplomas and Inquisition registers to recent state archives.
lisbon_torre_do_tombo.popupDesc: The Arquivo Nacional da Torre do Tombo is Portugal’s national archive and continues the name of a tower at the Castelo de São Jorge where royal documents were stored from the 14th century. The original tower was destroyed in the 1755 earthquake, and the holdings were moved several times before the current large concrete building next to the Cidade Universitária was completed in 1990, designed by Arsénio Cordeiro and Pedro Ferreira da Costa. The archive holds documents from the 9th century onward, including royal acts, maritime documents, Inquisition registers, state archives from the Estado Novo and the PIDE/DGS archive, as well as vast quantities of contemporary public documents. The Torre do Tombo is a crucial source for research on the Middle Ages, colonial history, dictatorship and the democratic transition, and runs digitalisation projects that make parts of the material available online. The building can be read as a case of how a state materialises its own memory, and how the archives function both as rule-of-law infrastructure and as a critical research resource.

lisbon_casa_museu_amalia_rodrigues.name: Casa-Museu Amália Rodrigues
lisbon_casa_museu_amalia_rodrigues.desc: House-museum of the fado singer Amália Rodrigues on Rua de São Bento, opened in 2001 in her former home. The museum preserves the interior, costumes and collections, and is a central arena for Portuguese celebrity memory and for fado as popular culture.
lisbon_casa_museu_amalia_rodrigues.popupDesc: The Casa-Museu Amália Rodrigues lies at Rua de São Bento 193 and was the former home of the fado singer Amália da Piedade Rebordão Rodrigues (1920–1999), who more than any other artist turned fado into an international art form in the second half of the 20th century. The museum opened to the public in 2001 and preserves her interior with furniture, stage costumes, records, photographs and personal belongings almost untouched, so that the home reads as a biographical device. Amália was at once a popular artist, an international stage name and a contested figure on account of her exposure under the Estado Novo, but after 1974 she was widely reclaimed as a national symbol and now lies at the Panteão Nacional. The museum is a concrete arena for reading fado as popular culture, celebrity memory and Portuguese canon, and how home and artist merge in a museological gaze. The site invites reflection on how popular culture is produced, managed and turned into public memory.

lisbon_feira_da_ladra.name: Feira da Ladra
lisbon_feira_da_ladra.desc: Traditional flea market on Campo de Santa Clara next to the Panteão Nacional, held on Tuesdays and Saturdays, with roots back to the Middle Ages and a fixed location in Santa Clara since the late 19th century. The market is an everyday arena of second-hand culture and informal trade.
lisbon_feira_da_ladra.popupDesc: The Feira da Ladra is held on Campo de Santa Clara between the Panteão Nacional and São Vicente de Fora and is one of Europe’s oldest still-active flea markets, with documented roots back to the 13th century and its present location since the late 19th century. The market is open on Tuesdays and Saturdays and contains everything from furniture, clothes, records, books, coins and ceramics to discarded-culture objects, curiosities and jewellery. The name «ladra» – the thief – points to the market’s historic reputation for selling used and sometimes dubiously sourced goods, and the market continues to be an everyday economic arena for migrants, artists, collectors and local traders. The site is useful for reading the link between informal trade, popular culture, history of use and memory objects, and how an open square organises a city life beyond the structure of shops. It also invites reflection on how tourism and gentrification press against traditional market forms.

lisbon_feira_do_livro.name: Feira do Livro de Lisboa
lisbon_feira_do_livro.desc: Annual book fair in the Parque Eduardo VII, organised in its current form since 1931 and a central arena for public reading culture in Portugal. The fair combines sales, talks and signings in park booths each spring and early summer.
lisbon_feira_do_livro.popupDesc: The Feira do Livro de Lisboa is the annual book fair held in the Parque Eduardo VII, with a tradition going back to 1931 and its current fixed form in the upper part of the park from the postwar period onward. The fair opens in May or June and brings Portuguese publishers, booksellers, antiquarian dealers and associations together in long rows of wooden booths along the park’s great axis, descending toward Marquês de Pombal and the Avenida da Liberdade. The programme includes signings, talks, readings and launches, and the fair is simultaneously a central commercial arena for the book trade and a popular festival of literature. The Feira do Livro is one of Europe’s largest open-air book fairs and must be read in connection with Portuguese reading culture, in which book prices, state support, small publishers and the reading community are matters of public debate. The site is useful for understanding how literature can become popular culture, how a park is temporarily transformed into a book space, and how popular culture and canonical literature can share the same table.

lisbon_marchas_populares.name: Marchas Populares de Lisboa
lisbon_marchas_populares.desc: Annual parade of Lisbon’s neighbourhood groups, held on the night of 13 June as part of the Santo António festivities, with organised structures since 1932. The parade descends Avenida da Liberdade and is a central collective performance of popular culture.
lisbon_marchas_populares.popupDesc: The Marchas Populares de Lisboa are an organised parade of local neighbourhood groups – marchas – each representing a bairro such as Alfama, Mouraria, Bica, Graça or Castelo, who compete in singing, dancing, costume and choreography on the night of 12 to 13 June in connection with the Santo António festivities. In its modern form, the parade was formalised from 1932, when the municipality and the regime helped institutionalise the popular festival, and it has since alternated between regime-curated folklore, democratic urban identity and contemporary commercialised mass event. The main procession marches down Avenida da Liberdade in a set order, while individual groups also hold concerts and rehearsals in their own neighbourhoods in the weeks before. The marchas tradition is a concrete arena for understanding how Portuguese popular culture, urban identity and ritual community are intertwined, and how a folklorised tradition can both express neighbourhood pride and become part of the municipal marketing of the city.

lisbon_santo_antonio_festival.name: Santo António festival in Lisbon
lisbon_santo_antonio_festival.desc: Lisbon’s major patron-saint festival, centred on Santo António on 12–13 June, with popular festivities in Alfama, Mouraria, Castelo and Graça. The festival combines religious liturgy, popular weddings, sardines and popular music.
lisbon_santo_antonio_festival.popupDesc: The Santo António festival is Lisbon’s most important patron-saint festival, tied to Santo António of Lisbon (also known as Saint Anthony of Padua), who was born in Lisbon and was later canonised. The main feast falls on 13 June, when the city celebrates him with mass at the Igreja de Santo António near the Sé, processions and popular festivities in the old neighbourhoods of Alfama, Mouraria, Castelo, Graça and Bica on the night of 12 to 13 June. The popular festival combines grilled sardines, caldo verde, ginja, street dance, manjericos and popular music in open streets, while several couples take part in the so-called Casamentos de Santo António – collective weddings organised by the municipality since 1958 and broadcast on national television. The festival in its modern form grew from the late 19th century and was institutionalised as the city’s official feast from the 1930s, with the Marchas Populares as a central element. The site is useful for reading how religious liturgy, popular culture, neighbourhood identity and municipal marketing fuse into one complex ritualised public sphere.

lisbon_tram_28.name: Tram 28 (Elétrico 28)
lisbon_tram_28.desc: Historic tram line 28, from Martim Moniz to Campo de Ourique, part of Lisbon’s everyday mobility since the 20th century and at the same time a powerful tourist magnet. The line has become an icon of popular culture and a contested field between transport, tourism and the cityscape.
lisbon_tram_28.popupDesc: Line 28 of the Carris tram network runs from Martim Moniz via Graça, Sé, Baixa, Estrela and Campo de Ourique and still uses the yellow, narrow Remodelado cars whose origin lies in the early 20th century. The line was established in its basic form in the early 1900s, and the combination of steep gradients, narrow streets through Alfama and a traditional car design has turned it into one of Lisbon’s strongest popular-culture icons – images of tram 28 appear on everything from postcards to music videos, and the line is routinely used as a visual synonym for the city. At the same time, the line remains part of the city’s public transport, used by elderly people, schoolchildren and commuters living along the route, and has in recent decades been in growing tension with tourist pressure, especially on the Alfama section, where overcrowded trams and pickpocketing dominate debate. The site is useful for reading how an everyday public-transport line becomes a symbol, how that symbol reflects back on everyday life, and how mobility, tourism and popular culture interlock in a historic city.

tullin.name: Tullinløkka
tullin.desc: Tullinløkka is named after the court steward Claus Tullin, who bought Ruseløkken in 1807. The state separated out the open space in 1869, and it was used for exhibitions, demonstrations, play and "velocipede riding". The Historical Museum was completed in 1903. After decades as a car park, the whole space was converted into a park and activity area in 2011.
tullin.popupDesc:
Tullinløkka lies between the Historical Museum and the former National Gallery. The name comes from the court steward Claus Tullin, who bought Ruseløkken in 1807. The state took over the property in 1837 and separated out the open ground in 1869. The undeveloped surface remained as a rare large space beside the new ceremonial street Karl Johan.

The space acquired many temporary uses early on. Children played here, soldiers drilled, and in winter the open surface could be used for activity on snow and ice. In 1885 the city's cyclists were given permission for "velocipede riding" between six and eight in the morning. The narrow time slot shows how unfamiliar and contested the new bicycle still was in the city's streets.

The Norwegian Industrial and Art Exhibition was held at Tullinløkka in 1883. As many as 2,245 exhibitors showed goods, machinery, crafts and industrial products in temporary halls. The exhibition turned the open ground into a large exhibition site for the young Norwegian state and showed how industry, art and national representation could be gathered in a single event.

In the 1890s Tullinløkka also became a political meeting place. Large demonstrations gathered here, and Bjørnstjerne Bjørnson was among the speakers. The open surface lay close to the university, the Storting and the city's institutions and could hold crowds that would not fit in ordinary streets and meeting halls.

The museum buildings gave the area a more permanent frame. The Sculpture Museum, the nucleus of the later National Gallery, opened in 1881. The Historical Museum was built in 1898–1903 to designs by Henrik Bull. Several competitions proposed new museums and extensions on the open ground itself, but none of the great monumental schemes was completed.

Through much of the twentieth century the space was used for car parking. A temporary art hall opened in 2005 but stood for only a few years. When it was decided that the new National Museum would be located at Vestbanen, Statsbygg laid out a park across the whole of Tullinløkka in 2011. The central field was kept as a flexible surface for markets, art, exhibitions and events. The space has therefore been exhibition hall, cycle track, demonstration ground, car park and park, but never received the permanent monumental building that so many plans tried to place here.

okern.name: Økern
okern.desc: Økern was farmland well into the twentieth century, but the municipality bought the Økern farm in 1938 and opened the area to industry, warehousing and road schemes. Standard Telefon og Kabelfabrik produced here from 1919. The metro station opened in 1966 and the Økern centre in 1969, with an 18-storey block as a landmark beside Ring 3.
okern.popupDesc:
Økern takes its name from the Økern farm and was long an agricultural area east of Sinsen. The landscape also held sand pits, brickworks and smaller quarries. From around 1910 a villa suburb grew up at Økernlund and Risløkka, but farming and open fields still characterised much of the area.

Industrialisation began before the municipality took over the farm. Skandinaviske Kabel- og Gummifabriker started production at Økern in 1919. The company was renamed Standard Telefon og Kabelfabrik, STK, in 1934 and became one of the area's largest employers. The factory produced telecommunications cables, telephone exchanges, radios, televisions, refrigerators, measuring instruments and electronics for ships and aircraft.

The City of Oslo bought the Økern farm and the remaining land in 1938. After the war the area was quickly zoned for industry, warehousing, roads and housing. The old Økern junction had small shops, a post office and housing, but much of this fabric disappeared when Ring 3, Østre Aker vei and larger commercial complexes were built.

STK's 62-metre factory tower was completed in 1962 and became a landmark. At its peak several thousand people worked for the company; around 1990 it had over 3,000 employees. Kabelgata, Standardveien and Tårngata have preserved the industrial memory in their street names. Cable production was wound up in 1992, and large parts of the factory site took on new functions.

Økern metro station opened on 16 October 1966 on the Grorud Line. Three years later, in June 1969, the Økern centre opened. The centre had more than thirty shops and an 18-storey office block that at the time of opening was the tallest building in the Groruddalen valley. Metro, shopping centre and road schemes made Økern a communications hub between the inner city and the valley.

When industry and the old centre lost their activity, a new transformation began. Factory halls were used for offices, retail, culture and other businesses, while new plans introduced housing, streets and urban spaces. In under a hundred years Økern has shifted from farmland to industrial community, traffic hub and dense urban development area. The factory tower, the street names and the large halls make the industrial period visible in the middle of the new city. The old farm name meanwhile lives on across the whole district.

skoyen.name: Skøyen
skoyen.desc: Skøyen station opened as Tyskestranden on the Drammen Line in 1872, was called Bygdø from 1876 and gained its present name in 1903. A large industrial area grew up around the tracks with Skabo Railway Carriage Works, Thune's Mechanical Workshop and NEBB. From the 1980s the workshop halls were gradually replaced or reused for offices, retail, housing and a transport hub.
skoyen.popupDesc:
Skøyen lies between Frognerkilen and Bestumkilen and was originally farmland belonging to the Skøyen farms. The Drammen Line opened in 1872 with the station Tyskestranden, named after the beach by Bestumkilen. The station was renamed Bygdø in 1876 and Skøyen in 1903. The railway made the area easily accessible for workers, goods and heavy equipment alike.

Skabo Railway Carriage Works moved its operations here in 1873 and began production at Skøyen the following year. The factory built railway carriages, trams and later buses. Frognerkilens Fabrik, which subsequently became part of Norsk Elektrisk & Brown Boveri, also established itself in the 1870s and produced electrical equipment.

Thune's Mechanical Workshop moved to Skøyen around 1901–02. The workshop made machinery and larger industrial products, while the Monier factory produced cement goods from the end of the nineteenth century. Eureka Mechanical Workshop came to the area in 1898. Goods sidings, cranes, workshop halls and factory chimneys made Skøyen one of the capital's largest industrial areas.

The area also held sport and leisure early on. A velodrome opened in 1887 and was given a timber surface in 1894. The cycle track was demolished in 1903 when other development took the site. Skøyen later gained both a riding hall and an exhibition hall, buildings that showed the large sites could be used for more than factories and warehouses.

From the 1970s and 1980s much of the industry closed, moved or merged. Thune left the area in 1976, and several production sites were transformed from the late 1980s. Office buildings, shops and housing replaced many halls, while some factory buildings and names were preserved and put to new use. Street names and surviving brick halls still tell which companies were based here.

Skøyen station was substantially extended and gained four tracks in 1998. The listed station building still stands beside the complex, 4.38 kilometres from Oslo Central Station. Trains, trams and buses meet close to the E18 and Ring 3, and large workplaces generate extensive commuting. Skøyen has thus gone from beach and farmland via railway workshops and electrical engineering industry to a dense hub of work and travel, with the industrial traces partly visible between the newer office buildings.

torshov.name: Torshov
torshov.desc: Torshovbyen was built by Kristiania municipality in 1917–25 with 18 blocks and around 1,760 flats. Harald Hals and Adolf Jensen Talberg combined a dense masonry city with green courtyards and curving streets. Torshov Park opened in 1931, the Soria Moria cinema in 1928, and the Torshov Theatre moved into the building in 1977 as the country's first permanent district stage.
torshov.popupDesc:
Torshov was farmland north of Kristiania before the municipality began large-scale housing construction. The municipality bought land in 1916 and built Torshovbyen between 1917 and 1925. The scheme consisted of 18 blocks and around 1,760 flats. City planning director Harald Hals and architect Adolf Jensen Talberg combined the dense European masonry city with English garden city ideals.

The blocks were laid out around large planted courtyards. Streets and rows of houses followed the terrain in curves rather than forming a strict grid. The flats were small by today's standards, but the project gave brighter rooms, better air and more green space than many older working-class tenements. The municipality planned the housing, the parks, the schools and the local services as parts of the same neighbourhood.

Torshov Park was kept free of building even though the elevation was attractive as a church site. Parks director Marius Røhne drew up the plan in 1924. The roughly 40-decare hilltop, 87 metres above sea level, was given continuous lawns, a bandstand, a playground and a paddling pool. Sigri Welhaven's children's sculpture arrived in 1928, and Wilhelm Rasmussen's bust of the women's rights campaigner Fernanda Nissen was unveiled at the official opening in 1931. During the occupation parts of the park were used for growing food and for private allotments.

Vogts gate became Torshov's retail and tram street. Here the Soria Moria cinema opened on 26 December 1928 in a neoclassical building designed by Thorvald Astrup. Rudolf Nilsen wrote the prologue for the opening. The main auditorium had a gallery and 1,012 seats, and the building also housed a restaurant and later a library branch. The domed ceiling and the columns in the auditorium were removed in a 1959 rebuilding.

The Torshov Theatre opened in 1977 in premises above the cinema as the National Theatre's first permanent district stage. A smaller cinema auditorium was built behind the screen in 1979. Cinema operation continued until 2008, while Cosmopolite took over the main auditorium as a music venue. The same building has thus served as a municipal public hall for film, theatre, library, restaurant and concerts.

The area was given street names after Norwegian composers, musicians and actors, among them Agathe Backer Grøndahl, Johan Svendsen and Erika Nissen. The names tied the housing project to a cultural programme later reinforced by the cinema, the theatre and the concerts. Torshovbyen also became a model for municipal housing construction. Rows of trees, front gardens and the large courtyards were meant to give families light and outdoor space without spreading the development as widely as an ordinary garden city. The continuous blocks meanwhile made it possible to build many homes quickly during the housing shortage after the First World War.

Torshov's distinctive character comes from housing policy and cultural institutions being built into the same plan. The green courtyards, Torshov Park, the tram in Vogts gate and Soria Moria are still within walking distance of one another. The area shows how Kristiania municipality tried early on to create a whole neighbourhood, not merely a collection of flats.

grorud.name: Grorud
grorud.desc: Grorud became a hub when the coaching station opened in 1831 and the Main Line gained a station in 1854. Quarries, copper mines, sawmills and factories supplied building stone, timber goods, textiles and metal products. Grorud school opened in 1900 and the church in 1902. During the war the large Nyland depot and prison camp lay here, before the metro arrived in 1966 and residential areas grew up around the old centre.
grorud.popupDesc:
Grorud lies in the upper part of the Groruddalen valley, where old travel routes, the Alna river, farmland and forest met. The farm name is known from the Middle Ages and probably means Gro's clearing. The area lay on road connections towards both Trondheim and Bergen. When a coaching station opened in 1831, Grorud became a regular stop for travellers, post and goods transport.

The Main Line between Christiania and Eidsvoll gained Grorud station in 1854. The railway made it easier to move heavy goods and strengthened industrial development. The area had copper mines, sawmills, a planing mill, textile production and ironware factories. The quarries became especially important. Nordmarkite from Grorud was used for paving stones and façades in the capital, and the sledgehammer in the district's later logo refers to that activity.

A local community grew up around the station, the industry and the main road. The Grorud residents' association was founded in 1897, Grorud school opened in 1900 and the stone church in 1902. The first prize ski race at Grorud was held as early as 1862, while Grorud Sports Club was established in 1917. By 1930 around 2,000 people lived in the early suburban development.

During the Second World War the Germans requisitioned Grorud school and built several military installations. The Nyland camp north of the railway consisted of more than 50 buildings and functioned mainly as a depot, but part of it was used as a prison camp for Soviet prisoners of war. The Norwegian State Railways' workshop on the southern side of the tracks was under German control. After liberation the armed forces took over the camp and used it as the Army's main arsenal until 1972. Only a few buildings and rows of trees have been preserved.

Large-scale housing construction came after the war. Farm and industrial areas were filled with small houses, blocks, schools and local centres. The Grorud Line opened in 1966 with Grorud as its terminus before it was later extended. The metro station, the shopping centre and public services shifted the centre of gravity, but the Main Line and the older roads continued to mark the area.

The stone industry is still visible in the materials. Grorud church is built of Grorud granite, and the cemetery lies on the slope south-west of the church. Trygve Lie is buried there, and a memorial stone commemorates local resistance members who fell during the war. Grorud school was designed by municipal architect Harald Bødtker and opened with eight classrooms, a craft room and a school kitchen. It was extended in 1913 and 1923. The same Bødtker designed Grorud church in local granite. The church was consecrated on 17 December 1902, and Per Vigeland completed the 200-square-metre fresco The Great White Host in 1936.

Grorud therefore holds far more than the post-war satellite town. The farm name, the coaching station, the railway, the stone industry, the church, the wartime camp and the metro are different layers around the same local hub. Grorud Park, opened in 2013, follows the Alna and ties newer public spaces to the river that once powered the industry.

gamlebyen.name: Gamlebyen
gamlebyen.desc: Historic urban area of Oslo with medieval traces, residential life and local activity venues.
gamlebyen.popupDesc:
Gamlebyen is the historic core where Oslo grew during the High Middle Ages, with church ruins, the Medieval Park and the layered traces of the early city still legible in the terrain. After the 1624 fire, the urban centre shifted west, leaving Gamlebyen as both archaeological landscape and contemporary residential neighbourhood.

The area is important because it makes the transition from medieval Oslo to the present city concrete. Walking through Gamlebyen means moving through several hundred years of urban history layered into the same terrain, alongside everyday housing and local activity venues.

frognerparken.name: Frogner Park
frognerparken.desc: Large urban park with walking lines, green areas and several activity and lingering zones.
frognerparken.popupDesc:
Frogner Park is one of Oslo’s largest urban parks, organised around long walking lines, generous green areas and several activity and lingering zones. The park functions both as a public landscape for everyday use and as a frame for the Vigeland sculpture installation, which gives the space a strong identity beyond ordinary park use.

The site is useful for reading how a major urban park can sustain many parallel uses: morning runs, sunbathing, picnics, school visits, tourist routes and quiet pauses, all within one continuous landscape.

kampen_park.name: Kampen Park
kampen_park.desc: Neighbourhood park in Kampen with hills, paths and lingering surfaces for everyday use.
kampen_park.popupDesc:
Kampen Park is a clear example of a neighbourhood park in eastern Oslo. The terrain combines hills, stairs, paths and open surfaces in a relatively compact area, with playgrounds, gravel pitches and seating that support everyday play, training and lingering.

The site is useful for reading how a smaller park can carry the social weight of a dense neighbourhood: a local public space that turns into running terrain, picnic ground, meeting point and informal arena depending on time of day and season.

bislett_stadion.name: Bislett Stadium
bislett_stadion.desc: Bislett Stadium is one of Oslo’s most distinct sporting sites, with a rare mix of athletics, football traces, speed-skating history, everyday running and international records. The place functions as a sporting urban stage where major meets, local training sessions and historic moments lie layered on top of one another in the same venue.
bislett_stadion.popupDesc: Bislett Stadium is a key arena for understanding Oslo as a sporting city. The first stadium form opened in 1922, and the site has been associated with athletics, speed skating, football, Olympic ceremonies and broad public use. For a Groundhopper mode, Bislett matters because the arena can be read both through numbers and memory: world records, the Bislett Games, former football matches, the history of the skating oval and today’s use of stands, running tracks and training rooms. The site makes sports statistics local: records get an address, older disciplines acquire a physical trace, and the player can collect arena, sport type, club affiliation and historic events at one point.

intility_arena.name: Intility Arena
intility_arena.desc: Intility Arena is Vålerenga’s modern home at Valle, and a central site for understanding recent club football in Oslo. The arena ties together top-flight football, supporter identity, women’s football, urban development and local ownership at a clear stadium point in the east of the city.
intility_arena.popupDesc: Intility Arena opened in 2017 and marks a shift in Oslo’s football geography: Vålerenga finally got a home of its own after many years at other arenas. For a Groundhopper mode this is a modern club ground with clear sports-statistical data: capacity, opening match, attendance records, home matches for the men’s and women’s teams, European nights and proximity to the wider Valle Hovin sporting environment. The site should be used for questions about club identity, stadium construction, supporter areas, artificial turf, floodlights, rivalry, and the difference between national arena and club home.

jordal_amfi.name: Jordal Amfi
jordal_amfi.desc: Jordal Amfi is Oslo’s most important ice-hockey arena, rooted in the 1952 Olympic facility and in a new arena form from 2020. The site brings together Vålerenga Ishockey, the east-side’s sporting memories, stand culture and the transition from old amphitheatre to modern hall.
jordal_amfi.popupDesc: Jordal Amfi is one of the strongest ice-hockey points in Oslo. The original arena was built in connection with the 1952 Winter Olympics, while today’s new Jordal Amfi opened in 2020. For History Go, Jordal should be the main site for hockey groundhopping in Oslo: here the player can collect ice-hockey arena, Vålerenga Ishockey, Olympic traces, district history, old and new stand layers, and concrete statistics such as capacity, opening year and home matches. The site also lends itself to questions about how a sports venue can be rebuilt without losing its old sporting identity.

holmenkollen_nasjonalanlegg.name: Holmenkollen National Arena
holmenkollen_nasjonalanlegg.desc: The Holmenkollen national arena is Norway’s most symbolic winter-sports site, with ski jump, ski stadium, cross-country skiing, biathlon and large public festivals. The complex turns skiing into local history: altitude, view, national mythology, World Cup competitions and audience rituals meet in a single landscape.
holmenkollen_nasjonalanlegg.popupDesc: Holmenkollen is one of the most charged sporting sites in Norway. The ski-jumping tradition goes back to 1892, while today’s national arena gathers ski jump, cross-country skiing, biathlon, museum, tower and major events. In Groundhopper mode, Holmenkollen should be the main node of winter sport: a place to collect ski jumping, cross-country, biathlon, World Cup, attendance records, hill records and national sporting memories. The site lends itself particularly well to questions that link concrete sports data to geography: altitude, hill profile, tracks, audience surfaces and the relationship between the facility and the surrounding forest.

frogner_stadion.name: Frogner Stadium
frogner_stadion.desc: Frogner Stadium is a historic sports facility next to Frogner Park, particularly important for speed skating, bandy, football, American football and old athletics traces. It is a good Groundhopper site because it shows how the same arena can shift sporting role across the year and across history.
frogner_stadion.popupDesc: Frogner Stadium has a long sporting history in Oslo. The stadium was moved to its present location in 1914, and has been used for speed skating, bandy, football, athletics and later also American football. Several skating records and championships are tied to the site, and its winter/summer use makes the arena a good example of multi-sport in an urban format. In History Go, Frogner should function as a classic multi-sport site where the player can collect skating history, bandy, football traces, stadium use and the relationship between park, city and sport.

valle_hovin_stadion.name: Valle Hovin Stadium
valle_hovin_stadion.desc: Valle Hovin Stadium is an artificial-ice facility at Valle that ties together speed skating, bandy, concert memories and the sporting weight of the Vålerenga area. The site matters as one of Oslo’s major ice-sport venues and as a historic neighbour to Intility Arena.
valle_hovin_stadion.popupDesc: Valle Hovin Stadium has a distinct place in Oslo’s skating and bandy history. The facility opened in 1966 as an artificial-ice rink and was later used both for ice sports and for major public events. After the rehabilitation in 2021–2023 and the official reopening in 2024, the site has entered a new phase as a modern artificial-ice facility. In a Groundhopper context, Valle Hovin should be read together with Intility and Vallhall: a complete sporting landscape at Valle where football, skating, bandy, training and major events lie close together.

daelenenga_idrettspark.name: Dælenenga sports park
daelenenga_idrettspark.desc: Dælenenga opened in 1916 as a football and athletics ground. Its velodrome, speedway era, 1952 Olympic matches, present artificial-turf pitch and Grünerhallen reveal successive layers of east-side sport.
daelenenga_idrettspark.popupDesc: Dælenenga at Seilduksgata 30 opened in 1916 on land previously used for clay extraction. A clubhouse followed in 1926 and a velodrome in 1929. Speedway races used the ground from 1947 to 1968, while ice hockey and bandy connected it to the 1952 Winter Olympics. Today the sports park combines an eleven-a-side artificial-turf pitch with Grünerhallen. The vanished cycling and speedway tracks must be read through sources rather than treated as present-day features.

gressbanen.name: Gressbanen
gressbanen.desc: Gressbanen at Holmen is a historic football and bandy ground, known as an early national-team venue and as the home of Ready. It matters particularly for Groundhopper because it shows football’s transition from early grass pitches and international matches to local club and bandy tradition.
gressbanen.popupDesc: Gressbanen opened in 1918 and was one of the earliest grass pitches in Norwegian football history. It was the main arena for the national team before Ullevaal took over the role, and has also been a cup-final venue and a bandy arena. In today’s History Go, Gressbanen should function as a historic groundhopper site: a point where the player can collect early national-team football, Ready, bandy, artificial ice, old crowd memories and the transition from national venue to local club ground. The site lends itself to questions about what a pitch was before stadium culture became standardised.

ekebergsletta.name: Ekebergsletta
ekebergsletta.desc: Ekebergsletta is one of Oslo’s largest grassroots-sport landscapes and the main site of Norway Cup. Here football is not just stadium, but field, tournament, teams, volunteering, logistics, international encounters and thousands of small matches on the same expanse of grass.
ekebergsletta.popupDesc: Ekebergsletta is crucial for the Groundhopper function because the site shows a different form of sports statistics than the stadiums. Here it is about the number of pitches, the number of teams, matches, age groups, tournament memories and the temporary sporting community that emerges during Norway Cup. The field also has older layers, with traces of airfield plans and outdoor leisure use, but in History Go the site should be used first and foremost as Oslo’s great stage for grassroots football. Ekebergsletta makes it possible to collect tournament sites, pitch areas, clubs from around the world and football as social infrastructure.

kfum_arena.name: KFUM Arena
kfum_arena.desc: KFUM Arena at Ekeberg is a modern club ground for KFUM Oslo, closely linked to Ekebergsletta and the club’s journey into Norwegian top-flight football. The site fits well in Groundhopper because it shows how a small arena can take on major sporting significance when the club rises.
kfum_arena.popupDesc: KFUM Arena is an important new Oslo site on the football map. The arena is located at Ekeberg and is used by KFUM Oslo, which in recent years has turned the club’s home ground into a visible point in top-flight football. For History Go, the site should generate questions about club growth, temporary stadium requirements, capacity, pitch dimensions, attendance records and the relationship between the grassroots-sport landscape at Ekeberg and the demands of the Eliteserien around a club ground. The Groundhopper logic here should be about proximity, small scale, club culture and statistics that change meaning when the division level changes.

nordre_aasen_idrettspark.name: Nordre Åsen Sports Park
nordre_aasen_idrettspark.desc: Nordre Åsen Sports Park is Skeid’s home area and an important football site in northeast Oslo. The site ties together club history, artificial turf, local recruitment, promotion and a stadium form smaller than the major arenas, but close to the club’s identity.
nordre_aasen_idrettspark.popupDesc: Nordre Åsen Sports Park is a natural Groundhopper site because it represents mid-level club football in Oslo. Skeid has been based here since the postwar period, and the ground has been upgraded for league play and modern requirements. In History Go, the site should be used for questions about Skeid, talent development, artificial turf, local stadium culture, capacity and the difference between a tradition-rich club ground and the major city arenas. The site also offers good comparisons with KFUM Arena, Intility and Ullevaal.

vallhall_arena.name: Vallhall Arena
vallhall_arena.desc: Vallhall Arena is a large indoor football and multi-use arena at Valle-Hovin, closely linked to the Vålerenga environment and winter training. The site enriches the Groundhopper map because it shows the arena behind the arena: training matches, indoor football, fairs and sporting infrastructure around Intility.
vallhall_arena.popupDesc: Vallhall Arena opened in 2001 and lies in the same sporting landscape as Intility Arena and Valle Hovin Stadium. It is used particularly for football, training, winter matches and major events. In History Go, Vallhall should not be treated as the main stadium for match mythology, but as an important support facility in the sporting city: the place where training logistics, indoor surfaces, club preparations and major events become part of the same system. For Groundhopper, Vallhall offers its own collection category for indoor football arenas and sporting infrastructure.

manglerudhallen.name: Manglerudhallen
manglerudhallen.desc: Manglerudhallen is the home arena of Manglerud Stars and an important eastern ice-hockey site in Oslo. The arena gives Groundhopper mode a local hockey rink beyond the most iconic city-centre points, with club history, ice-hall culture and proximity to everyday sport.
manglerudhallen.popupDesc: Manglerudhallen opened in 1979 and is the home arena of Manglerud Star Ishockey. It is important in Oslo sport because it represents club hockey at district level: a hall with its own rituals, local players, regular crowds and a history that is less monumental than Jordal, but no less relevant for understanding the hockey map. In History Go, Manglerudhallen should be used for questions about the ice-hall network, club affiliation, capacity, district sport and the difference between a local hockey hall and a major elite arena.

furuset_forum.name: Furuset Forum
furuset_forum.desc: Furuset Forum is an important ice-hockey and multi-use hall in the Groruddalen valley, linked to Furuset Ishockey and to eastern Oslo sporting circles. It gives the Groundhopper map a clear valley node, where ice hockey, handball, floorball and local club culture come together in one hall.
furuset_forum.popupDesc: Furuset Forum opened in its present form in 1998 and has a central role for Furuset Ishockey and other indoor sports. The hall is also interesting because Vålerenga Ishockey used it temporarily while the new Jordal Amfi was being built. For History Go, Furuset Forum should be a place where the player can collect hockey history, Groruddalen sport, temporary elite use, local club culture and multi-use hall as a sporting form. The site lends itself well to showing how major sporting narratives also live in smaller halls outside the city centre.

torshovdalen.name: Torshovdalen training and activity park
torshovdalen.desc: Long park valley between Torshov and Sinsen, with running, walks, ski and sledging play, ski-leik and a winter jib and snowboard park.
torshovdalen.popupDesc: Torshovdalen is a training site because the park has length, elevation difference and seasonal variation. Here you can run intervals, walk, roll, cycle, sledge, use the ski-leik area in winter and follow the park as a long training line between Torshov and Sinsen.

sognsvann.name: Sognsvann training loop
sognsvann.desc: Classic outdoor and training area at Sognsvann, with running, walking, swimming, forest trails and skiing in winter.
sognsvann.popupDesc: Sognsvann functions as a low-threshold training site for the whole city. The loop around the lake can be used for walking, jogging, intervals, easy recovery, swimming, forest trails and winter activity. In Wonderkammer, the site should show many ways of training without everything having to be organised sport.

bla.name: Blå
bla.desc: Concert venue by the Akerselva with graffiti, club culture and underground pulse.
bla.popupDesc:
Blå, by the Akerselva, has been a central venue for Oslo’s underground since the late 1990s. Around the venue, club culture, hip-hop, electronica, jazz, skateboarders and street art meet in an area where masonry walls, bridges and backyards have long been part of the city’s informal expression.

In the history of subculture, Blå matters as a site where music scenes, graffiti and nightlife overlap without being polished away. Here the urban space is about self-organised communities, DIY energy and audiences who actively use the area before, during and after concerts.

vulkan_murvegger.name: Vulkan walls and passages
vulkan_murvegger.desc: Passages and masonry surfaces around Vulkan where street expressions shift continuously with the urban life along the Akerselva.
vulkan_murvegger.popupDesc:
The Vulkan area combines bridges, back rooms and masonry walls used as visual surfaces in the transition between cultural venues, hospitality and night-time use. Here tagging, stickers, paste-ups and larger wall works appear side by side, often in rapid turnover.

The site is relevant in subculture because the expressions live in an everyday space with high throughflow, not in a closed gallery. The area shows how informal visual culture follows the rhythm of the city’s evening life, events and spontaneous encounters along the river.

hausmannsgate_aksen.name: Hausmannsgate axis
hausmannsgate_aksen.desc: Street axis with wall surfaces, posters and a DIY character around the Hausmannskvartalet block.
hausmannsgate_aksen.popupDesc:
Along Hausmannsgate and the side streets lies an urban space where street art, posters, political stencils and temporary expressions have been visible over a long period. The proximity to self-organised cultural communities means that visual traces often function as communication between scenes, audiences and activists.

In a subcultural sense, the axis matters because it shows how urban expressions emerge in friction between cultural activity, urban development and the everyday use of the street. Here the city is read through layer upon layer of temporary markings.

kolstadgata_toyen_vegger.name: Kolstadgata wall environment
kolstadgata_toyen_vegger.desc: Wall environment in Tøyen with local murals, tags and shifting street expressions.
kolstadgata_toyen_vegger.popupDesc:
Kolstadgata and the neighbouring passages in Tøyen are used regularly for visual expressions ranging from quick signatures to larger wall works. The area is closely linked to youth culture, music and local initiatives that actively use the urban space.

The site is relevant for subculture because the expressions do not stand still: they are painted over, updated and reinterpreted. That turns the street into an ongoing conversation about belonging, style and who shapes the neighbourhood.

gronland_underganger.name: Grønland underpasses
gronland_underganger.desc: Underpasses and technical surfaces at Grønland where tagging and street graphics shape the urban space.
gronland_underganger.popupDesc:
In the transitions between Grønland, Vaterland and the public-transport hub lie underpasses, pillars and walls with dense layers of tags, paste-ups and markings. Here the expressions are often quick and temporary, but they create a clear visual language for an area in constant movement.

This is subculture in practice: informal traces in a transit space where many pass through, few stop and new layers keep arriving. The area shows how street culture also lives in everyday infrastructure.

nybrua_pilarrom.name: Nybrua pillar space
nybrua_pilarrom.desc: Pillar space and wall surfaces by Nybrua used for graffiti, stickers and small-scale wall work.
nybrua_pilarrom.popupDesc:
The spaces under and around Nybrua are a classic transition site between the city centre, Vaterland and Grünerløkka. Pillars and side walls function as surfaces for quick tags, crew markings and layered expressions that change from week to week.

The site is subculturally relevant because it combines night-time use, throughflow and visual self-organisation. Here the city’s back rooms become an active stage for informal aesthetics and local presence.

schweigaards_gate_lodalen.name: Schweigaards gate–Lodalen wall axis
schweigaards_gate_lodalen.desc: Longer street axis with technical walls, track areas and varied street expressions.
schweigaards_gate_lodalen.popupDesc:
From lower Schweigaards gate toward Lodalen runs an axis of retaining walls, underpasses and technical surfaces that are regularly used for graffiti and other informal visual expressions. The environment is less polished than the more central hotspots and is marked by industrial edge and transport logic.

The axis is relevant in subculture because it shows another side of street art: everyday surfaces in the margin between housing, traffic and the railway. The expressions are often temporary, but over time they build a clear archive of the urban space.

kuba_akselpassasjer.name: Kuba passages along the Akerselva
kuba_akselpassasjer.desc: Passages near Kuba where walls, fences and back rooms are used for street-based expressions.
kuba_akselpassasjer.popupDesc:
Between Kuba, Nedre Foss and the riverbank lie narrow passages and back rooms where tagging, stencils and smaller wall works appear continuously. The area is used by people on their way to concerts, bars and late-night food, which gives a high turnover in the expressions.

The site fits subculture because it ties together social night life and informal visual production. Here street expressions are part of the city’s daily pulse, not a polished, curated end product.

grunerlokka_bakgardsvegger.name: Grünerløkka backyard walls
grunerlokka_bakgardsvegger.desc: Backyard and side-street walls in Grünerløkka with shifting graffiti and a DIY aesthetic.
grunerlokka_bakgardsvegger.popupDesc:
In the backyards and side streets of Grünerløkka lies a dense network of walls with tags, throw-ups, posters and small interventions. Many expressions live only briefly, but the sum of the layers gives the area a recognisable visual language tied to the music scene, night-time use and local creative practice.

This is subculturally relevant because it is about how the city is used outside the institutional venues. The back rooms function as informal surfaces for visibility, experimentation and belonging.

alnaelva_hovedsteder.name: Alnaelva
alnaelva_hovedsteder.desc: Oslo’s longest river, with its source in Lillomarka/Alnsjøen and outlet in Bjørvika, shaped at once by natural corridor, intervention and restoration.
alnaelva_hovedsteder.popupDesc:
The Alnaelva is Oslo’s longest river and runs through woodland, residential areas, industrial and logistics landscapes before discharging into Bjørvika. Along the river one finds both culverted and open stretches, traces of hard technical control and more recent efforts at restoration, reopening and the reinforcement of blue–green corridors.

In History Go, the Alnaelva should be read as a key natural-science site in which water system, green structure, pollution, restoration and nature–city friction take centre stage. Questions should start in the watercourse, water quality, green corridor, intervention, reopening and management, not in generic walking-trail romanticism.

nonneseter_kloster.name: Nonneseter convent
nonneseter_kloster.desc: Nonneseter was a Benedictine convent for women in medieval Oslo, first mentioned in 1161. The convent lay at Leiran beside the Hovinbekken stream and became a large landowner with farms across eastern Norway. After the Reformation the institution and its buildings disappeared, but street names, archaeological finds and the historical anchor show where women lived a religious, economic and organisational life.
nonneseter_kloster.popupDesc:
Nonneseter was a Benedictine convent for women in medieval Oslo. It is first mentioned in written sources in 1161 and was probably founded by the bishop of Oslo shortly before. The convent lay at Leiran, north of the Hovinbekken stream and west of today's junction between Schweigaards gate and Grønlandsleiret. No standing convent building marks the site today.

The nuns' daily life was organised around the canonical hours, services, work and shared rules. The convent gave women an institutional role in the church that differed from both marriage and ordinary household life. The abbess led the community and could manage property, income and connections on the convent's behalf.

Nonneseter became a significant landowner. According to the Oslo City Encyclopaedia, the convent at one point owned 272 farms in the eastern Norwegian region. The estate secured food, raw materials and income, but also made the convent an economic power. Traces of that ownership are found in the history of farms far outside the medieval town.

The convent's location shows how Oslo consisted of several religious institutions with different functions. The royal manor, the bishop's castle, men's monasteries, churches and Nonneseter all belonged to the same town, but represented different networks and forms of authority. The convent is therefore a reminder that medieval power was not exercised solely by kings, bishops and male religious orders.

After the Reformation in the sixteenth century, monastic life was wound up and the properties taken over by other authorities and owners. The buildings gradually disappeared. During an excavation in 1879 Peter Blix found skeletons and a corner of ashlar that may have belonged to the convent church, but the finds give no grounds for pretending that a visible ruin still exists.

Today's marker is therefore a historical, approximate anchor. Nonnegata and the former street name Klostergangen preserve the memory on the city map, while sources and archaeology must fill the empty space with knowledge. Nonneseter makes it possible to tell medieval history through women's religious life, property management and institutional power, while the absence shows how easily such places can vanish physically. The city around it has changed completely, but the convent's properties and names continue to shape how historians understand medieval Oslo. The invisible site therefore demands more source criticism than a ruin, not less.

oslo_ladegard.name: Oslo Ladegård
oslo_ladegard.desc: Oslo Ladegård was built as a country house in 1725 on the cellar walls of Christen Mule's house and above the ruins of the medieval bishop's castle. The name refers to the fact that old Oslo became the home farm of Akershus Castle after 1624. The building today houses interpretation, guided tours and events, and gives access to the reconstructed winter hall of the bishop's castle.
oslo_ladegard.popupDesc:
Oslo Ladegård was built as a country house in 1725. The main building stands on cellar walls from the house of mayor Christen Mule, which in turn stood over parts of the medieval bishop's castle. The site therefore gathers three distinct building layers: the bishop's seat of power, a wealthy mayor's house and an eighteenth-century Baroque country estate.

In Christen Mule's house the Scottish king James VI and the Danish-Norwegian princess Anne were married in 1589. When Christian IV moved the town westwards after the fire of 1624, the area in old Oslo was laid out as the home farm of Akershus Castle. From here, agriculture and resources were to contribute to supplying the fortress.

The name Ladegården comes from that function. The property changed owners and users before the present house was built. The Baroque complex was given a ceremonial main building and a garden that stood apart from the medieval ruins around it. At the same time, wall remains and terrain continued to carry the history of the bishop's castle beneath the new house.

By the side wing, a room from the bishop's castle has been reconstructed, often called Bishop Nikolas's chapel or the winter hall. It gives access to masonry from around the year 1200 and shows how the bishop lived and exercised power close to St. Hallvard's Cathedral. The room makes medieval institutions concrete beneath the floor of a later building.

The City of Oslo today uses Ladegården for interpretation, guided tours, meetings, concerts and events. Walks through the Medieval Park and the ruin areas start from here. The building therefore serves as a practical entrance to a historic landscape that can otherwise be hard to grasp between roads, railway and modern development.

Ladegården should not be read as an ordinary old farm. It shows how the city after 1624 took over and built above the former capital, and how heritage conservation has later opened these layers again. In one place, episcopal power, a royal wedding, the supply of a fortress, Baroque representation and today's public history all meet. The Baroque garden outside the house also carries forward the connection between building and landscape. It is reconstructed as an interpreted historical environment rather than preserved unchanged from the eighteenth century, and makes it possible to discuss both authenticity and historical reconstruction.

gamle_radhus.name: The Old Town Hall
gamle_radhus.desc: The Old Town Hall was built beside Christiania Torv in 1641 and served as the town hall until 1733. Here the magistracy met, the court sat and prisoners were held in the vaulted cellar. The building later housed church services, theatre, a masonic lodge and the Supreme Court. Today the ground floor is a restaurant and the first floor is used for concerts and performances.
gamle_radhus.popupDesc:
The Old Town Hall was built beside Christiania Torv in 1641, less than twenty years after Christian IV moved the town westwards following the fire of 1624. The building stood on the new town's central square and gave Christiania a permanent house for local government, justice and public assembly.

The town hall was originally a two-storey brick building with a stair tower, a steep pitched roof and Renaissance gables. The magistracy and the town council met here, while court proceedings and the lock-up were gathered in the same complex. The vaulted arrest cellar is the most important surviving part of the building's original interior.

The building served as the town hall until 1733, when decay led the administration to move to Rådhusgata 7. The large public room also had other functions. After Holy Trinity Church burned in 1686, the building was used for services, and travelling actors used it as a theatre hall.

After the town hall period the property was sold into private hands. It was a private residence and a masonic lodge on several occasions. Between 1815 and 1846 the Supreme Court sat here, so that the building continued to be a place of state judicial authority long after the municipal administration had moved out.

Restaurant operations began in a side wing in 1856 and moved into the main building in 1926. The restaurant was given an interior designed by Carl and Hagbart Berner. A fire in 1996 damaged the house, but the restaurant interior was recreated. Restored stepped gables from 1971 show at the same time how later periods have tried to return the building to a presumed older appearance.

Today Restaurant Gamle Raadhus occupies the ground floor, while Opera til folket and other organisers use the rooms above for concerts and performances. The Old Town Hall is therefore not merely a memory of the town council. The building gathers municipal power, imprisonment, church service, theatre, the Supreme Court, a restaurant and a cultural venue in one house beside the square that organised the new town after 1624. Its continued use shows how an institutional building can change role without losing its connection to the city's political and social history.

galgeberg.name: Galgeberg
galgeberg.desc: Galgeberg is named after Oslo's public place of execution, known as Martestokker since the Middle Ages. Executions were sited on the main road outside the town, where the punishment could be seen by travellers and townspeople. The original rock is much altered by later building and roads, but names such as Galgeberg and Justiskroken preserve the site of judgement on today's city map.
galgeberg.popupDesc:
Galgeberg is today a residential and traffic area between Vålerenga and Gamlebyen, but the name goes back to Oslo's old place of execution. In the Middle Ages the site was called Martestokker. Executions and other public punishments were placed outside the dense town, beside an important approach road, so that the authorities' power could be seen by travellers and residents alike.

The execution site lay on a rock in the area between today's Strømsveien, St. Halvards gate and Åkebergveien. Gallows, breaking wheels and other instruments of punishment turned the body into a public warning. The punishment was not meant only to strike the condemned; it was to show which acts society and the authorities defined as crimes.

Justiskroken, an old footpath traceable on maps from 1745, led up towards the execution site. The street name and the place name are therefore not incidental curiosities but sources for how the justice system was placed in the landscape. The path tied the town to the place where sentences were made physically visible.

Executions at Galgeberg continued into the early modern period. Gradually punishment was moved from open execution sites to houses of correction, workhouses and prisons. That transition changed the public sphere: the body disappeared from the town's view, while discipline, labour and isolation were organised behind walls and institutional gates.

The historic rock is largely gone or reshaped by roads, apartment blocks and other development. There is no preserved gallows that the marker can pretend to point to. A blue plaque and the names Galgeberg and Justiskroken are among the most important visible traces of the function.

Galgeberg should therefore be presented soberly as legal and social history. The place shows how punishment, shame and deterrence were built into the city's geography, and how modern urban development can erase the terrain itself without removing the name. Compared with the Penitentiary and Møllergata 19, Galgeberg makes the shift from public bodily punishment to closed institutions clear. It also provides a starting point for asking who was punished, who could judge, and how class, gender and social position shaped the encounter with the law. The history of the execution site is therefore about more than the executions themselves.

oslo_hospital.name: Oslo Hospital
oslo_hospital.desc: Oslo Hospital traces its history back to the Franciscan monastery of 1290. After the Reformation, Christian III made the complex the town's hospital in 1538, caring for the poor and the sick. The work later developed towards psychiatric treatment and continued on the site until 2018. The historic complex is now being converted into workplaces and open meeting areas in Gamlebyen.
oslo_hospital.popupDesc:
Oslo Hospital stands on the site where Franciscan friars established a monastery in 1290. The monastery lay outside the medieval town, beside the main road from the south.
