The friars maintained religious life and cared for the sick, for lepers and for other vulnerable people. Health and help were thus tied to the site long before modern hospitals existed.

After the Reformation, Christian III ordered in 1538 that the monastery buildings be taken over and used as the town's hospital. The Oslo Hospital foundation was established with responsibility for people who lacked family or others who could support and nurse them. Church care, poor relief and public control were closely interwoven.

Over the centuries both patient groups and forms of treatment changed. The complex housed a hostel, nursing care and eventually psychiatric treatment. Buildings were demolished, erected and rebuilt, but the institution kept its connection to the old monastic site. Gamlebyen church, also called Oslo Hospital's church, carries forward the religious part of the history.

The hospital was not merely a place of medical treatment. It shows how society organised responsibility for the poor, the sick and people with mental illness before the welfare state. Help could provide food and protection, but could also mean long-term institutionalisation and little control over one's own life.

Hospital operations continued until 2018. After the closure, an extensive transformation of the historic complex began. The plans involve offices, businesses, catering and meeting places, and the area is to be opened more towards the neighbourhood than it was under the closed institutional regime.

Oslo Hospital therefore holds over seven hundred years of monastic, hospital and psychiatric history. It should not be presented as a modern hospital still receiving patients, but as a historic institutional area in transition. As gates and courtyards open for new use, the question also arises of how the experiences of former residents and patients are to be preserved and conveyed. The ongoing transformation moreover shows that institutional history does not end when operations cease. Architecture, church, burial ground and the stories of the patients follow the area into its new office and meeting-place function. The history calls for careful interpretation.

botsfengselet.name: The Penitentiary
botsfengselet.desc: The Penitentiary opened at Grønland in 1851 as Norway's first modern national prison. The complex was built on the Philadelphia system, in which male long-term inmates were to work and repent in isolated single cells. Cell wings, chapel, exercise yards and a perimeter wall organised the control. "Botsen" was in use for more than 160 years and is listed as a principal work in Norwegian prison history.
botsfengselet.popupDesc:
The Penitentiary opened at Grønland in 1851 as a national prison for male long-term inmates. It was Norway's first prison built to a unified modern system and marked a break with houses of correction, fortress labour and other older forms of punishment. The sentence was not merely to inflict pain, but to shape the inmate through order, work, religion and repentance.

The plan was based on the Philadelphia system. Prisoners were held separately in single cells and were in principle to be shielded from one another's negative influence. The isolation was at the same time a severe psychological burden. The architecture made the system physical: cell wings, control points, chapel and exercise yards governed movement, sight and contact.

The single cell was at once living space, workplace and instrument of punishment. Inmates worked at various crafts and followed a class system in which good conduct could bring certain privileges. Morality, discipline and productivity were tied together. The prison therefore shows how nineteenth-century reform ideas could also create new forms of pervasive control.

The complex was altered many times as prisoner numbers, security requirements and views of punishment developed. The isolation gradually became less absolute, but the cell building and the perimeter wall continued to shape daily life. The Penitentiary became part of the larger Oslo Prison and was in operation for more than 160 years.

The prison's history encompasses staff, inmates, labour, conflicts and attempts at rehabilitation alike. The place must therefore not be reduced to spectacular prisoner stories or popular-culture associations. The most important questions concern what society wanted to achieve through punishment, and what consequences prolonged isolation had for the people held here.

The complex is listed and is regarded as a principal work of Norwegian prison architecture. It makes the transition from Galgeberg's open execution site to a closed institution clear. Behind the wall, punishment became less visible to the public but more minutely organised around the individual body and its time. The Penitentiary is thus at once reform history, architecture of power and social history. Its preservation offers a rare opportunity to examine the system through the spaces themselves, not only through laws and statistics. The width of the cells, the corridors and the exercise yards show how the ideas were translated into daily routine.

prinds_christian_augusts_minde.name: Prinds Christian Augusts Minde
prinds_christian_augusts_minde.desc: Prinds Christian Augusts Minde was founded in 1809 to help the poor and unemployed and bought Mangelsgården in 1812. From 1819 the complex developed into a workhouse, forced-labour institution, poor hospital, madhouse and asylum. The listed block in Storgata shows how care, work, discipline and exclusion were gathered in one of the city's most important social institutions.
prinds_christian_augusts_minde.popupDesc:
Prinds Christian Augusts Minde was established in 1809 by prosperous citizens of Christiania. The foundation was to help the poor and unemployed and was named after the governor Christian August. In 1812 it bought Mangelsgården in Storgata, an older country house that provided room for workshops, housing and eventually an extensive institutional complex.

The poor relief authority's spinning works were moved here, and in 1819 a permanent workhouse opened. The idea was that people without income should be given work and help. In practice the line between a voluntary offer and coercion blurred early. The poor, the unemployed, disabled people and others the authorities wished to control could be placed here.

Through the nineteenth century the complex grew with new wings and functions. It housed a work institution, forced labour, a poor hospital, a madhouse for people with mental illness and later an asylum and sheltered home. Different groups lived close together but were sorted by sex, capacity for work, health and the authorities' assessment of their worthiness.

Work was treated as help, moral education and discipline all at once. The institution shows how poverty was often understood as personal failing or disorder, and not only as the result of wages, housing conditions and illness. Care and punishment could therefore use the same rooms, rules and demands for labour.

The complex is known as Prindsen, Mangelsgården and "the quarter of the poor". The buildings and courtyards make it possible to follow more than two hundred years of social policy in one place. At the same time the history is fragmented, because the people who lived and worked here often left fewer sources of their own than the management and the authorities did.

Prindsen is listed and is today used by various social, cultural and municipal initiatives. New use gives access to parts of the block, but also makes the telling of its history important. The place should not merely relate a successful charitable foundation. It must show how help, forced labour, psychiatry, poor relief and exclusion were interwoven in the heart of the city. The courtyards and wings make it possible to compare the institution's many periods without compressing them into a single story. Charity, poverty policy and coercion must be kept visible at the same time.

bislett.name: Bislett
bislett.desc: Bislett grew up on the Bisaalit smallholding, where a brickworks stood in the nineteenth century. The municipality bought more than 60 decares in 1898 for a sports ground; Bislet baths opened in 1920 and the stadium in 1922. Around Oslo's first roundabout, trams, housing, a brewery and a tobacco factory met and together created the famous "Bislett smell" of malt and tobacco.
bislett.popupDesc:
The name Bislett goes back to the Bisaalit smallholding on the old road between Old Aker Church and Frogner. The area long lay outside the dense city. In the nineteenth century a brickworks operated here, while parts of the land were parcelled out for housing and industry. As the city grew northwards, the open ground became a rare expanse of space close to the new tenement blocks.

The City of Oslo bought more than 60 decares of the smallholding in 1898 to lay out a sports ground. Martinus Lørdahl had the area developed from 1907. The ground was used for athletics, skating and football, and in 1913 Norway met Sweden here in an international match. The sports ground became the centre of a district that soon took the name Bislett after the smallholding.

Bislet baths opened in 1920 in the building that replaced the old smallholding house. Harald Aars and Lorentz Ree designed the baths, which had Oslo's first indoor swimming hall. The pool measured 16 2/3 metres, and the facility also housed tub baths and other hygiene services at a time when many flats had no bathroom of their own. The sculpture After the Bath by Anders Svor was placed outside.

Bislett stadium was inaugurated in 1922 with a main stand and clubhouse designed by Ole Sverre. The complex was later extended and became known for speed skating, athletics and the 1952 Winter Olympics. The stadium gave the district an international name, but everyday life around it also consisted of trams, schools, shops, baths, workshops and dense housing. The old stadium was demolished in 2004 and replaced by today's facility in 2005.

Industry left a very concrete mark on the neighbourhood. The Frydenlund Brewery produced beer nearby, while Conrad Langaard's tobacco factory lay on the other side of the area. The smell of malt and tobacco mingled in the streets and became known as the "Bislett smell". The Anker Battery Factory and the Kristiania Bread Factory were also based in the district. Several former industrial sites were later taken over by college and university activity.

Between the stadium, Bislet baths and the residential blocks, Oslo's first roundabout was laid out. It made Bislett a local traffic hub where several streets and transport lines met. The district is therefore not merely the name of a stadium. It is a former smallholding and brickworks area where sport, public health, industry, housing and transport were built tightly together.

saga_kino.name: Saga cinema
saga_kino.desc: Saga cinema opened in the Odd Fellow building in Stortingsgata in 1934 as Oslo Kinematografer's great functionalist cinema. The opening film was Sinners in the Sun, and the Philharmonic Society Orchestra played in the auditorium. After conversion into six screens in 1981, Saga became a model for modern multiplex cinemas and later a city-centre venue for children's and family films.
saga_kino.popupDesc:
Saga cinema opened on 14 February 1934 in the Odd Fellow building at Stortingsgata 28. The architects Gudolf Blakstad and Herman Munthe-Kaas designed both the building and the cinema as a flagship for the municipal company Oslo Kinematografer. The original auditorium had a gallery, boxes and 1,482 seats in total, and formed part of one of the most striking functionalist buildings of the interwar years in central Oslo.

The opening was staged as a major cultural event. The Philharmonic Society Orchestra, today's Oslo Philharmonic, played music by Edvard Grieg and Christian Sinding under Olav Kielland. The opening film was the Norwegian Sinners in the Sun, based on Sigurd Hoel's novel. Audiences were met by uniformed ticket collectors and ushers, and a special short film showed how the cinema had been built from excavation to finished structure.

Saga early became more than a place for ordinary film screenings. In 1937 the Women's League for Peace and the Socialist Cultural Front demonstrated against the war film The Lost Squadron. It was the first organised political protest against a film screening in Norway. In 1973 the cinema was also used for the public meeting that led to the founding of Anders Lange's Party, the forerunner of the Progress Party.

The single large auditorium was later judged inflexible in the face of a new cinema market. After a complete rebuilding, Saga reopened on 1 December 1981 as a cinema complex with six screens. The solution was a commercial success and a model for the later subdivision of large cinemas in Oslo and other Norwegian cities. The place therefore also tells the story of the shift from the monumental premiere cinema to multiplex operation.

The Odd Fellow building around the cinema has had a far darker parallel history. During the occupation the Reichskommissariat requisitioned the building, which the Germans called "Kabahaus". It held offices, radio communications, a canteen and a large switchboard. The cinema's history therefore lies inside a building that also carries clear traces of the occupying power and of shifting post-war uses.

Saga was later profiled as a children's and family cinema in the city centre. After a lengthy closure it was modernised and reopened in November 2025 with respect for its historic identity. Today Saga is both an active cinema and a layered piece of urban history: functionalist architecture, an orchestral opening, film protests, the founding of a political party, occupation history and the development of the modern Norwegian multiplex all meet in the same building.

klingenberg_kino.name: Klingenberg cinema
klingenberg_kino.desc: Klingenberg cinema opened in 1938 on the site of the Circus Building in Christiania Tivoli. Gudolf Blakstad and Herman Munthe-Kaas designed the monumental main auditorium, which quickly became Oslo's foremost premiere venue. Here came the city's first late-night cinema in 1970, the art-house screen Veslefrikk in 1972 and later Kinoteket, a forerunner of the Cinemateket.
klingenberg_kino.popupDesc:
Klingenberg cinema opened on 6 October 1938 at Olav V's gate 4, then Roald Amundsens gate. The cinema was built for Oslo Kinematografer to designs by Gudolf Blakstad and Herman Munthe-Kaas. The site had previously held the Circus Building in Christiania Tivoli, a venue for circus, concerts, sport and film. The first public film screenings in Norway were held in the Tivoli area in 1896.

At its opening the main auditorium had 1,215 seats and was described as Oslo's finest cinema. The inaugural film was The Kid, based on Oskar Braaten's play, with Eva Sletto and Harald Heide Steen. The large auditorium, the foyer and the central location beside the National Theatre made Klingenberg the capital's most important venue for gala premieres, Norwegian first screenings and major international launches.

During the occupation the auditorium was also used politically. Nasjonal Samling and the German authorities held meetings here, including with Vidkun Quisling as speaker, and the building was used in recruiting front-line volunteers. After the war it returned as a national premiere venue. King Haakon VII attended the world premiere of The Battle of Heavy Water in 1948, among other occasions, and had a fixed seat in the so-called royal row.

A succession of Norwegian films had their first large public screenings here, including Operation Leafspring, An-Magritt and Pinchcliffe Grand Prix. On 26 June 1970 Klingenberg held Oslo's first late-night screening with MASH. The main auditorium was adapted for the wide CinemaScope format as early as 1955, and the cinema has since taken 70-millimetre film into use for productions requiring a particularly large image and rich detail.

Klingenberg also became a laboratory for alternative forms of exhibition. The art-house screen Veslefrikk opened in the basement in 1972 and made the complex Oslo's first multi-screen cinema. Biografen followed in 1975, and in 1980 Kinoteket was established as a cinema for older films. Kinoteket is regarded as a forerunner of the Cinemateket. A third small auditorium opened in 1984, and the complex was marketed as Klingenberg 1–4.

The main auditorium was restored and reduced to 766 seats in the 1990s. The interior and foyer were treated as heritage, and the cinema is listed. Klingenberg is therefore not merely an old cinema but a physical archive of Norwegian film exhibition: from municipal cinema policy and royal premieres to occupation propaganda, art house, late-night screenings, the Cinemateket and today's large-format projection.

gimle_kino.name: Gimle cinema
gimle_kino.desc: Gimle cinema opened at Frogner in 1939 as a premiere cinema, designed by Gunnar T. Schultz and Ragnvald Tønsager. The cinema developed a clear profile for European quality film and an adult audience. After modernisation in 1997 the auditorium gained greater comfort and wine service, and from 2008 live opera, ballet and theatre entered the programme.
gimle_kino.popupDesc:
Gimle cinema was inaugurated on 23 August 1939 at Bygdøy allé 39. It was built for the municipal company Oslo Kinematografer to designs by the architects Gunnar T. Schultz and Ragnvald Tønsager. With its location in the middle of Frogner, Gimle took over the role of the district's premiere cinema, while the older Frogner cinema was used more for repeat screenings.

The cinema was smaller than the monumental city-centre venues Saga and Klingenberg. Precisely its size and its closeness to the residential streets gave it a different character. Gimle became a cinema one could return to as part of everyday life at Frogner, while its programme had a more strongly curated profile than the broad capital-city cinemas.

The expression "a Gimle film" came in time to be used for European dramas, literary adaptations and other quality films for an adult audience. The profile was not merely a marketing device but a lasting part of Oslo's film culture. Gimle showed that a municipal cinema system could give different houses distinct roles, and that a single auditorium could build a stable audience through repertoire and continuity.

In 1997 the cinema was renovated and modernised by architect Kirsti Skulberg. The upgrade placed great emphasis on comfort, service and a more exclusive cinema experience. Wine service became part of the offer. Gimle thereby also became an example of how older single-screen cinemas could survive competition from large multiplexes by refining their distinctive character rather than copying them.

Digitisation in 2008 opened the way for new kinds of content. Gimle began screening live opera, ballet and theatre, including performances from the Metropolitan Opera in New York. The cinema screen thus became a stage for live art produced elsewhere, and the distinction between film cinema and international cultural venue grew less clear.

Gimle is today operated by Nordisk Film Kino and continues to combine ordinary film screenings with quality film, senior cinema, special events and stage art on screen. The place's history is therefore not about the largest auditorium or the most premieres. It is about how a district cinema from 1939 has survived through a consistent programming profile, a recognisable audience and the ability to change its technology without losing its identity.

vika_kino.name: Vika cinema
vika_kino.desc: Vika cinema opened beside the Oslo Concert Hall in 1997 as a four-screen complex designed by Arcasa Arkitekter. Its largest auditorium was the first in Oslo with THX sound. The cinema tied film exhibition to the modern office, retail and cultural district of Vika and is today used for the ordinary repertoire, festival films, previews and guest events alike.
vika_kino.popupDesc:
Vika cinema lies at Ruseløkkveien 14 with its entrance from Johan Svendsens plass, close to the Oslo Concert Hall. Today's cinema opened on 12 December 1997 and was built for the municipal company Oslo Kinematografer to designs by Arcasa Arkitekter. The complex was given four screens and became part of the modern cultural and service city that grew up in Vestre Vika.

The area around the cinema had been completely transformed several decades earlier. Older small houses, bazaars and the working-class Vika community were demolished, and from the 1960s came office buildings, shops, a concert hall and wide traffic arteries. The cinema was therefore not placed within an old cinema district, but in a planned central area where work, retail, representation and culture were to lie close together.

The largest auditorium was the first cinema in Oslo with THX. The system had been developed to ensure that sound equipment, acoustics and playback met strict technical requirements. This made Vika a clear example of the 1990s emphasis on standardised sound quality, multi-channel formats and a more controlled film experience than older auditoriums were originally built for.

The four screens made it possible to combine broad popular films with smaller releases. The location near the National Theatre, Aker Brygge, City Hall and the transport hubs gave the cinema an audience of commuters, office workers, residents and visitors alike. An evening at the cinema could be linked directly to a restaurant, a concert, work or shopping without the audience having to leave the city centre.

Vika has also been used for film festivals, previews, director visits, panel discussions and curated film weekends. Such events make the cinema more than an automatic screening machine. Audiences meet film-makers and critics, and films that might otherwise have had short ordinary runs are given a clear frame and a gathered audience.

The cinema is today operated by Nordisk Film Kino. It tells a different Oslo story from Saga, Klingenberg and Gimle: not the municipal cinema palace of the interwar years, but the compact multi-screen complex of the 1990s integrated into a modernised district. Vika shows how the cinema became part of the city centre's service economy, while festivals and special screenings can still make it a public meeting place.

hartvig_nissens_skole_skam.name: Hartvig Nissen School (SKAM)
hartvig_nissens_skole_skam.desc: Hartvig Nissen School was founded as Nissen's Girls' School in 1849, while today's main building at Frogner was completed in 1898. The school gained Norway's first music programme in 1955 and a drama programme in 1969. From 2015 its corridors, schoolyard and façades became internationally known as the main setting of NRK's youth series SKAM.
hartvig_nissens_skole_skam.popupDesc:
Hartvig Nissen School was founded by the educator Ole Hartvig Nissen in 1849 as Nissen's Girls' School. The school was an important institution for girls' education at a time when the path to higher education and working life was far narrower for women. After several addresses in the city centre it moved to Frogner, where today's main building was erected in 1898 to designs by architect Henrik Nissen.

The building was sized for around 400 pupils. A gymnasium was added in 1905, and the complex was later extended with neighbouring buildings. The school also ran teacher training for women and had a student class of its own. The municipality took over its operation in 1919, but the institution's long history as a girls' school continued to shape its identity.

During the Second World War the school buildings were requisitioned several times. They were used by the Red Cross, German forces, the home forces and Allied troops. Teaching had to be relocated or shared with other schools. This wartime layer is barely visible in the school's later popular-cultural fame, but shows that the building has also been a military site and a temporary barracks.

In 1955 male pupils were admitted when the school established Norway's first music programme of its kind, on the initiative of Ingeborg Kindem. The school was named Hartvig Nissens skole in 1963 and established a drama programme in 1969. Music, dance and drama thus became a lasting part of the school several decades before it became the setting for one of Norway's best-known television series.

NRK's SKAM used the school as its main setting from 2015. The series followed teenagers through school life, friendship, first love, religion, identity and mental health. Episodes and short clips were published continuously online in the same rhythm as the story unfolded. The digital publishing format meant viewers could follow the characters between television episodes and experience the school as an ongoing social space.

The series ran for four seasons, won numerous awards and reached audiences far beyond Norway. The façade, the schoolyard and the nearby streets became destinations for fans and the starting point for national remakes. Hartvig Nissen School is therefore both a historic educational institution and a media location. The place shows how a real school can retain its ordinary function while television fiction turns it into an international symbol of Norwegian youth culture.

sagene_skole.name: Sagene School
sagene_skole.desc: Sagene School traces its history back to Aker's first parish school of 1741; the oldest surviving building, designed by Jacob Wilhelm Nordan, was completed in 1861. The school gave children in the industrial district teaching, food and help with hygiene. Under Anna Sethne the Sagene experiments from 1930 became an internationally known laboratory for activity-based schooling and Norwegian progressive education.
sagene_skole.popupDesc:
The history of Sagene School goes back to 1741, when the first parish school in Aker was established at Sagene. Over time the provision was divided among several schools. As the factories along the Akerselva drew ever more workers and families to the area, a larger school complex was needed in the new industrial district.

The oldest surviving school building was designed by Jacob Wilhelm Nordan and completed in 1861. It was the second oldest municipally built school building in Christiania. Around the school lay textile factories, a mill, a brewery, workers' housing, public baths and assembly halls. The school became part of a local system of work, housing, hygiene and upbringing.

Many pupils came from families with little financial security. The school was to teach the children to read, write and count, but its work also covered meals, clothing and hygiene. The writer Oskar Braaten was a pupil here and later used the environment along the Akerselva in plays and novels. The schoolyard was thus part of the same working-class city his literature described.

A new school building from 1926 became a model for later school construction. Anna Sethne was head teacher from 1919 to 1938 and made Sagene an internationally known model school. From 1930 she was allowed to carry out the Sagene experiments, in which activity, cooperation, workshop practice and the pupils' own experience were given more room than rote learning and passive listening. The principles influenced later Norwegian schooling.

During the Second World War the buildings were requisitioned as German barracks, and teaching had to be dispersed to temporary premises. After the war the school acquired its own camp site at Hadeland. Vesle Sagene opened in 1951 as Norway's first outdoor school and was to give city children nature, fresh air and practical learning.

Sagene School continued to be an arena for social change. One of Norway's first bilingual classes was established here in 1982. When neo-Nazis threatened the school's participation in the 17 May celebrations in 1983, pupils, parents and politicians responded by defending an inclusive celebration; the following year the pupils carried the slogan "17 May for everyone". The whole complex is listed and was rehabilitated up to 2003. The school is still in operation, in the middle of the cultural environment that shaped it.

trefoldighetskirken.name: Trinity Church
trefoldighetskirken.desc: Trinity Church was consecrated at Hammersborg in 1858 in response to Christiania's rapid growth. Alexis de Chateauneuf won the architectural competition, while Wilhelm von Hanno completed the neo-Gothic central church in red brick. The building has housed large congregations, church movements and public debate, and since 2020 has held a special mandate as a church of peace and reconciliation.
trefoldighetskirken.popupDesc:
Trinity Church was consecrated at Hammersborg in 1858. Christiania had grown sharply, and Oslo Cathedral could not serve the new population alone. The church therefore became the first in a series of large church buildings that followed the capital's expansion in the nineteenth century. When it opened, it stood close to simple timber housing and to families on low incomes.

Alexis de Chateauneuf won the architectural competition in 1849. After he fell ill and died, the work was carried on by his pupil Wilhelm von Hanno. The result was a monumental central church in red brick with an octagonal ground plan, a tall tower and neo-Gothic detailing. The plan gathered the congregation around a central space rather than a long traditional nave.

Construction was demanding and the plans were adjusted along the way. Materials, structure and decoration had both to withstand the Norwegian climate and to give the capital a modern European monumental building. The exposed brick architecture distinguishes the church from the rendered Oslo Cathedral and shows how the neo-Gothic was used to express both historical continuity and new urban self-confidence.

The church has been a setting for services, funerals, concerts, organisational life and religious movements. The large dome and the central space have provided good conditions for music and for large gatherings. At the same time its location between the Supreme Court, the district court, the government quarter and central media houses has made the church a neighbour to several of the state's institutions of power.

Over the years the building has been restored, closed and reopened in step with technical needs and changes in church use. Trinity Church is listed as heritage, but is not merely a preserved work of architecture. Congregations and new user groups have continually given the building tasks other than those envisaged in 1858.

Since 2020 the church has held a special mandate as a church of peace and reconciliation in Oslo. This ties the architecture and the location to conversations about conflict, religion, human rights and social responsibility. Trinity Church can therefore be read both as a product of nineteenth-century urban growth and as an active institution attempting to create a different kind of public space in the midst of the judiciary, politics and the media.

fredriksten_festning.name: Fredriksten Fortress
fredriksten_festning.desc: Border fortress in Halden, begun in 1661 after the loss of Bohuslän. Fredriksten was never captured in battle and is especially known for the siege in 1718, when Charles XII was shot and killed here.
fredriksten_festning.popupDesc: Fredriksten Fortress is one of Østfold’s strongest historic places. The fortress was built to protect the new southeastern border after Norway lost Bohuslän and Bohus Fortress to Sweden. It was attacked several times, but never captured in battle. The event that made the place nationally known was the siege in 1718, when the Swedish king Charles XII was killed at the fortress. In History Go, Fredriksten should be used for border history, defence, state formation, Swedish-Norwegian wars and national symbols.

fredrikstad_festning_gamlebyen.name: Fredrikstad Fortress / Old Town
fredrikstad_festning_gamlebyen.desc: Norway’s only preserved fortified town and one of Europe’s best-preserved fortress towns. Fredrikstad Fortress was begun in 1663 after the loss of Bohuslän and shows the interaction between garrison, citizens, moats and bastion system.
fredrikstad_festning_gamlebyen.popupDesc: Fredrikstad Fortress is the core of the Old Town. It was laid out from 1663 after Norway lost Bohuslän and Bohus Fortress to Sweden, and was designed according to the Old Dutch bastion system with earth ramparts, water-filled moats and bastions. The place is distinctive because military and civilian life have existed side by side inside the fortified town for more than 350 years. In History Go, the place should be used to show how an entire town could be part of the realm’s border defence.

eidsvoll_verk_andelva.name: Eidsvoll Verk / Andelva
eidsvoll_verk_andelva.desc: Historic works and industrial landscape around the Andelva river, closely linked to Eidsvoll Manor and Carsten Anker’s milieu. The place gives background to how economy, industry and politics met before 1814.
eidsvoll_verk_andelva.popupDesc: Eidsvoll Verk and Andelva make the history of 1814 more material. Before Eidsvoll Manor became a national symbol, it stood in a works environment where iron production, hydropower, ownership and international connections were important. The place should be used to show that political history also has economic and technological surroundings: who owned the site, what resources existed, and why could a private estate become the setting for a national assembly?

fetsund_lenser.name: Fetsund Timber Booms
fetsund_lenser.desc: National cultural heritage site where the Glomma flows into Øyeren, established as part of timber floating. Fetsund lenser shows how rivers functioned as industrial infrastructure.
fetsund_lenser.popupDesc: Fetsund lenser is a clear site of labour and transport history. Here timber was sorted and guided through a large installation in the water, where the Glomma meets Øyeren. The place shows how forestry, river, workers, technology and market were connected before modern roads and trucks took over. In History Go, the place should be used for timber floating, labour history, river history and the interaction between nature and culture.

kjeller_flyplass.name: Kjeller Airfield
kjeller_flyplass.desc: Norway’s first military airfield and a key site in Norwegian aviation history. Kjeller links early flight, defence, technological development and preservation issues.
kjeller_flyplass.popupDesc: Kjeller Airfield is one of Norway’s most important aviation-history sites. The first flight from Kjeller came in 1912, and the place has since been closely connected to military aviation, technical maintenance, research and aircraft history. During the Second World War the airfield became part of war history, and in recent times the area has been contested as a cultural environment and development area.

trandumskogen.name: Trandum Forest
trandumskogen.desc: National war memorial at Trandum, where the German occupying power executed prisoners during the Second World War. The place is a serious point of memory for occupation, terror and postwar remembrance work.
trandumskogen.popupDesc: Trandum Forest is one of the darkest and most important war memorial sites in Akershus. During the Second World War, prisoners were executed here by the occupying power and placed in mass graves. After liberation, the graves were found, identification and remembrance work began, and the place gained a central role in national war memory. In History Go, Trandum Forest must be treated as a place for occupation history, source criticism, memory, justice and human dignity.

baerums_verk_jernverk.name: Bærums Verk
baerums_verk_jernverk.desc: Historic ironworks environment by the Lomma river, with roots in the early 1600s. Bærums Verk makes industrial history concrete through mining, smelting works, hydropower, labour, ownership and reuse.
baerums_verk_jernverk.popupDesc: Bærums Verk shows how natural resources, hydropower, ore, privileges and labour organization could create an entire local community around iron production. At the same time, it is a clear example of historical reuse: old production environments have gained new functions as commerce, culture and experiences. In History Go, the place should be used for industrial history, labour history, resource use and cultural environment.

hadeland_glassverk.name: Hadeland Glassworks
hadeland_glassverk.desc: Norwegian glassworks founded in 1762 by Randsfjorden at Jevnaker. Hadeland Glassworks makes industrial history, craft, design and living production visible in the same cultural environment.
hadeland_glassverk.popupDesc: Hadeland Glassworks is one of the most important industrial sites in Akershus after Jevnaker became part of the county. The glassworks was founded in 1762 at the southern end of Randsfjorden, on land under the Mo farm, and production began in 1765. At first it made bottles, apothecary glass and household glass, before production later developed toward utility glass, crystal, art glass and Norwegian design. In History Go, the place should be used as an entry to industrial history, craft knowledge, material understanding, design history and continuity in production.

kistefos_traesliperi.name: Kistefos Wood Pulp Mill
kistefos_traesliperi.desc: Former wood pulp mill by Kistefossen in the Randselva river, founded in 1889 and in operation until 1955. Kistefos shows wood processing, hydropower, forest resources and factory work as a physical industrial environment.
kistefos_traesliperi.popupDesc: Kistefos Træsliberi was established by Anders Sveaas in 1889 by Kistefossen in the Randselva river. The factory produced wood pulp from 1890 to 1955, based on hydropower from the waterfall and timber from large forest estates. Today the area is preserved as an industrial museum, sculpture park and art institution, but the History Go trail should first read the place as a factory, workplace, power landscape and history of wood processing.

hvitsten_sjobodene.name: Hvitsten Seaside Storehouses
hvitsten_sjobodene.desc: Historic port of call and seaside storehouse environment by the Oslofjord. Hvitsten was linked to timber, shipping, ice, shipowning and later summer and artist culture.
hvitsten_sjobodene.popupDesc: The Hvitsten seaside storehouses make the fjord history of Akershus concrete. The old storehouses on the quay are a local cultural monument, and Hvitsten grew as a port of call and shipping harbour for timber and ice. Later the place became a summer resort, artist place and part of the Fred. Olsen family’s maritime history. The place should be used to show how small coastal places could be connected to international trade, the capital’s recreation culture and local identities.

roald_amundsens_hjem_uranienborg.name: Roald Amundsen’s home Uranienborg
roald_amundsens_hjem_uranienborg.desc: Roald Amundsen’s home at Svartskog, bought in 1908 and called Uranienborg. The house stands as he left it when he disappeared during the rescue operation after Umberto Nobile in 1928.
roald_amundsens_hjem_uranienborg.popupDesc: Uranienborg is a rare personal-history site because Roald Amundsen’s home is preserved as a concrete work and living space. The property was originally a tenant smallholding under Bålerud, before Amundsen bought it in 1908 and gave it the name Uranienborg. The house stands as he left it in 1928. In History Go, the place should be used for polar history, technological development, celebrity culture, private life and the relationship between world history and a withdrawn home by Bunnefjorden.

drobak_kirke.name: Drøbak Church
drobak_kirke.desc: Timber church consecrated in 1776, financed by the timber merchant and shipowner Niels Carlsen and his wife Martha Zachariasdatter. The church shows the port town’s economy and social power in the age of timber trade.
drobak_kirke.popupDesc: Drøbak Church, Church of Our Saviour, was consecrated on 29 October 1776. It was built in timber as a cruciform church, and the businessman, timber merchant and shipowner Niels Carlsen and his wife Martha Zachariasdatter took financial responsibility for the construction. The church shows how a wealthy fjord and port town could build its own institutions through trade, shipping, timber and a local elite. It should be used together with Drøbak’s trade and harbour history, not only as church history.

nostvet_boplass.name: Nøstvet Settlement Site
nostvet_boplass.desc: Key archaeological site at Nøstvet in Ås, where Early Stone Age finds gave their name to the Nøstvet culture.
nostvet_boplass.popupDesc: The Nøstvet settlement site is one of Akershus’ most important prehistoric places. Stone tools, especially the Nøstvet axe, make very old human traces visible in the landscape and open questions about the Stone Age, changing shorelines, hunter-gatherer culture and archaeological method.

raknehaugen.name: Raknehaugen
raknehaugen.desc: One of Northern Europe’s largest burial mounds, raised in the Migration Period as a visible monument to power and memory in Romerike.
raknehaugen.popupDesc: Raknehaugen is a major prehistoric site in Akershus. The large mound at Ljøgot shows how power could be expressed in the landscape before written sources, as an Iron Age landmark that required organization, resources and an audience.

nes_kirkeruiner.name: Nes Church Ruins
nes_kirkeruiner.desc: Ruins of a medieval church where the Glomma and Vorma meet, bringing church power, travel, war, fire, rebuilding and decay into one landscape.
nes_kirkeruiner.popupDesc: Nes Church Ruins stand where the Glomma, the Vorma, old routes, church power and rural communities meet. The church was built in the Middle Ages, burned during conflict with Sweden, rebuilt and later left as a ruin after an 1800s fire.

blaker_skanse.name: Blaker Fortification
blaker_skanse.desc: Protected defensive work by the Glomma, built as part of the defence line against Sweden.
blaker_skanse.popupDesc: Blaker Fortification links landscape, military strategy and the relationship between Norway and Sweden. Its ramparts, star-fort geometry and position by the Glomma show how early modern defence used terrain, rivers and form.

tertitten_urskog_holandsbanen.name: Tertitten / Urskog-Høland Railway
tertitten_urskog_holandsbanen.desc: Narrow-gauge museum railway from Sørumsand, preserved from the Urskog-Høland Railway.
tertitten_urskog_holandsbanen.popupDesc: Tertitten shows a railway history different from the large main lines. The narrow-gauge line connected inner Akershus to transport networks and markets, carrying people and goods tied to farming, forestry and local economy.

tanum_kirke.name: Tanum Church
tanum_kirke.desc: Medieval Romanesque church on the Tanum plateau in Bærum, linked to older roads, burial mounds and church power.
tanum_kirke.popupDesc: Tanum Church stands high on Tanumåsen and shows how Christianization and medieval church building entered older landscapes of power and culture. The church dates from the first half of the 1100s, while nearby burial mounds are from the Early Iron Age.

haslum_kirke.name: Haslum Church
haslum_kirke.desc: Medieval church in Bærum, built in whitewashed masonry in the 1100s and later reshaped as a cruciform church.
haslum_kirke.popupDesc: Haslum Church makes the Middle Ages concrete in today’s suburban Bærum. Built in the 1100s, later extended and restored, it shows how old road junctions, farm landscapes, monastery links, pilgrimage routes and local churches structured everyday life.

skedsmo_kirke.name: Skedsmo Church
skedsmo_kirke.desc: Medieval church at Skedsmo, completed around 1180 and dedicated to St. Olav.
skedsmo_kirke.popupDesc: Skedsmo Church is a key medieval site in Romerike. The original Romanesque stone long church preserves or documents thick walls, a baptismal font and an older bell, while later 1800s rebuilding raises questions about continuity and restoration.

enebakk_kirke.name: Enebakk Church
enebakk_kirke.desc: Medieval church in Kirkebygda in Enebakk, traditionally dated to the early 1100s.
enebakk_kirke.popupDesc: Enebakk Church is a key place for medieval Follo. The old stone church lies by older rural and church structures and shows how Christian institutions became fixed points in the landscape, linking church, agriculture, local organization, travel and continuity.

asker_kirke_kirkested.name: Asker Church / old church site
asker_kirke_kirkested.desc: Church site in Asker where a medieval church from the 1100s stood before it burned in 1878.
asker_kirke_kirkested.popupDesc: Asker Church matters as a church site, not only as today’s building. The old medieval stone church burned in 1878, and the neo-Gothic brick church from 1879, the churchyard, nearby burial mounds and rescued furnishings make the place historically layered.

gamle_hvam_museum.name: Gamle Hvam Museum
gamle_hvam_museum.desc: Historic manor farm and museum in Romerike, rooted in long settlement and agricultural history.
gamle_hvam_museum.popupDesc: Gamle Hvam Museum is mainly the former manor farm Store Hvam. The yard shows a large farm environment with buildings, status markers and work spaces, making agricultural history concrete through questions about residence, animals, tools, wealth and the farm as an economic and social centre.

heggedal_hovedgard.name: Heggedal Manor Farm
heggedal_hovedgard.desc: Old Asker farm known from Bishop Eystein’s land register, later protected through local preservation work in the 1970s.
heggedal_hovedgard.popupDesc: Heggedal Manor Farm brings together local history, farming and building preservation. Known from medieval land-register material, it was church property, Crown property and a private farm before decay and demolition threats led to preservation of the buildings.

son_ladested.name: Son historic trading port
son_ladested.desc: Historic trading port by the Oslofjord, shaped by timber, customs, harbour activity and trade.
son_ladested.popupDesc: Son is an old trading port and harbour environment where the fjord, timber, trade and customs income shaped the settlement. Important from the 1500s and granted customs rights in 1604, it still has older buildings that make the trading place readable.

holen_ladested.name: Hølen historic trading port
holen_ladested.desc: Historic trading port and marketplace by the Såna, known for old bridges, sawmills and important routes southward.
holen_ladested.popupDesc: Hølen shows how small places could gain importance through location. It lay by main routes south, had sawmills along the Såna for export timber, became a customs place from the mid-1600s and later a small administrative unit.

hurdal_verk_glassverk.name: Hurdal Verk / Hurdal Glassworks
hurdal_verk_glassverk.desc: Former glassworks and industrial site in Hurdal, operated from 1755 to 1895.
hurdal_verk_glassverk.popupDesc: Hurdal Verk shows how an industrial enterprise could create a local community. Around 1800 it was the country’s largest glassworks, with hundreds of workers, its own school, poor relief, general store and many buildings; later uses added new historical layers.

vollen_maudbukta.name: Vollen / Maud Bay
vollen_maudbukta.desc: Coastal culture site where Roald Amundsen’s polar ship Maud was launched in 1917.
vollen_maudbukta.popupDesc: Vollen and Maud Bay make polar history local. Maud was built by the local boatbuilder Christian Jensen and launched here in 1917; the site connects boatbuilding, fjord life, polar expeditions and later industrial history at Arnestad Bruk.

stunner_boplass.name: Stunner Stone Age settlement site
stunner_boplass.desc: Archaeological find site in eastern Ski with traces of an approximately 11,000-year-old Stone Age settlement.
stunner_boplass.popupDesc: Stunner is one of Akershus’ most important prehistoric sites. Finds began when farmer Johannes Mikkelsen found flint in a field in 1928, and Anders Nummedal linked them to the Fosna complex, showing how early human traces can be small finds in soil and landscape.

ski_middelalderkirke.name: Ski Medieval Church
ski_middelalderkirke.desc: Medieval church in Ski, built around 1150 on a central site in the village.
ski_middelalderkirke.popupDesc: Ski Medieval Church is one of Follo’s central stone churches. Built around the mid-1100s, probably on a site of earlier local importance, it lies by older routes and shows how Christianization and church building organized rural communities.

krakstad_kirke_og_gravhaug.name: Kråkstad Church and burial mound
krakstad_kirke_og_gravhaug.desc: Medieval church in Kråkstad, in an area with Iron Age burial mounds.
krakstad_kirke_og_gravhaug.popupDesc: Kråkstad Church stands in an older cultural landscape with Iron Age burial mounds, including the mound regarded as Follo’s largest. The site shows the transition from pre-Christian power and burial landscapes to a Christian church site.

lunner_kirke.name: Lunner Church
lunner_kirke.desc: Medieval stone church at Lunner, later expanded into a timber cruciform church.
lunner_kirke.popupDesc: Lunner Church is an important medieval site in new Akershus. Its oldest part is a 1100s stone church, expanded in timber in 1782 and altered in the late 1800s, with links to Hadeland pilgrimage routes and Akershus’ northern historical geography.

hakadal_verk.name: Hakadal Works
hakadal_verk.desc: Former ironworks in Hakadal, probably among the oldest in Norway. Hakadal Works shows how ore, charcoal, forests, privileges and works labour shaped early Norwegian industrial history.
hakadal_verk.popupDesc: Hakadal Works, also known as Hakedals Verk, was probably one of Norway’s oldest ironworks. Operations began around 1550 as a public enterprise by royal order, using ore from Grua in Hadeland and charcoal from large forest areas. In the 1600s and 1700s the works became linked to privileges, estates and families that ran the site as its own works community. In History Go, the place should be used to show the connection between mining, iron production, forestry, state power and local communities.

nesodden_kirke.name: Nesodden Church
nesodden_kirke.desc: Medieval stone church at Kirkekrysset on Nesodden, built around 1175. The church site shows the relationship between fjord, travel routes, local community and church in the Middle Ages.
nesodden_kirke.popupDesc: Nesodden Church is the village’s oldest building and a stone church from around 1175. The church stands at a historic crossroads, with views toward Bunnefjorden, and in earlier times many people rowed to church via Kirkevika below. The protected cultural landscape around the church makes the site well suited for reading medieval geography: church, fjord, farms, routes and local community.

seiersten_skanse.name: Seiersten Fortification
seiersten_skanse.desc: Defensive installation on the landward side east of Oscarsborg and the Oslofjord, established in 1894–1902. Seiersten fortification shows how Drøbaksundet was also defended from land.
seiersten_skanse.popupDesc: Seiersten fortification was established in 1894–1902 on the landward side east of Oscarsborg and the Oslofjord. The installation consisted of a closed fortification with strong earth ramparts, parapets, quarters, ammunition rooms and firing positions. The site broadens the defence history around Drøbaksundet beyond Oscarsborg alone: it shows how the entrance to the capital was secured through several layers of coastal and land defence in the period before the dissolution of the union and 1905.

raelingen_bygdetun.name: Rælingen Local Heritage Museum
raelingen_bygdetun.desc: Open-air local museum at Fjerdingby with a main building from 1814, a storehouse from the 1850s and older traces beneath the house. The site shows a farm environment, royal road, church hill and local public life.
raelingen_bygdetun.popupDesc: Rælingen Local Heritage Museum lies at Fjerdingby, close to Rælingen Church. The main building is from 1814 and was formerly the farmhouse at Søndre Fjerdingby, while the storehouse is from the 1850s. Beneath the house are traces of an older building, probably from the 1600s. Fjerdingby was a central junction where roads met, and the old royal road crossed the farmyard. The site is therefore suited to showing how farm, church, road, assembly site, announcements and social life were connected in rural society.

losby_gods.name: Losby Estate
losby_gods.desc: Historic estate and forest property in Lørenskog, rooted in sawmills, timber trade, tenant farms, hunting and recreation. Losby shows how large forest estates organized work and landscape around Oslo.
losby_gods.popupDesc: Losby Estate is more than a hotel. Losby’s history is about forest properties, sawmills, timber trade, tenant farmers, servants, hunting, recreation and wealthy Christiania owners. Losby, Vestmork and Østmork were gathered into a larger estate and forestry environment, and smallholders and workers were tied to sawmills and forestry. In History Go, the site should be used to show how the forest around Oslo was also a working landscape with ownership, class differences and resource economy.

frogner_gamle_kirke.name: Frogner Old Church
frogner_gamle_kirke.desc: Medieval stone church from around 1180, later damaged by fire in 1918 and restored through the 1900s. Frogner Old Church makes Romerike’s Middle Ages and modern preservation work visible in the same building.
frogner_gamle_kirke.popupDesc: Frogner Old Church is a stone long church from around 1180. It was struck by fire in 1918, the walls were repaired in 1936, the floor and roof in 1948, and the restoration was completed in 1977. The site should be used in History Go to show how a medieval church is both an old building and the result of modern restoration, fire history and preservation choices.

sorum_kirke.name: Sørum Church
sorum_kirke.desc: Medieval stone church from the 1100s, linked to Sørum as an old church site and to the historical importance of the Sudreim area in Romerike.
sorum_kirke.popupDesc: Sørum Church is one of Romerike’s old stone churches. It is usually dated to the 1100s, and the site is linked to the old Sørum name and the Sudreim milieu. Here the player can read how church buildings, farm names, local aristocratic history and the village centre were connected in the Middle Ages. Sørum Church should be used as a pure history point, not as a generic church marker.

feiring_jernverk.name: Feiring Ironworks
feiring_jernverk.desc: Ironworks established in 1798 and operated from 1806 to 1818 as part of Eidsvoll Verk under Carsten Anker. Feiring Ironworks has one of the country’s best-preserved blast furnaces and clear ruins of a small industrial community.
feiring_jernverk.popupDesc: Feiring Ironworks was established in 1798 and operated from 1806 to 1818. The works were part of Eidsvoll Verk, owned by Carsten Anker, and therefore belong to the material background of the 1814 milieu. At its peak, 168 men, women and children lived in the industrial community, working in the mines, timber felling, transport, charcoal burning and roasting. The blast furnace and the ruins of the charcoal house, bake oven, manager’s residence and office building make the site very well suited for industrial-history interpretation.

gardermoen_militaerleir_tunet.name: Gardermoen Military Camp / Tunet
gardermoen_militaerleir_tunet.desc: Historic military area at Gardermoen, with Lilleplassen as one of Norway’s oldest drill grounds. Tunet at Ullensaker Museum gathers buildings from Sør-Gardermoen military camp.
gardermoen_militaerleir_tunet.popupDesc: Gardermoen was a military area long before it became the main airport. Lilleplassen was established in 1740 as a cavalry drill ground, and in the 1850s Gardermoen was the main camp for all of Eastern Norway and the country’s largest military camp. The buildings at Tunet by Ullensaker Museum were moved from Sør-Gardermoen military camp and show both military and civilian history. The development of Oslo Airport marked the end of about 250 years of military activity at Gardermoen.

ullensaker_kirke_kirkested.name: Ullensaker Church / Ullinhof church site
ullensaker_kirke_kirkested.desc: Church site with roots back to the Middle Ages and a name pointing to pre-Christian cult linked to Ullr. Today’s Ullensaker Church from 1958 is known as Romeriksdomen and has Alf Rolfsen’s monumental frescoes.
ullensaker_kirke_kirkested.popupDesc: Ullensaker Church is important as a layered church site. Today’s church is from 1958, but church history goes back to the Middle Ages, when a wooden church stood somewhat farther north. The older name Ullinhof suggests that the place may have had pre-Christian significance linked to the god Ullr. The site can therefore be used to show a long transition: pre-Christian cult, medieval church, later church buildings and modern monumental church art in Romeriksdomen.

aurskog_holand_bygdetun.name: Aurskog-Høland Local Heritage Museum
aurskog_holand_bygdetun.desc: Open-air local museum at Hemnes, opened in 1964 and based on Warrant Officer August Krogh’s collections. The museum consists of old houses from across Aurskog-Høland and presents work, household life, school, tenant farming and Finnish immigration.
aurskog_holand_bygdetun.popupDesc: Aurskog-Høland Local Heritage Museum has been a meeting place at Hemnes for more than fifty years. It consists of buildings from across the municipality: tenant cottages, brewhouse, barn, cowshed, stable, storehouse, drying kiln and the main Kinnestad building from Setskog. The museum opened in 1964, with roots in Warrant Officer August Krogh’s collections, and presents everyday life, traditional food, working horses, a schoolroom and Finnish immigration. In History Go, the site should be used for local social history, not only as a nostalgic museum.

nannestad_bygdemuseum.name: Nannestad Local Museum
nannestad_bygdemuseum.desc: Local museum established in 2007 on the basis of Tore G. Solheim’s monetary gift and collections. The museum presents Nannestad’s farm, everyday and institutional history through interiors, objects and permanent collections.
nannestad_bygdemuseum.popupDesc: Nannestad Local Museum was established in 2007 on the basis of a monetary gift from Tore G. Solheim, who wanted younger people to learn about the village’s history. Solheim also contributed objects, furniture and interiors from the family farm Grindaker in Bjerke parish. The museum has permanent collections, including a reconstructed doctor’s office after Dr. Habberstad. The site should be used to show how local history is also about who collects, preserves and decides what the village should remember.

borgarsyssel_museum_olavsbyen.name: Borgarsyssel Museum / Olav’s town Sarpsborg
borgarsyssel_museum_olavsbyen.desc: Museum and medieval area in Sarpsborg, linked to Olav Haraldsson’s founding of the town in 1016, Borgarsyssel and the ruins of the medieval St. Nicholas Church.
borgarsyssel_museum_olavsbyen.popupDesc: Borgarsyssel Museum lies by the ruin park for St. Nicholas Church and presents Østfold’s cultural history with special emphasis on the medieval town of Borg/Sarpsborg. Sarpsborg was founded by Olav Haraldsson in 1016 by Sarpsfossen, and the name Borgarsyssel refers to the old name for Østfold. The site should be used in History Go as a main entry point to Østfold’s Middle Ages, the Olav tradition, church ruins, county history and how a town can be moved, destroyed and continue as historical memory.

solbergfeltet_helleristninger.name: Solbergfeltet rock carvings
solbergfeltet_helleristninger.desc: Rock-carving field in Skjeberg with ships, wagons, sun wheels, people and cup marks. Solbergfeltet is one of the clear Bronze Age sites along Oldtidsveien in Østfold.
solbergfeltet_helleristninger.popupDesc: Solbergfeltet is a Bronze Age field in Skjeberg with around one hundred figures, including ships, wagons, sun wheels, people and cup marks. The field lies along Oldtidsveien and shows how Østfold’s landscape contains religious, ritual and maritime ideas from the Bronze Age. The site should be used in History Go to ask about symbols, cult, sea routes, sun religion and how archaeologists interpret images in rock.

hunnfeltet_gravfelt.name: Hunnfeltet burial field
hunnfeltet_gravfelt.desc: Large burial field at Borge/Fredrikstad with burial mounds, stone settings and ancient traces. Hunnfeltet shows Østfold as one of Norway’s richest ancient landscapes.
hunnfeltet_gravfelt.popupDesc: Hunnfeltet is a large ancient and burial landscape at Borge in Fredrikstad. The area contains burial mounds, stone settings and traces of long-term use through the Iron Age. Together with the rock-carving fields along Oldtidsveien, Hunnfeltet shows how Østfold’s landscape was densely filled with ritual and social markers long before medieval towns and fortresses. In History Go, the site should be used for burial customs, power, kinship, rituals and archaeological landscape reading.

tune_skipet_funnsted.name: Tune ship find site
tune_skipet_funnsted.desc: The find site of the Tune ship, a Viking ship from around AD 900 found in a burial mound on Rolvsøy in 1867. The ship is one of the major Norwegian Viking-ship finds.
tune_skipet_funnsted.popupDesc: The Tune ship was found in a burial mound on Rolvsøy in 1867, in an area that then belonged to Tune. The ship is dated to around AD 900 and is now among the central Norwegian Viking-ship finds. The find site is important because it makes the Viking Age local in Østfold: the ship burial shows elite, burial ritual, craftsmanship, seafaring and archaeological history. In History Go, the site should be used to show the difference between the find site itself and the museum where the ship was later exhibited.

moss_jernverk_konventionsgarden.name: Moss Ironworks / Konventionsgården
moss_jernverk_konventionsgarden.desc: Historic ironworks area in Moss, established in 1704. The administration building Konventionsgården is known as the place where the Convention of Moss was negotiated in August 1814.
moss_jernverk_konventionsgarden.popupDesc: Moss Ironworks was a large industrial environment and a central workplace in Moss from 1704. The works produced cannons, iron goods and other cast products, and the owner circles around the works were closely linked to Norwegian economy and politics. In 1814 the administration building, Konventionsgården, became headquarters and negotiation site during the war against Sweden. The Convention of Moss was negotiated here in August 1814 and laid the foundation for the ceasefire, the Storting’s continued role and the union with Sweden. The site should therefore be asked about as both industrial history and constitutional history.

hafslund_hovedgard.name: Hafslund Manor
hafslund_hovedgard.desc: Manor near Sarpsborg with roots in older farm history and a main building from 1761. Hafslund connects estate ownership, forest, waterfall, industry and later hydropower development.
hafslund_hovedgard.popupDesc: Hafslund Manor lies in one of Østfold’s most resource-rich landscapes, close to Sarpsfossen and old travel routes. The farm is known in sources from the Middle Ages, and today’s main building was erected in 1761 after a fire in 1757. Hafslund is linked to owners, sawmills, forest resources, industry and later hydropower development. In History Go, the site should be used to show how manor, natural resources and modernization can be connected over many hundreds of years.

rod_herregard.name: Rød Manor
rod_herregard.desc: One of Norway’s best-preserved manors, with roots back to the 1600s and especially linked to the Tank and Anker families from 1733. Rød Manor shows elite culture, trade, art, gardens and political connections in the border landscape.
rod_herregard.popupDesc: Rød Manor in Halden is one of Østfold’s most important manor environments. The property has roots back to the late 1600s, but was especially shaped by the Tank and Anker families from 1733 and through the 1700s and 1800s. Buildings, interiors, art collections, arms collections, baroque garden and landscape garden make the site a rare whole. The site should be used in History Go to show connections between trade, officialdom, European culture, border politics and local power.

gjellestadskipet_jellhaugen.name: Gjellestad ship / Jellhaugen
gjellestadskipet_jellhaugen.desc: Viking-ship find by Jellhaugen in Halden municipality, detected with ground-penetrating radar in 2018. Gjellestad shows how modern technology can uncover old power landscapes with ships, burial mounds and longhouses.
gjellestadskipet_jellhaugen.popupDesc: The Gjellestad ship was detected with ground-penetrating radar by Jellhaugen in 2018. The investigations showed traces of a Viking ship, burial mounds and buildings from the Iron Age. The site is therefore not only a ship find, but an entire power landscape where elite burial, longhouses and monumental topography belong together. In History Go, Gjellestad should be used for the Viking Age, archaeological method, digital ground-penetrating radar, burial rituals and how new finds can change the understanding of a landscape.

bantjern_salamanderlokalitet.name: Båntjern salamander site
bantjern_salamanderlokalitet.desc: The Båntjern area in Nordmarka is used as a pedagogical nearby anchor for older salamander records in the pond environment by Bånntjernveien.
bantjern_salamanderlokalitet.popupDesc:
The Båntjern area shows how small ponds in the transition between villa districts, forest and the Marka can contain important amphibian values. Norsk Naturarv documents great crested newt, smooth newt and toad in the pond environment by Bånntjernveien, with older records from 1988/89.

In History Go, this place should be used carefully: the point is not to send the player into private ponds, but to explain how amphibians often live in small water surfaces on the edge between housing, gardens, forest and walking terrain. Good questions should address habitat quality, fish-free ponds, forest contact and why protection also applies to small and less visible natural places.

tjernsmyr_salamanderlokalitet.name: Tjernsmyr salamander site
tjernsmyr_salamanderlokalitet.desc: Wetland area by Lysaker where smooth newt and great crested newt have been recorded in a heavily developed transport and construction landscape.
tjernsmyr_salamanderlokalitet.popupDesc:
Tjernsmyr is a good example of how salamander sites are not found only in quiet forest ponds, but also close to major roads, construction areas and urban development. The Norwegian Public Roads Administration describes finds of both smooth and great crested newts at Tjernsmyr, and how knowledge about overwintering, migration routes and habitats must be used when E18 work is planned.

In History Go, Tjernsmyr should be used as a case for nature considerations in the building zone. Questions should connect wetland, red-listed species, environmental DNA, construction work and the Nature Diversity Act, but always in a concrete, place-based way: Why must a small wetland area be surveyed before major technical interventions? What happens when species migration routes cross road systems?

blindern_forskningsparken_salamanderdam.name: Blindern/Forskningsparken salamander pond
blindern_forskningsparken_salamanderdam.desc: Pond environment by Forskningsparken at Blindern, used by Oslo Municipality as an example in the city’s mapping of amphibian ponds.
blindern_forskningsparken_salamanderdam.popupDesc:
The pond by Forskningsparken at Blindern is a good example of how important urban nature can lie right between research, campus, public transport and dense building zones. Oslo Municipality uses salamanders in a pond by Forskningsparken as an image and example in its work to map Oslo’s unknown amphibian ponds.

In History Go, this place should be used to explain how the municipality, biologists and nature maps can make small natural places visible. Good questions should address why ponds are mapped, what biologists look for, how ponds become overgrown, and why amphibians need open water, vegetation and careful management.

naturhistorisk_museum.name: Natural History Museum
naturhistorisk_museum.desc: The Natural History Museum at Tøyen manages scientific collections in zoology, botany, geology and palaeontology. Specimens, fossils, minerals and their associated data are used in research, species identification, conservation and teaching. The museum is a broad institution and must be distinguished from the Botanical Garden and Klimahuset, which have map sites of their own.
naturhistorisk_museum.popupDesc:
The Natural History Museum at Tøyen is the University of Oslo's museum for zoology, botany, geology and palaeontology. The map point represents the broad museum institution and the collection work. The Botanical Garden is a living collection site of its own, and Klimahuset is a separate building for public engagement; they are not to be merged with the museum marker.

The museum's scientific collections consist of animals, plants, fossils, rocks, minerals and other natural history objects with documentation. A specimen acquires research value when its identity, find site, date, collector and treatment can be traced. Without such metadata it becomes harder to compare the material or check earlier conclusions.

Collections make it possible to study nature across long spans of time. Researchers can compare older and newer specimens, revise species identifications and analyse material with methods that did not exist when it was collected. A museum object is therefore not only an exhibition object, but possible documentation for future questions.

The exhibitions translate parts of the collections and the research into public presentation. Display cases, reconstructions and explanations select particular narratives and must be read as scholarly interpretations, not as the whole collection. New finds can change names, relationships or reconstructions, and the museum must therefore update its knowledge.

Collection management also involves ethics and responsibility. Material may be fragile, have an unclear collecting history or be regulated by laws and agreements. Conservation requires control of light, temperature, pests and physical handling. Digitisation increases accessibility, but does not always replace the original specimen.

On site the user can ask what makes an object scientific evidence. Is it correctly identified, documented and preserved, and can other researchers examine it? The Natural History Museum shows how knowledge of nature is built through the combination of fieldwork, collections, laboratory methods and critical revision. The museum should therefore be understood as active research infrastructure, not merely as a place where finished facts are presented behind glass. Collection numbers and databases make it possible to link publications back to particular specimens, so that analyses can be checked or repeated with new methods. The site should therefore be examined through documented sources, a clear method and precise limits on what the observations can actually support.

botanisk_hage.name: The Botanical Garden
botanisk_hage.desc: The Botanical Garden at Tøyen was established in 1814 and is a living scientific collection. Plants are cultivated with known identity, origin and documentation for research, teaching, conservation and public engagement. The garden must be distinguished from wild nature: the beds are curated experiments and collections where species can be compared over time.
botanisk_hage.popupDesc:
The Botanical Garden at Tøyen was established in 1814 and is a living scientific collection under the Natural History Museum. The map point covers the whole garden area, not just one entrance, the glasshouses or Klimahuset. The garden is at once a park, a teaching arena and research infrastructure, but the plants stand here through planned collecting, cultivation and documentation.

A botanical collection differs from an ordinary park in that the plants' identity and origin are recorded. Labels, databases and collection records make it possible to know what is being grown and where the material comes from. Without such documentation the plant loses much of its value as research and comparison material.

Living collections can be used to study form, relationship, growth, flowering and adaptation. When observations are repeated across years and seasons, researchers and gardeners can follow how species respond to climate, soil, disease and management. The garden can also preserve material from rare or threatened plants.

Visitors meet systematics and plant geography in physical form. Species can be arranged by relationship, habitat or use, so that differences become visible outside the textbook. But the placement of the beds is a pedagogical and practical choice; it must not be confused with how the species naturally grow together in an ecosystem.

The garden is also a place for source criticism. A species name can change when new research on relationships is published. A plant may be misidentified, hybridised or affected by growing conditions. Collection work therefore involves revision, checking and traceability, not just the upkeep of beautiful beds.

On site the user can look for labels and ask what information makes a plant scientifically documented. The Botanical Garden shows how living organisms can form part of long-term systems of knowledge. It should be distinguished both from the Natural History Museum as a broad institution and from Klimahuset as a separate building for public engagement. Comparison between beds, glasshouses and natural habitats can moreover show how temperature, light and management affect the form of a plant, without a single cultivated plant alone proving how the whole species behaves in nature. The living collection also makes time part of the research material. Seeds germinate, plants flower and individuals age across many seasons. Such processes cannot always be replaced by photographs or dried specimens. At the same time the growing conditions must be documented, because warmth, watering and soil can shape the plant differently than in its natural habitat.

forskningsparken.name: Forskningsparken
forskningsparken.desc: Forskningsparken at Gaustadalléen 21 opened in 1989 and gathers research communities, laboratories, incubators, start-ups and established knowledge businesses. Its closeness to the University of Oslo and Oslo University Hospital makes the site a link between academic research, clinical practice, technology development and commercialisation. Here science and business meet in shared development environments.
forskningsparken.popupDesc:
Forskningsparken at Gaustadalléen 21 opened in 1989 as a meeting place between research, business and public innovation. Today several hundred businesses, networks, incubators and research communities are based in the complex. The map point concerns the building complex, not the metro station or the whole area between Blindern and Gaustad.

The closeness to the University of Oslo and Oslo University Hospital is a central part of the model. Researchers, clinicians, founders and companies can meet at a short physical distance. Laboratories, offices and shared arenas make it possible to develop ideas further than an ordinary office building would allow.

Forskningsparken houses communities in technology, health, life science and energy, among other fields. Incubators can offer laboratory space, networks, business development and contact with investors. The aim is often to turn research results or technical expertise into products, services and new businesses.

Research and innovation are nevertheless not the same thing. A promising experiment is not automatically a working product, and a commercial idea is not necessarily scientifically documented. The transition requires testing, regulation, financing, production and an assessment of whom the solution actually helps or burdens.

Co-location can create collaboration, but the building does not produce innovation on its own. Results depend on expertise, trust, access to data and equipment, and the ability to handle failed attempts. Narratives of growth should therefore be supplemented by questions about evidence, risk, ownership and long-term public benefit.

On site the user can examine where in the chain a business stands: basic research, prototype, clinical trial, market test or established operation. Forskningsparken makes the knowledge economy physical, but also shows that the road from discovery to application consists of many institutions, checkpoints and possible interruptions. An idea can change direction several times, and a failed commercial project can still yield useful methodological knowledge if the attempts are documented and the experience shared. The park also makes visible that different kinds of knowledge have different time horizons. A software prototype can be tested quickly, while medical technology may require laboratory experiments, regulatory assessment and clinical studies over several years. The same building therefore houses both rapid development cycles and slow documentation, and the user should ask what kind of evidence a business actually needs before its solution is put into use.

meteorologisk_institutt.name: The Norwegian Meteorological Institute
meteorologisk_institutt.desc: The Norwegian Meteorological Institute at Henrik Mohns plass 1 is Norway's national body for weather, climate and meteorological forecasts. Since its establishment in 1866 the institute has linked observations, measurement networks, satellite data and numerical models. Here continuous streams of data are turned into forecasts, hazard warnings, climate statistics and open services for society and research.
meteorologisk_institutt.popupDesc:
The Norwegian Meteorological Institute at Henrik Mohns plass 1 is Norway's national body for weather, climate and meteorological forecasts. The institute was established in 1866. The map point concerns the main building at Blindern, not weather stations, radars, research facilities or observation networks elsewhere in the country.

Weather forecasting begins with observation. Temperature, precipitation, wind, air pressure and other quantities are measured from the ground, the sea, aircraft, radar and satellites. The measurements are checked before they are combined, because a faulty sensor, a wrong location or missing data can affect the analysis the models start from.

Numerical weather models calculate the development of the atmosphere using physical laws. Computers divide the atmosphere into a grid and calculate changes forward in time. The model is a simplification, and small differences in the initial state can produce larger differences later. Several model runs and professional judgement are therefore used.

A forecast is not just an icon with sun or rain. Meteorologists assess probability, local conditions and possible consequences. Hazard warnings require particularly clear communication: the recipient must understand what may happen, how certain it is, and which areas or activities are most exposed.

The institute also manages long climatic time series. Climate describes patterns over longer periods, while weather describes the atmosphere at a given moment. A cold day therefore does not contradict global warming, and one record alone does not explain a trend. Comparable measurements and documented changes in instruments and stations are decisive.

On site the user can follow the chain of knowledge from sensor to social decision: observation, quality control, model, meteorological interpretation and published forecast. The Norwegian Meteorological Institute shows that a forecast can be professionally sound without being certain.
